3.h: Jesus Our Apostle and High Priest
3.ctx: Moses was the most honoured figure in Judaism, the one through whom the law came. God himself called him ‘faithful in all My house’ (Numbers 12:7).
3.mean: ‘Holy brothers, who share in the heavenly calling, set your focus on Jesus, the apostle and high priest whom we confess.’ He is the ‘apostle’ (the one sent from God to us) and the high priest (the one who represents us to God). The writer honours Moses: both were faithful. But Moses was faithful ‘as a servant in all God’s house’, while ‘Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house’. A servant in a house and the son who owns it are not on the same level. Then a challenge: ‘And we are His house, if we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope of which we boast.’
3.big: Jesus is greater than Moses as a son is greater than a servant in the household.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

3.ctx: A long quotation of Psalm 95, recalling Israel’s rebellion in the wilderness when they refused to enter the promised land (Numbers 13–14).
3.mean: ‘Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts, as you did in the rebellion.”’ The generation that came out of Egypt saw God’s works for forty years, yet their hearts were ‘always going astray’. So God swore, ‘They shall never enter My rest.’ The writer introduces a psalm written by David as what ‘the Holy Spirit says’, in the present tense. Scripture is not just an old record but God speaking now, and the word ‘Today’ is addressed to every new reader.
3.big: Scripture speaks with a present voice, ‘Today’, and warns against the hardness that kept Israel out of the promised land.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

3.ctx: The writer applies Psalm 95 directly to his readers.
3.mean: ‘See to it, brothers, that none of you has a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God. But exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today, so that none of you may be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness.’ Sin deceives. It hardens gradually, and the remedy is mutual: every believer has a responsibility to encourage the others, every day. ‘We have come to share in Christ if we hold firmly to the end the assurance we had at first.’ The wilderness generation had all left Egypt and seen the miracles, yet ‘it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter’.
3.big: Believers guard one another against the slow hardening of sin by daily encouragement.
3.diff: Verse 13’s call to ‘exhort one another daily’ sits close to the group’s anchor text in chapter 10. On what verse 14 implies about whether believers can fall away, see the note on 6:1.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL
T. R. Schreiner, Hebrews, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham)

4.ctx: The argument about Israel’s failure to enter the land continues, now applied to the rest God offers.
4.mean: ‘While the promise of entering His rest still stands, let us be careful that none of you be deemed to have fallen short of it.’ The writer argues from Scripture. God’s rest has existed since creation, when ‘on the seventh day God rested from all His works’. Israel failed to enter it. Joshua brought them into the land, but that was not the final rest, because centuries later, through David, God still said ‘Today’. So ‘There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God.’ Entering it means resting from our own work, as God did from his. ‘Now we who have believed enter that rest.’ Yet it is also still ahead: ‘Let us, therefore, make every effort to enter that rest.’
4.big: God’s true rest, pictured by the Sabbath and the promised land, is entered by faith now and enjoyed fully in the age to come.
4.diff: Christians differ over what this means for a weekly day of rest. The Westminster Confession (21.7–8) teaches that the Sabbath command continues as the ‘Christian Sabbath’, the Lord’s Day, Sunday. Many other Christians see the Sabbath as fulfilled in Christ (compare Colossians 2:16–17) while keeping Sunday as the day of worship. Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday. Most interpreters read this passage chiefly as being about salvation, rest begun now by faith and completed in the age to come, rather than about which day to keep.

src.l: Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text), ch. 17, 21, 29
Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

4.ctx: A famous passage on God’s word, then the introduction of the letter’s main theme: Christ as high priest.
4.mean: ‘For the word of God is living and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword, it pierces even to dividing soul and spirit, joints and marrow. It judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart.’ The word that warned Israel still exposes us. ‘Nothing in all creation is hidden from God’s sight.’ That could be terrifying, but the writer immediately turns to comfort. ‘Since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold firmly to what we profess. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin. Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need.’ The throne of the judge is, for believers, a throne of grace.
4.big: Because our high priest was tempted as we are yet without sin, believers can approach God’s throne with confidence.
4.diff: Verse 15 is central to the church’s teaching on Christ’s true humanity. Theologians have discussed whether Christ could have sinned. Traditionally, many theologians have held that he could not, because he is God the Son, while insisting that his temptations were real and costly. Some evangelical theologians argue that real temptation requires a real possibility of sinning. Either way, the point of the text is that his sympathy is genuine: he knows the full force of temptation, perhaps more than anyone, because he never gave in.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

5.ctx: The writer explains what a high priest is, in terms of the Old Testament priesthood, especially Aaron.
5.mean: ‘Every high priest is appointed from among men to represent them in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.’ Two qualifications follow. He must be able to sympathise: ‘He is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is subject to weakness.’ And he must be called: ‘No one takes this honor upon himself.’ Christ meets both. He was appointed by God, who said ‘You are My Son’ (Psalm 2:7) and ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek’ (Psalm 110:4). And he knows weakness from the inside: ‘During the days of Jesus’ earthly life, He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence.’ This recalls Gethsemane. ‘Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered. And having been made perfect, He became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him.’
5.big: Jesus is a true high priest, appointed by God and made perfect through suffering.
5.diff: ‘Learned obedience’ does not mean he was ever disobedient. He learned by experience what obedience costs, all the way to the cross, which is part of his genuine humanity. ‘He was heard’ does not mean he escaped death. God answered his prayer by raising him from death, and Jesus himself prayed ‘not My will, but Yours’.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

5.ctx: The writer breaks off from Melchizedek to rebuke his readers.
5.mean: ‘We have much to say about this, but it is hard to explain, because you are dull of hearing.’ The problem is not that the subject is too hard but that the readers have become sluggish. ‘Although by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to reteach you the basic principles of God’s word. You need milk, not solid food!’ Maturity is not just knowing more; it is trained judgment: ‘solid food is for the mature, who by constant use have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil.’
5.big: Believers are meant to grow up in understanding and discernment, not stay on spiritual milk.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

6.ctx: One of the most difficult and most discussed passages in the New Testament. Read it together with verses 9–12.
6.mean: ‘Let us leave the elementary teachings about Christ and go on to maturity.’ The foundations are listed: repentance and faith, ‘instruction about baptisms’, the laying on of hands, the resurrection and eternal judgment. Then the warning. ‘It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have shared in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the coming age—and then have fallen away—to be restored to repentance, because they themselves are crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting Him to open shame.’ ‘Fallen away’ here means abandoning Christ altogether, not ordinary sins and failures. Calvin calls it ‘a total defection or falling away from the Gospel’. An illustration follows: land that drinks the rain and produces a crop is blessed; land that produces only thorns is cursed. Then the writer’s tone changes: ‘Even though we speak like this, beloved, we are convinced of better things in your case—things that accompany salvation. For God is not unjust. He will not forget your work and the love you have shown.’ He wants them to show diligence ‘to the very end, in order to make your hope sure’.
6.big: Turning away from Christ after knowing him is the most serious danger there is, and the writer warns because he is confident of better things for his readers.
6.diff: Christians read this warning in four main ways. (1) Professing but not truly converted: many Reformed interpreters hold that it describes people who experienced much of the church’s life, even the Spirit’s influence, without being born again. Calvin argued that God may give the reprobate ‘some taste of his grace’, while the Spirit of regeneration is given to ‘the elect alone’. (2) A real warning that God uses to keep believers: others in the Reformed tradition, such as Thomas Schreiner, argue that the language describes real Christians. The warning is not about something that will happen to true believers, but is one of the means by which God preserves them. They heed it and so do not fall away. (3) Arminian (Wesleyan): it describes genuine believers who can, and sometimes do, finally fall away. Wesley read the passage as ‘not a supposition, but a plain relation of fact’ about people who ‘were renewed once’. (4) Hypothetical: some read it as an impossible case used for argument (‘if this could happen…’), though most commentators think this weakens the writer’s urgency. Most interpreters agree on three things. The sin in view is deliberate, total rejection of Christ, not ordinary failure. The writer himself is ‘convinced of better things’ for his readers (verse 9). Many pastors add that someone anxious about having committed it shows, by that very concern, that they have not turned their back on Christ.

6.ctx: In the ancient world an oath sworn by a greater authority settled a dispute. God, having no one greater, swore by himself (Genesis 22:16).
6.mean: ‘When God made His promise to Abraham, since He had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself.’ Abraham waited patiently and obtained the promise. God did not need to swear; he did it for our sake, ‘to make the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear to the heirs of the promise’. ‘Thus by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie’, his promise and his oath, ‘we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged. We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf.’ The image is striking: an anchor is usually thrown down into the sea, but this one is fixed upward, in heaven, where Jesus has gone ahead.
6.big: Believers’ hope is anchored in God’s unbreakable promise and in Jesus, who has gone before them into God’s presence.
6.diff: Verse 19 is the verse behind the Community of Brothers’ anchor emblem.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

7.ctx: Melchizedek appears briefly in Genesis 14:18–20 as king of Salem (probably Jerusalem) and priest of God Most High, who blessed Abraham. Psalm 110:4 promises a king who will be ‘a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek’.
7.mean: The writer draws out what Genesis says, and what it leaves out. Melchizedek’s name means ‘king of righteousness’, and ‘king of Salem’ means ‘king of peace’. Scripture records him ‘Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God’. For a priest, missing ancestry was remarkable, since Levitical priests had to prove their descent. Then the argument: ‘Consider how great Melchizedek was: Even the patriarch Abraham gave him a tenth of the plunder.’ ‘And indisputably, the lesser is blessed by the greater.’ And in a sense Levi, the ancestor of Israel’s priests, ‘paid the tenth through Abraham’. So the order of Melchizedek ranks above the Levitical priesthood.
7.big: Melchizedek, greater than Abraham, foreshadows a priesthood greater than Israel’s.
7.diff: Some have thought Melchizedek was an appearance of Christ himself before the incarnation. Most interpreters, including Calvin, read the writer as saying that Melchizedek resembles the Son because Scripture records no beginning or end for him, not that he literally had none. He was a real king, made by God’s providence into a picture of Christ.

hist.t: Melchizedek in the Dead Sea Scrolls
b: Melchizedek appears only twice in the Old Testament (Genesis 14:18–20; Psalm 110:4), but he fascinated Jewish writers. A fragmentary scroll from Cave 11 at Qumran, known as 11QMelchizedek, pictures him as a heavenly figure appointed by God as judge in the heavenly court, bringing liberation at the end of the age.

This shows that speculation about Melchizedek was alive among Jews in the century before Hebrews. Hebrews takes a different and more restrained line. It builds only on what Scripture says, and on what it does not say: Genesis gives him no genealogy, birth or death, which makes him a fitting picture of the Son of God, who truly has no beginning or end of life (7:3).

7.ctx: The writer argues that a new priesthood means the old system was never meant to be final.
7.mean: ‘If perfection could have been attained through the Levitical priesthood…why was there still need for another priest to appear?’ Psalm 110 shows the old priesthood was temporary, and ‘when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed as well’. Jesus came from Judah, not Levi. He became a priest ‘not by a law of succession, but by the power of an indestructible life’, and with an oath: ‘The Lord has sworn and will not change His mind’. ‘Because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood. Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them.’ He is ‘holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners’. ‘Unlike the other high priests, He does not need to offer daily sacrifices, first for His own sins and then for the sins of the people; He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself.’
7.big: Jesus’ priesthood is permanent and his sacrifice complete, so he saves completely those who come to God through him.
7.diff: ‘The law must be changed’ (verse 12) refers to the law of the priesthood and sacrifices, which Christ fulfils and ends. Most Christian traditions distinguish this from God’s moral will, which the new covenant writes on the heart (8:10).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

8.ctx: The writer summarises his main point. The tabernacle was built to a pattern Moses was shown on the mountain (Exodus 25:40), which Hebrews reads as a copy of the heavenly reality.
8.mean: ‘The point of what we are saying is this: We do have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, and who ministers in the sanctuary and true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man.’ The earthly priests serve in ‘a copy and shadow of what is in heaven’. That is why Moses was told: ‘See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.’ The earthly tabernacle was real and God-given, but it pointed beyond itself.
8.big: Christ serves in the true sanctuary, of which the earthly one was only a copy.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

8.ctx: The longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament: Jeremiah 31:31–34, a promise made around the time of the Babylonian exile.
8.mean: ‘Jesus has received a much more excellent ministry, just as the covenant He mediates is better and is founded on better promises.’ The problem with the first covenant lay with the people: ‘God found fault with the people’. So God promised a new covenant that would succeed where the old failed. ‘I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people.’ All will know him, ‘from the least of them to the greatest’. ‘For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.’ ‘By speaking of a new covenant, He has made the first one obsolete; and what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear.’
8.big: Christ mediates the new covenant God promised, which writes his law on hearts and fully forgives sin.
8.diff: ‘Will soon disappear’ (verse 13) may hint that the temple was still standing when the letter was written (see When, and to whom? above). Christians differ on how the new covenant relates to Israel. Some see the church as the fulfilment of the promise to ‘the house of Israel’. Dispensationalists expect a future fulfilment for the nation of Israel as well.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL
‘Hebrews, Epistle to the’ and F. F. Bruce, ‘Melchizedek’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

9.ctx: The writer describes the tabernacle, the portable sanctuary of Israel’s wilderness years (Exodus 25–40), and the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16).
9.mean: The tabernacle had two rooms. The first, the Holy Place, held the lampstand, the table and the consecrated bread. ‘Behind the second curtain was a room called the Most Holy Place’, with the ark of the covenant, the cherubim and the mercy seat. The priests went into the first room every day. ‘But only the high priest entered the second room, and then only once a year, and never without blood’, for his own sins and the people’s. The very layout taught something: ‘By this arrangement the Holy Spirit was showing that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed as long as the first tabernacle was still standing.’ Its gifts and sacrifices ‘were unable to cleanse the conscience of the worshiper’. They were ‘external regulations imposed until the time of reform’.
9.big: The old system, by its very design, showed that the way to God was not yet fully open.
9.diff: Two details are often raised. (1) Verse 4 links ‘the golden altar of incense’ with the Most Holy Place, but Exodus 30:6 places it in front of the curtain. The altar stood just outside, but it belonged to the inner room in use. 1 Kings 6:22 speaks of the ‘altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary’, and on the Day of Atonement incense from it was taken inside the veil (Leviticus 16:12–13). The Greek word could also mean a golden censer. (2) Verse 4 says the jar of manna and Aaron’s staff were in the ark, but 1 Kings 8:9 says that in Solomon’s day there was nothing in it but the tablets. Exodus 16:33–34 and Numbers 17:10 place the jar and staff ‘in front of the Testimony’. Hebrews describes the wilderness tabernacle as Jewish tradition remembered it, and by Solomon’s time the items may have been lost.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

9.ctx: The heart of the letter’s argument about Christ’s sacrifice, set against the Day of Atonement.
9.mean: ‘He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption.’ If animal blood made people ceremonially clean, ‘how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God!’ Christ is the mediator of a new covenant. The writer then plays on a Greek word that means both ‘covenant’ and ‘will’: a will takes effect only when someone dies, and even the first covenant was put into effect with blood (Exodus 24:8). ‘Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.’ Christ entered ‘heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God’, and not repeatedly: ‘now He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself. Just as man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment, so also Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many; and He will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him.’
9.big: Christ’s one sacrifice of himself achieves what all the old sacrifices could only picture: eternal redemption.
9.diff: Verse 14 names the Father, the Son and the eternal Spirit together in the one act of Christ’s self-offering. Verse 27 (‘appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment’) is a key text against reincarnation.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

10.ctx: The conclusion of the argument about sacrifice begun in chapter 7. If the temple was still standing, sacrifices were being offered every day as the writer wrote.
10.mean: ‘For the law is only a shadow of the good things to come, not the realities themselves.’ If its sacrifices could have cleansed, they would have stopped. Instead, ‘those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.’ So Christ came, in the words of Psalm 40: ‘Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me…I have come to do Your will, O God.’ The incarnation was necessary for the atonement: the Son took a body in order to offer it. ‘And by that will, we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.’ Then a picture. ‘Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices’. There were no chairs in the tabernacle; the work was never done. ‘But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God.’ ‘By a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified.’ The Spirit confirms it from Jeremiah: ‘Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more.’ ‘And where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed.’
10.big: Christ’s single sacrifice, once for all, has done what endlessly repeated sacrifices never could.
10.diff: The Lord’s Supper and sacrifice. This passage is central to a historic disagreement. Protestant churches hold that Christ’s sacrifice was offered once and is complete, so the Lord’s Supper is not itself a sacrifice for sin. The Westminster Confession says it is ‘only a commemoration of that one offering up of himself, by himself, upon the cross, once for all’ (29.2), though Reformed believers hold that Christ is truly, spiritually present to faith. Catholic teaching agrees that Christ’s sacrifice cannot be repeated, and does not claim that the Mass repeats it. The Catechism says the Eucharist ‘re-presents (makes present) the sacrifice of the cross’, so that the cross and the Mass are ‘one single sacrifice’, and ‘only the manner of offering is different’ (1366–1367). The question is whether ‘once for all’ and ‘no longer needed’ rule out any ongoing offering (the Protestant view), or are honoured by a sacrament that makes the one offering present (the Catholic view).

10.ctx: The practical application of everything since 4:14, and the passage from which the Community of Brothers takes its name and shape (verses 23–25).
10.mean:
Three invitations (verses 19–25). Because we have ‘confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body’, and a great priest over God’s house: ‘let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith’; ‘Let us hold resolutely to the hope we profess, for He who promised is faithful’; and ‘let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.’ Faith, hope and love; God, the future, and one another. Meeting together is not optional extra: it is how believers keep each other going.

A warning (verses 26–31). ‘If we deliberately go on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no further sacrifice for sins remains’. In context, the sin is rejecting Christ’s sacrifice, the only one there is: having ‘trampled on the Son of God’ and ‘insulted the Spirit of grace’. ‘It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.’

Encouragement (verses 32–39). ‘Remember the early days’, when they endured ridicule, persecution and the confiscation of property ‘joyfully’. ‘So do not throw away your confidence; it holds a great reward.’ ‘But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.’
10.big: Because Christ has opened the way to God, believers must draw near, hold fast, and keep meeting together to encourage one another.
10.diff: Verses 26–31 raise the same questions as 6:4–6 (see the note there for the four main readings). ‘Deliberately go on sinning’ does not mean any sin committed knowingly. The writer has in mind persistent, settled rejection of Christ, the ‘shrinking back’ of verse 39. The writer again ends with confidence: ‘we are not of those who shrink back’.

b: The readers had suffered public insult, imprisonment of some members, and confiscation of property, but ‘not yet’ to the point of bloodshed (12:4). If the letter was sent to Rome, two known events are candidates.

Claudius, AD 49. The Roman historian Suetonius records that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were constantly rioting ‘at the instigation of Chrestus’. Many historians think this refers to disputes about Christ in the synagogues. Acts 18:2 mentions the same expulsion, which brought Aquila and Priscilla to Corinth. Expulsion would have meant loss of property, but not martyrdom. That fits these verses well.

Nero, AD 64. After the great fire of Rome, Tacitus records that Nero blamed the Christians, and that some were torn to death by dogs or burned as torches. Since the readers had ‘not yet’ shed blood, many date the letter before this. Some think the writer is preparing them for exactly such a storm.
The link to Rome is likely but not certain, so these identifications remain suggestions.

11.ctx: Chapter 11 answers 10:38–39 (‘My righteous one will live by faith’) with a gallery of Old Testament examples, often called the ‘hall of faith’.
11.mean: ‘Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see. This is why the ancients were commended.’ Faith is not wishful thinking. It is confidence in what God has promised (the future) and in what he has revealed (the unseen). It begins with creation: ‘By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible.’
11.big: Faith is confident trust in what God has promised but cannot yet be seen.
11.diff: Verse 1 is less a full definition than a description of faith’s character, which the chapter then illustrates. Verse 3 is a key text for creation ‘out of nothing’: the visible world was not made from pre-existing visible material.

11.h: The Faith of Abel, Enoch, Noah
11.ctx: The first examples come from Genesis 4–6, before the flood.
11.mean: ‘By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did’, and ‘by faith he still speaks, even though he is dead’. ‘By faith Enoch was taken up so that he did not see death’, because he pleased God. Then a principle for every reader: ‘And without faith it is impossible to please God. For anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him.’ ‘By faith Noah, when warned about things not yet seen, in godly fear built an ark to save his family.’ He believed God about a flood no one had seen, and acted on it for years.
11.big: From the beginning, people have pleased God by trusting him and acting on his word.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

11.h: The Faith of Abraham and Sarah
11.ctx: Abraham, honoured by Jews as father of their nation and by Paul as the father of all who believe (Romans 4), gets the longest treatment.
11.mean: ‘By faith Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going.’ He lived in the promised land in tents, as a foreigner, ‘For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God.’ By faith Sarah, though barren and past age, conceived. ‘All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised.’ ‘They acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth.’ ‘Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.’ The greatest test came when Abraham offered Isaac, the son of the promise. ‘Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.’
11.big: Faith obeys God’s call and lives as a stranger on earth, looking for the city God is building.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

11.h: The Faith of Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph
11.ctx: The patriarchs at the end of their lives (Genesis 27–50). Each blessing or instruction looked forward to promises none of them lived to see fulfilled.
11.mean: ‘By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future.’ By faith the dying Jacob blessed Joseph’s sons. ‘By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones.’ Joseph was the most powerful man in Egypt, yet he did not want to be buried there. He was sure God would bring his people out, and wanted his bones to go with them (Exodus 13:19).
11.big: Faith looks beyond death to the fulfilment of God’s promises.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

11.ctx: Moses, the central figure of the old covenant, was raised in Pharaoh’s court with every advantage Egypt could give (Exodus 2; Acts 7:22).
11.mean: By faith Moses’ parents hid him, ‘unafraid of the king’s edict’. ‘By faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. He chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin. He valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to his reward.’ ‘Disgrace for Christ’ probably means the reproach borne by God’s people and their coming Messiah, which Moses shared by identifying with them. ‘He persevered because he saw Him who is invisible.’ By faith he kept the Passover, and the people crossed the Red Sea.
11.big: Faith chooses suffering with God’s people over the passing pleasures of sin.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

11.ctx: The chapter speeds up, moving from Joshua through the judges, kings and prophets, to the martyrs of the period between the Testaments.
11.mean: ‘By faith the walls of Jericho fell’. ‘By faith the prostitute Rahab…did not perish’. ‘Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets’. Through faith some ‘conquered kingdoms’, ‘shut the mouths of lions, quenched the raging fire, and escaped the edge of the sword’. But faith did not always lead to rescue. ‘Others were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection.’ ‘They were stoned, they were sawed in two, they were put to death by the sword.’ ‘The world was not worthy of them.’ ‘These were all commended for their faith, yet they did not receive what was promised. God had planned something better for us, so that together with us they would be made perfect.’
11.big: Faith sometimes brings deliverance and sometimes brings suffering, and God commends both.
11.diff: The list includes deeply flawed figures such as Samson and Jephthah. The chapter commends their faith, not everything they did.

b: No Old Testament person is said to have been sawn in two. But an ancient Jewish tradition held that the prophet Isaiah was killed in this way under the wicked King Manasseh (compare 2 Kings 21:16). Justin Martyr, writing around AD 155, refers to it in debate with a Jewish teacher: Isaiah, ‘whom you sawed asunder with a wooden saw’. Hebrews probably alludes to it. Verse 35 (‘tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection’) likewise recalls the Jewish martyrs under Antiochus IV in the 160s BC. In 2 Maccabees 7 a mother and her seven sons are tortured to death for refusing to break God’s law, one saying they look for the hope ‘that we will be raised up again by him’.

12.ctx: The ‘cloud of witnesses’ refers back to the heroes of chapter 11. The picture is a race run in a crowded stadium.
12.mean: ‘Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us. Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.’ The witnesses are not so much spectators as examples: they testify that the race can be finished. Jesus is more than an example. He is the pioneer who ran the whole course first and brings faith to completion. ‘Consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.’
12.big: Believers run the race of faith by keeping their eyes on Jesus, who ran it first.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

12.ctx: The readers had faced public insult, imprisonment and loss of property (10:32–34), but not yet martyrdom.
12.mean: ‘In your struggle against sin, you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.’ They have forgotten Proverbs 3:11–12: ‘My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you. For the Lord disciplines the one He loves.’ Hardship is not a sign that God has abandoned them but that he is treating them as sons. ‘For what son is not disciplined by his father?’ Earthly fathers disciplined us for a short time as they thought best, ‘but God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in His holiness. No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it.’ So, ‘strengthen your limp hands and weak knees’.
12.big: Hardship, received rightly, is the loving training of a Father, not a sign of his absence.
12.diff: ‘Discipline’ here means training more than punishment. Not all suffering is discipline for a particular sin (compare John 9:1–3); the writer presents hardship as something God uses for his children’s good.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

12.ctx: Practical warnings drawn from the argument. The story of Esau selling his birthright for a meal comes from Genesis 25:29–34 and 27:30–40.
12.mean: ‘Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.’ Three dangers. Falling short of God’s grace. A ‘root of bitterness’ that ‘springs up to cause trouble and defile many’ (one bitter person can poison a church). And being ‘godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright’. ‘Afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. He could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.’ Esau traded what was eternal for what was immediate, and could not undo it.
12.big: Holiness and perseverance in grace matter; Esau shows the cost of trading eternal things for passing ones.
12.diff: ‘No ground for repentance’ is read in two ways: Esau could not get his father Isaac to change his mind, or Esau himself could not find true repentance. Either way, his tears were for the lost blessing rather than for his sin. ‘Holiness, without which no one will see the Lord’ does not teach that holiness earns salvation. Protestants read it as the holiness that always grows from saving faith; Catholics as the holiness of grace that must be kept to the end.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

12.ctx: A contrast between Mount Sinai, where the law was given in fire and terror (Exodus 19), and Mount Zion, God’s heavenly city.
12.mean: ‘For you have not come to a mountain that can be touched and that is burning with fire; to darkness, gloom, and storm’. At Sinai the sight was so terrifying that even Moses trembled. ‘Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You have come to myriads of angels in joyful assembly, to the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven. You have come to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.’ Abel’s blood cried for justice; Jesus’ blood speaks forgiveness. When believers gather to worship, they join this heavenly assembly. Then a final warning: God will shake heaven and earth once more, so that ‘the unshakable may remain’. ‘Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe. “For our God is a consuming fire.”’
12.big: Believers have come not to the terror of Sinai but to the joyful assembly of heaven, which calls for grateful, reverent worship.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

13.ctx: Practical instructions for the community’s life together. Travelling believers relied on hospitality, and prisoners in the Roman world often depended on friends for food.
13.mean: ‘Continue in brotherly love. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it’, as Abraham did (Genesis 18). ‘Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them, and those who are mistreated as if you were suffering with them.’ ‘Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.’
13.big: Brotherly love shows itself in hospitality, care for those who suffer, and faithfulness in marriage.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

13.ctx: The instructions rest on Christ’s unchanging faithfulness. Animal sacrifices and food rules were still central to the temple worship the readers had known.
13.mean: ‘Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, for God has said: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.”’ Contentment rests on God’s presence. ‘Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.’ So, ‘Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings’. The heart is strengthened ‘by grace and not by foods’. ‘We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat.’ On the Day of Atonement the bodies of the sacrificed animals were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). ‘And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate’. ‘Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore. For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.’
13.big: Because Christ never changes and never leaves, believers can be content and bear disgrace for him.
13.diff: ‘We have an altar’ (verse 10) is read differently. Calvin and most Protestant commentators take the altar to be Christ’s sacrifice on the cross, on which believers ‘feed’ by faith. Some interpreters see a reference to the Lord’s Table. Either way, the writer’s point is that clinging to the old system cuts a person off from Christ’s sacrifice.

src.l: Calvin on Hebrews 13:10–15, CCEL

13.ctx: With Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice complete, the writer names the offerings that remain for God’s people.
13.mean: ‘Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name. And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.’ The sacrifices are now praise and generosity. ‘Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch over your souls as those who must give an account. To this end, allow them to lead with joy and not with grief.’ Leaders are accountable to God for their people; the people can make that task a joy or a burden. ‘Pray for us’.
13.big: The old sacrifices give way to praise, generosity, and glad support of faithful leaders.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

13.ctx: One of the best-loved blessings in Scripture, and the letter’s closing.
13.mean: ‘Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, equip you with every good thing to do His will. And may He accomplish in us what is pleasing in His sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.’ It is the only mention of the resurrection in so many words in the whole letter. God equips us, and God works in us: our obedience is his work. The writer calls his letter a brief ‘word of exhortation’, mentions that ‘our brother Timothy has been released’, and sends greetings from ‘Those from Italy’.
13.big: The God who raised the great Shepherd will equip his people to do his will.
13.diff: The mention of Timothy and ‘those from Italy’ links the letter with Paul’s circle and possibly with Rome (see History & setting of Hebrews above).

1.ctx: Paul writes from Ephesus, about AD 53–55, to the church he had founded a few years earlier. Sosthenes may be the synagogue leader in Corinth who was beaten in front of Gallio (Acts 18:17), now a believer and with Paul, though we cannot be sure.
1.mean: Paul calls himself ‘called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God’. That matters, because some in Corinth were questioning his authority (chapters 4 and 9). He writes ‘To the church of God in Corinth’: the church belongs to God, not to Corinth and not to any leader. Its members are ‘sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy’. Holiness is first something God has given them (they are set apart as his) and then something they must live out. Paul also reminds them they belong with ‘all those everywhere who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ’. Corinth is not the only church in the world.
1.big: A church full of problems is still God’s holy people, and must start living like it.
1.diff: Calling on the name. ‘Call on the name of the LORD’ is Old Testament language for worshipping the one God (Joel 2:32). Paul applies it, without explanation, to Jesus. Little more than twenty years after the crucifixion, Jewish believers like Paul were calling on Jesus as Lord.

src.l: ‘Corinthians, First Letter to the’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

1.ctx: Ancient letters usually opened with a thanksgiving. Paul’s thanksgivings often hint at the themes to come.
1.mean: Paul thanks God for the grace given them. They have been ‘enriched in every way, in all speech and all knowledge’ and ‘do not lack any spiritual gift’. These are the very things the Corinthians were proud of, and which Paul will later correct (chapters 12–14). But he thanks God for them first, because they are gifts. The confidence for the future rests on God, not on them: ‘He will sustain you to the end, so that you will be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.’ ‘God, who has called you into fellowship with His Son Jesus Christ our Lord, is faithful.’
1.big: God’s faithfulness, not the church’s performance, guarantees that he will finish what he began.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

1.ctx: The first problem Paul tackles. Greek cities admired public speakers and teachers, and students took pride in which famous teacher they followed. Apollos was an eloquent Jewish teacher from Alexandria who had worked in Corinth after Paul (Acts 18:24–19:1). Cephas is Peter’s Aramaic name.
1.mean: Some of ‘Chloe’s household’ had told Paul about quarrels. People were saying, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ or ‘I follow Christ.’ Even the last group was using Christ as a party badge. Paul’s answer is three blunt questions: ‘Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized into the name of Paul?’ He is relieved he baptised so few of them. He is not belittling baptism; he wants no one to think they were joined to him rather than to Christ. His calling was ‘to preach the gospel, not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power’.
1.big: Loyalty to human leaders divides the church, which belongs to Christ alone.

src.l: ‘Corinthians, First Letter to the’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
1 Clement 47 (trans. Roberts and Donaldson), New Advent

1.ctx: Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, kept for slaves and rebels. Preaching a crucified man as Lord sounded absurd to Greeks and offensive to Jews, who read Deuteronomy 21:23 as putting a hanged man under God’s curse.
1.mean: ‘The message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.’ Quoting Isaiah 29:14, Paul says God has turned the world’s wisdom upside down: ‘the world through its wisdom did not know Him’, so God chose to save people through a message that sounds foolish. ‘Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles’. To those God calls, the crucified Christ is ‘the power of God and the wisdom of God’.
1.big: The cross looks like weakness and foolishness, but it is God’s power and wisdom for salvation.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

1.ctx: Paul points to the Corinthian church itself as evidence. Most members were ordinary people: workers, freed slaves and slaves. A few, like Crispus, Gaius and Erastus, were people of some standing.
1.mean: ‘Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth.’ God deliberately ‘chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise’, and the weak, lowly and despised, ‘so that no one may boast in His presence.’ Their salvation was God’s doing: ‘It is because of Him that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption.’ So the only boasting left is the kind Jeremiah 9:24 allows: ‘Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.’
1.big: God chooses the unimpressive so that all glory goes to him and all boasting is in Christ.
1.diff: ‘God chose’. Reformed readers see here God’s free choice of whom he will save: the Corinthians are in Christ ‘because of Him’, not because they were wiser or better than others (compare Westminster Confession 3). Arminian (Wesleyan) readers agree that salvation is entirely God’s gift and leaves no room for boasting, but take ‘chose’ here to describe the kind of people God delights to save, rather than a fixed decision about particular individuals. Both agree on Paul’s point: the church is made up of people God has rescued, not people who impressed him.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

2.h: Paul’s Message by the Spirit’s Power
2.ctx: Travelling speakers in Corinth were judged on their delivery, looks and polish. Paul had arrived from Athens, where few had believed (Acts 17:32–34).
2.mean: Paul deliberately did not try to impress. ‘I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified.’ He came ‘in weakness and fear, and with much trembling’. Yet people believed, because his preaching came ‘with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power, so that your faith would not rest on men’s wisdom, but on God’s power.’ This is not a rejection of careful thought; Paul argues carefully all through this letter. It is a refusal to make the speaker, rather than Christ, the attraction.
2.big: Faith that rests on God’s power, not on persuasive technique, is the kind that lasts.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

2.ctx: Having rejected the world’s wisdom, Paul says there is a true wisdom. Some Corinthians thought of themselves as the ‘spiritual’ elite; Paul turns their own words back on them.
2.mean: There is a ‘mysterious and hidden wisdom of God’, planned ‘before time began’. The powerful did not grasp it: ‘if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.’ It cannot be discovered by human cleverness (‘No eye has seen, no ear has heard’), but ‘God has revealed it to us by the Spirit.’ Only God’s Spirit knows God’s thoughts, as only a man’s own spirit knows his. ‘The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned.’ Believers, by contrast, ‘have the mind of Christ.’
2.big: God’s wisdom is grasped only as his Spirit opens our understanding.
2.diff: The ‘natural man’ (verse 14). Reformed theology reads this as showing that, without the Spirit’s new birth, no one can truly receive the gospel; the Spirit must first open the heart. Arminian (Wesleyan) theology agrees that no one can come to God unaided, but teaches that God’s ‘prevenient’ grace (grace that goes before) is at work in everyone, enabling them to respond. Both reject the idea that people find God by their own intelligence. ‘The Lord of glory’ (verse 8) echoes Old Testament language for God (compare ‘the King of glory’ in Psalm 24:7–10), here given to the crucified Jesus.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

3.ctx: Paul returns to the factions of chapter 1. The Corinthians thought themselves spiritually advanced; Paul says the opposite.
3.mean: ‘I could not address you as spiritual, but as worldly—as infants in Christ.’ The proof is their ‘jealousy and dissension’. Rivalry between fan clubs is just ordinary human behaviour. As for the leaders they are fighting over: ‘What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? They are servants through whom you believed’. ‘I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow.’ The workers are ‘one in purpose’ and each will be rewarded for his own work. The church belongs to neither: ‘you are God’s field, God’s building.’
3.big: Leaders are only servants; God alone gives growth.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

3.ctx: Paul develops the building picture. Corinth’s own history gave it force: the city had been sacked and burned in 146 BC, and was probably rebuilt partly from the stone and metal that survived.
3.mean: Paul laid the foundation ‘as an expert builder’, and others are building on it. ‘No one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.’ What is built on it may be durable (‘gold, silver, precious stones’) or flimsy (‘wood, hay, or straw’). On the Day of judgement, ‘the fire will prove the quality of each man’s work.’ Work that survives will be rewarded. If it burns, the builder ‘will suffer loss. He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames.’ Like a man escaping a burning house he built badly, he is rescued, but his work is lost.
3.big: Everything must be built on Christ, and each person’s work will be tested by God.
3.diff: Who is in view? Many commentators (including Calvin, who says ‘Paul assuredly speaks of ministers alone’) think Paul is speaking first of church leaders and teachers. Others apply it to every believer’s life’s work. Purgatory? Catholic teaching cites this verse among others when it speaks of a purification after death for those who die in God’s grace but still need cleansing: ‘the tradition of the Church, by reference to certain texts of Scripture, speaks of a cleansing fire’ (Catechism 1031). Protestants read the fire as the testing of each person’s work on the Day of judgement, not a cleansing of the soul after death. Calvin called purgatory ‘silly trifles’; Wesley said this text ‘utterly overthrows’ it. They point out that the fire tests works, not souls, and that it comes on ‘the Day’ of Christ’s return rather than at each person’s death. Many modern commentators of different traditions likewise read the passage as about the final judgement of believers’ work. All agree that the one who is saved is saved by Christ, the foundation, not by the quality of his work.

3.ctx: Corinth had many temples. Destroying or defiling a temple was treated as a serious crime by Jews and Gentiles alike.
3.mean: ‘Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?’ The ‘you’ is plural: the church together is where God now lives. So: ‘If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him’. Splitting the church is not a minor matter. Paul then deflates the pride behind the factions. The world’s wisdom is foolishness to God, so ‘stop boasting in men.’ It is backwards to say ‘I follow Paul’ (1:12), because the truth is the other way round: ‘All things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future… and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.’
3.big: The church is God’s temple, and those who divide it answer to God.
3.diff: Here the temple is the church as a whole. In 6:19 Paul applies the same picture to each believer’s body.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

4.ctx: The Corinthians were ranking their teachers. Paul answers with some of his sharpest irony.
4.mean: Apostles are ‘servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God’, and ‘it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.’ So Paul is not troubled by their verdicts on him, or even his own: ‘It is the Lord who judges me.’ ‘Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time’. Then a question that undercuts all pride: ‘What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?’ The Corinthians act as if they had already arrived: ‘Already you have become rich. Without us, you have become kings.’ By contrast the apostles are like condemned prisoners at the end of a procession, ‘a spectacle to the whole world’, hungry, homeless, ‘the scum of the earth’.
4.big: Christian leaders answer to the Lord, and everything we have is a gift, so there is no room for pride.

b: Corinth had a large theatre, seating about 14,000, and some scholars (such as Jerome Murphy-O’Connor) suggest Paul had public spectacles like those in mind when he wrote that the apostles had become ‘a spectacle to the whole world’ (verse 9). It is a reasonable suggestion, but Paul does not say so.

src.l: Matthew S. Beal, ‘Corinth’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Murphy-O’Connor, Thiselton, Engels, Strabo, Pliny)
Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

4.ctx: A change of tone, from irony to appeal. A ‘guardian’ (Greek paidagōgos) was a household slave who took children to school and kept them in line; he was not their father.
4.mean: ‘I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.’ They may have ‘ten thousand guardians in Christ’, but only one father: ‘in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.’ So ‘I urge you to imitate me.’ He is sending Timothy to remind them how he lives, which is ‘exactly what I teach everywhere in every church.’ Some have grown arrogant, thinking Paul will not come back. He will, and ‘the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power.’ ‘Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and with a gentle spirit?’
4.big: Paul corrects the church as a father who brought them to faith, and he expects to be imitated.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

5.ctx: A case the church was tolerating. The law of Moses forbade a man to have sexual relations with his father’s wife (Leviticus 18:8), and Paul says even pagans would not accept it.
5.mean: ‘A man has his father’s wife’, a kind of immorality ‘intolerable even among pagans’. Worse, the church was proud of its tolerance, perhaps as proof of its freedom. They should have grieved and ‘removed from your fellowship the man who did this’. When they meet, with Paul present in spirit and ‘the power of the Lord Jesus’, they are to ‘hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord.’ The aim is rescue, not revenge. Sin left alone spreads: ‘a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough’. As Israel cleared out yeast at Passover, so they must clear out sin, ‘For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.’
5.big: Tolerating open, unrepentant sin harms the whole church; discipline aims at the sinner’s rescue.
5.diff: ‘Hand this man over to Satan’. Most take this to mean putting him out of the church’s fellowship into the world, ‘Satan’s territory’, where he will feel the full weight of his sin and, it is hoped, repent. ‘The destruction of the flesh’ is read either as the destruction of his sinful nature, or as physical suffering (compare 11:30). 2 Corinthians 2:5–11 may describe a repentant offender being welcomed back, though whether it is the same man is debated. Churches differ in how formal discipline is carried out, but almost all agree it must be done carefully, through proper leadership, and with restoration as the goal.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

5.ctx: Paul had written to them before (verse 9). That earlier letter is lost, and they had misunderstood it.
5.mean: ‘I wrote you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people.’ He did not mean people outside the church; ‘In that case you would have to leave this world.’ He meant ‘anyone who claims to be a brother but is sexually immoral or greedy, an idolater or a verbal abuser, a drunkard or a swindler. With such a man do not even eat.’ ‘God will judge those outside.’ The church’s job is to hold its own members to account, quoting Deuteronomy: ‘Expel the wicked man from among you.’
5.big: The church is to hold its own members to account, not withdraw from unbelievers.
5.diff: Notice that greed, abusive speech and drunkenness appear in the same list as sexual sin. Churches are often stricter about some of these than others.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL
‘Corinthians, First Letter to the’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

6.ctx: Lawsuits were heard in public, in the civic courts. Verses 7–8 show that some members were using them to cheat fellow believers.
6.mean: ‘If any of you has a grievance against another, how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints!’ If believers will one day share in judging the world and even angels, they can surely settle everyday disputes. ‘Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between his brothers?’ Suing one another at all is already a defeat. ‘Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?’ Instead they are the ones doing the cheating, ‘even against your own brothers!’
6.big: Believers should settle disputes within the church, even at personal cost, rather than shame Christ in public.
6.diff: Paul is speaking about civil disputes between believers, not about reporting crimes. Romans 13:1–4 says the authorities are God’s servants to punish wrongdoing, and churches today rightly report abuse and other crimes to the police.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

6.ctx: Some Corinthians seem to have argued that what they did with their bodies did not matter spiritually. Paul quotes their slogans (‘Everything is permissible for me’; ‘Food for the stomach’) and answers them.
6.mean: ‘Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who submit to or perform homosexual acts, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God.’ Then the turn: ‘And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.’ As for their slogans: ‘not everything is beneficial’, and ‘I will not be mastered by anything.’ ‘The body is not intended for sexual immorality, but for the Lord’. God will raise our bodies, they are ‘members of Christ’, so uniting them with a prostitute is unthinkable.
6.big: The gospel names sin plainly and transforms sinners: ‘that is what some of you were. But you were washed’.
6.diff: The words in verse 9. The BSB’s ‘men who submit to or perform homosexual acts’ translates two Greek words. Malakos literally means ‘soft’ and was used of men who took the passive role in sex with men. Arsenokoitēs is a rare compound of ‘male’ and ‘bed’ (a word for sexual intercourse). It may have been coined from the Greek translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, where the same two words stand side by side. Where scholars stand. Most commentators (for example Fee, Garland, Thiselton) conclude that the two words refer to the passive and active partners in male same-sex intercourse; Garland translates them ‘those males who are penetrated sexually by males’ and ‘those males who sexually penetrate males’. In 1980 the historian John Boswell argued that the words did not condemn homosexual relationships as such. Some scholars since have argued that Paul had in mind only exploitative forms common in his day, such as the sexual use of boys or slaves, or prostitution. Most commentators have not been persuaded, noting that Paul draws on the Leviticus wording, which is general, and on Jewish teaching that rejected all such acts. Churches. Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches teach that sexual intimacy belongs only within marriage between a man and a woman. Some Protestant denominations have changed their teaching in recent decades. The pastoral point. This is one item in a list that also includes greed, drunkenness and abusive speech, and Paul says ‘some of you were’ these things. He is writing to forgiven people. The church is a community of washed sinners, not of people who were never tempted.

6.h: The Temple of the Holy Spirit
6.ctx: Paul draws the practical conclusion of verses 12–17.
6.mean: ‘Flee from sexual immorality.’ Not argue with it or manage it: run. Sexual sin is unique because the person ‘sins against his own body.’ And the body is not ours to do with as we like: ‘your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.’
6.big: The body matters to God: it is the Spirit’s temple and belongs to Christ, who bought it.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

7.ctx: Paul turns to the questions the Corinthians had written to him. ‘It is good to abstain from sexual relations’ (verse 1) is probably their slogan, which Paul quotes and then qualifies. Some of them seem to have thought that sex, even within marriage, was unspiritual.
7.mean: Marriage is the right place for sex: ‘each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.’ Within marriage, each has a duty to the other. Strikingly for his time, Paul says it equally of both: ‘The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife.’ They may abstain for a time of prayer, by agreement, but must come together again. Paul values singleness, but ‘each man has his own gift from God’. To the married he passes on the Lord’s own command: no divorce. If a believer is married to an unbeliever who is willing to stay, they must not divorce, because the unbelieving spouse and the children are ‘sanctified’ through the believer. ‘But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases.’
7.big: Marriage is good and mutual, and should be kept wherever possible.
7.diff: Deserted by an unbelieving spouse (verse 15). ‘Not bound’ is read in two main ways. Many Protestants take it to mean the deserted believer is free to remarry. The Westminster Confession allows divorce for ‘adultery, or such willful desertion as can no way be remedied by the church, or civil magistrate’ (24.6). Others take it to mean only that the believer need not fight to keep the marriage, and should not remarry. Catholic canon law calls this the ‘Pauline privilege’: a marriage between two unbaptised people is dissolved when one is baptised, the other departs, and the baptised person marries again (canon 1143). ‘Your children… are holy’ (verse 14). The word does not mean they are automatically saved, but that they are set apart, belonging within the circle of God’s people. Calvin used this to argue for infant baptism: ‘If the Lord admits them into the Church by his word, why should we refuse them the sign?’ Baptists, who baptise only those who profess faith, reply that the same verse calls the unbelieving husband ‘sanctified’, and no one baptises him on that basis. Practical note. Questions about divorce and remarriage are painful and personal. They are best worked through with a church’s own leaders.

7.ctx: A principle Paul applies to circumcision, slavery and marriage alike. Some Jewish men in the Greek world had surgery to hide their circumcision; some Gentile converts wanted to be circumcised.
7.mean: ‘Each one should lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him and to which God has called him.’ Becoming a Christian does not require changing your outward situation. ‘Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing. Keeping God’s commandments is what counts.’ To slaves: ‘Do not let it concern you—but if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity.’ In Christ the slave is ‘the Lord’s freedman’ and the free man is ‘Christ’s slave’. ‘You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men.’
7.big: Christians can serve God where they are, because their calling in Christ matters more than their status.
7.diff: Paul does not approve of slavery here. He tells slaves to take freedom if they can, and his teaching that slave and master are brothers in Christ (Philemon 16) undermined the whole system.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

7.ctx: Paul turns to the unmarried, in light of ‘the present crisis’. This may refer to a local hardship such as famine, or to the pressures of the last days in general.
7.mean: Paul gives ‘a judgment’ rather than a command from the Lord. Because of the present crisis, it is good to stay as you are. ‘But if you do marry, you have not sinned.’ ‘The time is short’ and ‘this world in its present form is passing away’, so believers should hold everything loosely: marriage, grief, joy, possessions. The unmarried person can give ‘undivided devotion to the Lord’; the married person rightly gives attention to pleasing their spouse. A widow may remarry, ‘as long as he belongs to the Lord.’
7.big: Both singleness and marriage are good gifts, and singleness offers particular freedom to serve the Lord.
7.diff: Paul’s own judgement. Paul distinguishes the Lord’s command (verse 10) from his own advice (verses 12, 25). Most Christians still treat his advice as inspired Scripture (he adds, ‘I think that I too have the Spirit of God’), but as wise counsel for circumstances rather than a rule binding everyone. Catholic and Orthodox traditions have drawn on this chapter in honouring vowed celibacy. Protestants have emphasised that marriage is honourable and not a lesser calling (Hebrews 13:4).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

8.ctx: Little meat was available in Corinth that had not come from animals sacrificed at a temple, and meals were held in temple precincts (verse 10 mentions ‘eating in an idol’s temple’). Refusing every such meal could cost a believer friendships and business.
8.mean: The ‘strong’ Corinthians said, ‘We all have knowledge’: idols are nothing, so eating is harmless. Paul agrees with the theology: ‘an idol is nothing at all in the world’. But ‘Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.’ ‘For us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist.’ Not everyone has this knowledge. A believer with a weak conscience, seeing a stronger Christian ‘eating in an idol’s temple’, may be drawn back into idolatry. ‘So this weak brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge.’ ‘Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again’.
8.big: Love for a weaker brother matters more than the freedom that knowledge gives.
8.diff: One God, one Lord (verse 6). Paul takes the Shema, Israel’s confession that ‘the LORD our God, the LORD is One’ (Deuteronomy 6:4), and divides its words between the Father (‘one God’) and Jesus (‘one Lord’). He also names Jesus as the one ‘through whom all things came’, that is, the Creator. This is one of the earliest places where Jesus is included within the identity of the one God, and it may have shaped the Nicene Creed’s confession of ‘one God, the Father Almighty’ and ‘one Lord Jesus Christ’.

9.ctx: Paul uses himself as an example of giving up rights for others, following on from chapter 8. Some in Corinth questioned whether he was a real apostle, partly because he refused their money and worked as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3).
9.mean: ‘Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?’ The church itself is proof: ‘you are the seal of my apostleship’. Paul has every right to be supported, like soldiers, farmers, shepherds and priests. The Law says so too: ‘Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.’ And ‘the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel.’ ‘But we did not exercise this right. Instead, we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ.’ Preaching is not optional for him: ‘Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!’ His reward is to offer it ‘free of charge’.
9.big: Paul gave up his own rights so that nothing would hinder the gospel.
9.diff: Paying ministers. This chapter is the main New Testament basis for churches supporting their pastors (compare 1 Timothy 5:17–18). Paul’s own choice to work for a living shows that ministers may also choose not to be paid, when that helps the gospel. The Lord’s brothers (verse 5): see History & setting of James for how different traditions understand them.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

9.ctx: Paul’s missionary principle, still within his argument about giving up rights for others.
9.mean: ‘Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible.’ Among Jews he kept Jewish customs; among Gentiles he did not, though he was never ‘outside the law of God but am under the law of Christ’. ‘To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some.’
9.big: Paul adapts everything except the gospel itself in order to reach people.
9.diff: ‘All things to all people’ is about cultural flexibility (food, customs, approach), not changing the message or compromising on right and wrong. Paul immediately adds that he is under ‘the law of Christ’.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

9.ctx: Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games, one of the great athletic festivals of the Greek world. See The Isthmian Games below.
9.mean: ‘Run in such a way as to take the prize.’ Athletes train ‘with strict discipline’ for ‘a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable.’ Paul does not run aimlessly or shadow-box: ‘I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified.’
9.big: The Christian life calls for disciplined, purposeful effort toward a prize that lasts.
9.diff: ‘Disqualified’. Reformed readers generally take this as a real warning that God uses to keep his people persevering; those truly in Christ will heed such warnings and be kept. Some take ‘disqualified’ to mean losing reward or usefulness in ministry, rather than salvation. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers take it to mean that even an apostle could fall away; Wesley glossed it ‘Disapproved by the Judge, and so falling short of the prize.’ All agree Paul took his own spiritual discipline seriously.

b: Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, at the sanctuary of Poseidon near the city. They drew crowds from all over Greece, and one of the city’s leading officials was the president of the games. In Paul’s day the victor’s crown was made of plants, which soon withered. Paul’s ‘crown that is perishable’ (verse 25) would have meant something to every reader.

10.ctx: Some Corinthians seem to have felt safe because they had been baptised and shared the Lord’s Supper. Paul shows that Israel had similar privileges and still fell.
10.mean: Israel’s ancestors were all ‘baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea’, all ate the same spiritual food and drank from ‘the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ.’ ‘Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them’. They fell into idolatry, sexual immorality, testing God and grumbling. ‘These things… were written down as warnings for us’. ‘So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall.’ Then encouragement: ‘No temptation has seized you except what is common to man. And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.’
10.big: Privileges do not guarantee faithfulness, but God is faithful to provide a way through every temptation.
10.diff: A misused verse. Verse 13 is often quoted as ‘God won’t give you more than you can handle’. Its subject is temptation to sin, not suffering in general; Paul himself was at times ‘under a burden far beyond our ability to endure’ (2 Corinthians 1:8). ‘That rock was Christ’. Paul sees Christ present with Israel in the wilderness, providing for them, which assumes that Christ existed before he was born as a man.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

10.ctx: Paul now rules out sharing in meals that were part of pagan worship.
10.mean: ‘Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.’ ‘Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?’ ‘Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body’. Eating at a sacrificial meal joins people to what is worshipped there. Idols themselves are nothing, but ‘the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God.’ ‘You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too’.
10.big: Believers share in Christ at his table, and so cannot share in pagan worship.
10.diff: ‘Participation’ (Greek koinōnia, also ‘fellowship’, ‘sharing’) in Christ’s body and blood. All Christians agree the Lord’s Supper is a real sharing in Christ and makes the church one body. They differ on how Christ is present. Wesley called the cup ‘The means of our partaking of those invaluable benefits, which are the purchase of the blood of Christ.’ See the glossary entry ‘Lord’s Supper’ for the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and memorial views in their own words.

10.ctx: Paul sums up his guidance on disputed matters. ‘Everything is permissible’ was probably a Corinthian slogan, which Paul quotes and qualifies.
10.mean: ‘“Everything is permissible,” but not everything is beneficial.’ ‘No one should seek his own good, but the good of others.’ In practice: ‘Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience’, because ‘The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.’ If an unbeliever invites you to dinner, eat what is served. But if someone points out that the food was offered to idols, do not eat it, for the sake of their conscience. ‘So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God.’
10.big: Christian freedom is used for others’ good and for God’s glory.

b: Paul’s word for ‘meat market’ in verse 25 is makellon, borrowed from the Latin macellum. Excavators at Corinth have identified the city’s meat market. Much of the meat sold there had come from animals sacrificed in the city’s many temples, which is why the question of conscience arose.
