11.ctx: In public worship, men and women in Corinth were praying and prophesying. Something about how they covered (or did not cover) their heads was causing offence. See Head coverings in Roman Corinth below.
11.mean: ‘The head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God.’ So a man who prays or prophesies ‘with his head covered dishonors his head’, and a woman who does so ‘with her head uncovered dishonors her head’. Paul argues from creation: ‘woman from man’, and ‘woman for man’. So ‘a woman ought to have a sign of authority on her head, because of the angels.’ Then he balances it: ‘In the Lord, however, woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman. For just as woman came from man, so also man is born of woman. But everything comes from God.’ He appeals to what is fitting and to the practice of all the churches.
11.big: Worship should honour God by respecting the difference between men and women, within their mutual dependence in the Lord.
11.diff: One of the hardest passages in Paul. What ‘head’ means. Some scholars argue the Greek kephalē here means authority (for example Robertson and Plummer; Ciampa and Rosner, who ground it in the order of creation). Others argue it means source or origin, since woman came from man (Fee; Barrett). A third view is ‘pre-eminence’. Calvin took it as authority: the man holds ‘the office of the head in respect of ruling her.’ Complementarians (who hold that men and women are equal but have different roles in marriage and church leadership) generally read ‘authority’; egalitarians (who hold that roles are open to both) generally read ‘source’. Are head coverings for today? A minority of churches (for example some Brethren, Mennonite and Reformed congregations) still ask women to cover their heads in worship. Most churches see the covering as the way that culture expressed a lasting principle. Calvin, who thought the covering right in his day, said ‘the one rule to be observed here is το πρέπον — decorum.’ Because of the angels. No one knows for sure. The commonest view is that angels are present at worship and care that it is fitting. Note that Paul assumes women pray and prophesy aloud in the gathering (verse 5). That shapes how chapter 14:34–35 is read.

b: What the Corinthians were doing is not fully clear, and scholars disagree. For men, Roman religion had a well-known custom: a man leading a sacrifice or prayer pulled his toga up over his head (capite velato, ‘with covered head’). A famous statue of the emperor Augustus (about AD 12–14) shows him like this. Some commentators (for example Ciampa and Rosner) think Paul did not want Christian men to look like pagans at worship. Others (for example Garland) think the issue was a hairstyle rather than a cloth covering, though Garland too connects it with pagan sacrifice. Gordon Fee, after weighing the options, concludes we do not know for certain what Paul had in mind for the men.

For women, Paul plainly regards the head covering as a mark of propriety and modesty. He compares an uncovered head with a shaved one, which he calls shameful (verse 6), and he treats leaving it off as a kind of rebellion. Why some Corinthian women were doing so is not clear.

11.ctx: The early church ate the Lord’s Supper as part of a real meal, usually in a wealthier member’s home. Corinth had great gaps between rich and poor. Some scholars think the poorer members, including slaves, arrived late after work to find the food gone.
11.mean: ‘Your gatherings do more harm than good.’ There are divisions: ‘While one remains hungry, another gets drunk.’ So ‘it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat’, and they ‘humiliate those who have nothing’. Paul reminds them what he ‘received from the Lord’: ‘The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread, and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, “This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me.”’ And the cup: ‘This cup is the new covenant in My blood’. ‘For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.’ So eating ‘in an unworthy manner’ is serious. ‘Each one must examine himself’, for whoever eats ‘without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.’ The practical answer: ‘when you come together to eat, wait for one another.’
11.big: The Lord’s Supper proclaims Christ’s death, and must be shared in a way that honours all his people.
11.diff: The earliest account. This is the earliest written record of the Lord’s Supper, earlier than the Gospels, and Paul says he had passed it on to them when he founded the church around AD 50. ‘Without recognizing the body’ (verse 29). Calvin read it as failing to distinguish the Lord’s body ‘as a sacred thing from a profane’, treating the Supper like ordinary food. Many modern commentators think ‘the body’ here also, or mainly, means the church as Christ’s body (compare 10:17; 12:27), since the sin Paul is correcting is despising poorer members. How Christ is present. Christians differ: Catholic and Orthodox teach that the bread and wine are changed into Christ’s body and blood; Lutherans that Christ’s true body and blood are present ‘under the bread and wine’; the Reformed that believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (Calvin: ‘Christ is not a deceiver, to mock us with empty representations’); and many evangelicals stress remembrance. See the glossary entry ‘Lord’s Supper’. Examine yourself is meant to lead to repentance and coming, not to staying away; the Supper is for sinners who trust Christ.

12.ctx: The Corinthians prized dramatic gifts, especially tongues, as signs of spiritual status. Many had come from pagan religion, where ecstatic speech was also known.
12.mean: The first test of the Spirit’s work is what is said about Jesus: ‘no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except by the Holy Spirit.’ ‘There are different gifts, but the same Spirit. There are different ministries, but the same Lord. There are different ways of working, but the same God works all things in all people.’ ‘Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.’ Paul lists wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues and interpretation. ‘All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines.’
12.big: Every gift comes from the one Spirit, for the good of the whole church, not for status.
12.diff: Spirit, Lord, God. Verses 4–6 name the Spirit, the Lord (Jesus) and God (the Father) side by side as the one source of the gifts, one of the patterns in Paul that the church later expressed in the doctrine of the Trinity. ‘As He determines’ presents the Spirit as a person who decides, not an impersonal force. Do all the gifts continue today? Cessationists, including many Reformed Christians, hold that the miraculous gifts confirmed the apostles’ message and ceased with them. B. B. Warfield argued they were ‘part of the credentials of the Apostles’ and ‘necessarily passed away with’ the apostolic church. Continuationists (including many evangelicals, charismatics and Pentecostals) hold that all the gifts continue until Christ returns. See the glossary entry ‘Spiritual gifts’.

12.ctx: Ancient writers often compared a city or society to a body. Paul uses the picture to honour the members who seem weakest.
12.mean: ‘The body is a unit, though it is composed of many parts… So it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink.’ No part can say it does not belong, and no part can say to another, ‘I do not need you.’ In fact ‘the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable’, and God gives ‘greater honor to the parts that lacked it’. ‘If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it.’
12.big: Every believer is a needed part of Christ’s body, and all share one another’s sufferings and joys.
12.diff: ‘Baptized… in one Spirit’ (verse 13). Most Protestants and Catholics read this as describing what happens to every believer at conversion and baptism: all are joined to Christ’s body by the Spirit. Pentecostals agree that every believer receives the Spirit at the new birth, but teach a further ‘baptism in the Spirit’, ‘distinct from and subsequent to the experience of the new birth’ (Assemblies of God), drawing mainly on Acts.

12.ctx: Paul applies the body picture to the roles God gives in the church.
12.mean: ‘Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it.’ God has appointed ‘first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers’, then other gifts. Tongues, which the Corinthians prized most, comes last. ‘Are all apostles? Are all prophets?… Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?’ In Greek each question expects the answer ‘No’. ‘But eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now I will show you the most excellent way.’
12.big: God gives different gifts to different people, and no single gift is expected of everyone.
12.diff: ‘Do all speak in tongues?’ The expected answer is no. Many cite this against the Pentecostal teaching that tongues is the necessary first sign of baptism in the Spirit. Pentecostals commonly reply that Paul is speaking of the ongoing gift of tongues used in church, which not all have, rather than the initial sign which, they hold, all who are baptised in the Spirit receive. ‘The most excellent way’ introduces chapter 13: love.

13.ctx: Often read at weddings, but written to correct a church proud of its gifts and failing in love. Every phrase in verses 4–7 corrects something the Corinthians were doing.
13.mean: ‘If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal.’ Prophecy, knowledge, faith and even self-sacrifice without love are ‘nothing’. ‘Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs.’ ‘It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails.’ The gifts are temporary: ‘we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away.’ ‘Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face.’ ‘And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love.’
13.big: Without love even the greatest gifts are worthless, and love will outlast them all.
13.diff: ‘When the perfect comes’. Most interpreters, across traditions, take this to be Christ’s return, when we will see ‘face to face’. Calvin said the perfection ‘begins, indeed, at death’ but will not be fully seen ‘until the day of judgment’, and that applying the passage to the time in between is a mistake; Wesley put it ‘At death and in the last day.’ Some cessationists have taken ‘the perfect’ to mean the completed New Testament, but many cessationists do not rest their case on this verse. Love here is agapē, love that seeks the other’s good at cost to oneself, as Christ did.

b: Corinth was famous for its bronze, which the Roman writer Pliny said was valued ‘before silver and almost even before gold’. The architect Vitruvius mentions bronze in connection with the acoustics of theatres. Some scholars (such as Jerome Murphy-O’Connor) suggest that Paul’s ‘ringing gong or a clanging cymbal’ (13:1) would have called these to mind for Corinthian readers: loud, impressive and hollow. It is an attractive suggestion but cannot be proved.

14.ctx: Paul applies chapter 13 to the gifts the Corinthians were misusing, especially speaking in tongues in church without interpretation.
14.mean: ‘Earnestly pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, especially the gift of prophecy.’ Someone speaking in a tongue speaks to God, and ‘no one understands him’; prophecy ‘speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort.’ ‘The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but the one who prophesies edifies the church.’ Paul himself speaks in tongues ‘more than all of you’, yet ‘in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.’ If outsiders hear uninterpreted tongues they will think ‘you are out of your minds’; if they hear prophecy, they may be convicted and say, ‘God is truly among you!’
14.big: What is said aloud in church must be understandable and build others up.
14.diff: What were tongues and prophecy? At Pentecost, tongues were human languages the speakers had not learned (Acts 2:6–11). Some think Corinthian tongues were the same; others think they included non-human speech, the ‘tongues of men and of angels’ (13:1), since ‘no one understands him’. New Testament prophecy is understood by some as Spirit-given speech that must be weighed (14:29), not equal to Scripture; others hold that true prophecy carried God’s authority and belonged to the founding of the church. Do they continue? See the glossary entry ‘Spiritual gifts’. All agree on Paul’s rules: love first, intelligible speech in church, and everything for building others up.

14.ctx: Early Christians met in homes, where many people could take part. Paul gives practical rules to keep the gathering orderly. The BSB footnote notes that ‘Some manuscripts place verses 34–35 after verse 40.’
14.mean: ‘When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church.’ Two or three may speak in tongues, in turn, and only with interpretation. Two or three prophets may speak, ‘and the others should weigh carefully what is said.’ ‘The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets’; no one is swept along out of control. ‘For God is not a God of disorder, but of peace’. Then: ‘Women are to be silent in the churches. They are not permitted to speak, but must be in submission, as the law says. If they wish to inquire about something, they are to ask their own husbands at home’. Paul ends: ‘be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner.’
14.big: Worship should be orderly and build others up, because it reflects the God of peace.
14.diff: ‘Women are to be silent’ (verses 34–35). This is hard, because in 11:5 Paul assumes women pray and prophesy aloud in church. Where scholars stand. There is no consensus. The main readings are: (1) a general rule, women are not to speak in the assembly (for example Robertson and Plummer); (2) women are not to take part in the judging of prophecies (verse 29), which would put them in authority over men (for example Kistemaker); (3) Paul is stopping disruptive questioning during worship, perhaps by wives questioning their husbands’ prophecies (for example Thiselton; Ciampa and Rosner); (4) the verses were added to the letter later by a copyist (Fee). The last view rests on the fact that some Western manuscripts put the verses after verse 40. Every surviving manuscript contains them somewhere, and many scholars hold that they are Paul’s. Reformed and Wesleyan voices. Calvin read it as forbidding women to teach in public ‘referring to ordinary service, or where there is a Church in a regularly constituted state’, and allowed that ‘a necessity may occur’. Wesley read it as forbidding women to speak ‘By way of teaching in public assemblies’, unless ‘under an extraordinary impulse of the Spirit’. Today. Churches that do not have women as pastors or elders (complementarian) usually read this with 1 Timothy 2:12 as about authoritative teaching. Churches that do (egalitarian) usually read it as a local problem of disorder. Very few churches today forbid women to speak in church at all, which shows that nearly everyone reads it in light of chapter 11. This is a matter on which faithful Christians differ; it is worth discussing with a church’s own leaders.

15.ctx: Some in Corinth were saying ‘there is no resurrection of the dead’ (verse 12). Greek thought often looked down on the body and hoped for the soul to escape it; a raised body seemed absurd (compare Acts 17:32). Paul starts with what everyone in the church already believed.
15.mean: Paul reminds them of the gospel ‘by which… you are saved’. ‘For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve.’ Then to ‘more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living’, then to James, then to all the apostles, ‘And last of all He appeared to me also’. Paul, once the persecutor, says: ‘by the grace of God I am what I am’. ‘This is what we preach, and this is what you believed.’
15.big: The gospel rests on events in history: Christ’s death for sins, his burial, his resurrection and his appearances to many witnesses.
15.diff: ‘For our sins’ and ‘according to the Scriptures’ probably point especially to Isaiah 53, where the servant suffers for the sins of others. ‘He was buried’ matters: in a Jewish setting, saying someone who was buried was raised meant the body was no longer in the grave. Witnesses. Calvin notes that Paul’s list is not complete: ‘He does not, however, adduce them all, for he makes no mention of women.’ The Gospels say women were the first to see the risen Jesus; why this formal summary leaves them out is not certain.

b: Paul says he ‘received’ and ‘passed on’ this summary (15:3), the technical words for handing on a tradition. The language is not typical of Paul, and it uses Peter’s Aramaic name ‘Cephas’. For these reasons scholars across the spectrum treat verses 3–5 (or 3–7) as a creed Paul was taught, not something he composed.

When did he receive it? Paul visited Peter and James in Jerusalem about three years after his conversion (Galatians 1:18–19), and his conversion was within a few years of the crucifixion. As Kirk MacGregor notes in a survey of the scholarship, virtually all critical scholars agree that Paul received it within about five years of the crucifixion, and many date it earlier. This is not only a believing view. The sceptical scholar Gerd Lüdemann wrote that ‘all the elements in the tradition are to be dated to the first two years after the crucifixion’. Scholars disagree on what lay behind the appearances, but most agree that the claim that Jesus had been raised and had appeared to named people was being taught within a very few years of his death, not developed decades later as legend.
Paul adds that most of the more than 500 witnesses were ‘still living’ when he wrote (15:6): in effect, ‘go and ask them’.

15.ctx: The Corinthian doubters seem to have accepted that Jesus rose, but denied that believers’ bodies would be raised.
15.mean: Paul follows their view to its end. ‘If there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith.’ The apostles would be ‘false witnesses about God’. ‘And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins.’ Those who have died in Christ would be lost. ‘If our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all men.’
15.big: Christianity stands or falls on the bodily resurrection of Jesus.
15.diff: Paul does not treat the resurrection as a symbol or a spiritual experience. He says that if it did not happen, Christian faith is false and pointless. This is one reason the evidence matters (see An early creed in the previous note).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

15.ctx: ‘Firstfruits’ were the first sheaf of the harvest, offered to God as the pledge that the rest would follow (Leviticus 23:10–11).
15.mean: ‘But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.’ ‘For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.’ There is an order: ‘Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him.’ Then the end, when Christ ‘hands over the kingdom to God the Father after He has destroyed all dominion, authority, and power.’ ‘The last enemy to be destroyed is death.’ Finally ‘the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all.’ Paul adds an argument from practice: why are some ‘baptized for the dead’, and why does he risk death daily, if the dead are not raised? Without resurrection, ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.’ ‘Bad company corrupts good character’, he warns, probably quoting the Greek playwright Menander.
15.big: Christ’s resurrection is the first of the harvest, guaranteeing the resurrection of all who belong to him.
15.diff: The Son made subject (verse 28). In the 4th century the Arians used this verse to argue that the Son is less than the Father. The historic churches answer that it concerns the Son’s work as the incarnate mediator, not his divine nature. Calvin: Christ ‘is inferior to God, in respect of his human nature’, yet is ‘of one essence with him, and is therefore himself God’; the handing over of the kingdom ends his work as mediator, not his deity. ‘Baptized for the dead’ (verse 29). No one knows for certain what Paul meant, and there are dozens of proposals. (1) Some Corinthians were being baptised on behalf of believers who had died unbaptised (Conzelmann and others). Paul mentions it without approving it, simply to show they believed in the resurrection. (2) People were being baptised ‘because of’ the dead, moved by the hope of rejoining believers who had died (Ciampa and Rosner). (3) Calvin thought it meant people seeking baptism when they were dying, ‘who are looked upon as already dead’; he could not ‘by any means be persuaded’ that proxy baptism was meant. Wesley: ‘Perhaps baptized in hope of blessings to be received after they are numbered with the dead.’ (4) The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints practises proxy baptism for the dead, citing this verse. The mainstream churches have not practised it, because elsewhere the New Testament ties baptism to each person’s own repentance and faith (Acts 2:38), and because one obscure verse is a weak basis for a practice found nowhere else in Scripture.

15.ctx: The doubters’ question was practical: what could a raised body be like, once the old one has rotted?
15.mean: ‘How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?’ Paul answers with a seed: ‘What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.’ The plant is continuous with the seed, yet far more glorious. God already makes many kinds of bodies, earthly and heavenly. ‘So will it be with the resurrection of the dead: What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.’ Adam, ‘of the dust of the earth’, became a living being; Christ, ‘the last Adam’, is ‘a life-giving spirit’. ‘And just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man.’
15.big: The resurrection body is continuous with the present one but transformed, as a plant is from its seed.
15.diff: ‘Spiritual body’ does not mean a body made of spirit, or no body at all. Paul’s word means a body fully given life and governed by the Holy Spirit, as ‘natural’ means a body animated by ordinary human life. The risen Jesus could be touched and ate food (Luke 24:39–43). The Westminster Confession says the dead will be raised ‘with the selfsame bodies, and none other’ (32.2), though changed.

src.l: Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text), chs. 1, 24, 29, 32

15.h: Where, O Death, Is Your Victory?
15.ctx: The climax of the chapter, looking to Christ’s return.
15.mean: ‘Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God’, so we must be changed. ‘Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed—in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.’ The dead will be raised imperishable, and those still living will be transformed. Then Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14 will come true: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory.’ ‘Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?’ ‘The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!’ So: ‘be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain.’
15.big: Christ’s victory over death means that nothing done for him is ever wasted.
15.diff: ‘Flesh and blood’ means human nature in its present, mortal state, not bodies as such; the whole chapter insists on a bodily resurrection. Paul expects some believers to be alive when Christ returns (compare 1 Thessalonians 4:15–17), but does not say when that will be.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

16.ctx: Paul was collecting money from Gentile churches for poor believers in Jerusalem, a project he cared about deeply (Romans 15:25–27; 2 Corinthians 8–9).
16.mean: ‘On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up, so that when I come no collections will be needed.’ The church will choose trusted people to carry the gift to Jerusalem, with letters from Paul.
16.big: Regular, planned giving is part of church life, and it binds believers of different backgrounds together.
16.diff: Paul’s care for transparency (the church chooses who carries the money) is a good model for handling church funds today.

b: ‘The first day of every week’ (verse 2) is our Sunday, the day of Jesus’ resurrection (Mark 16:2). Acts 20:7 shows believers gathering ‘on the first day of the week’ to break bread. The Didache, a church manual from the late 1st or early 2nd century, says: ‘every Lord’s day gather yourselves together, and break bread’.

16.ctx: Paul’s plans later changed, which caused friction (2 Corinthians 1:15–2:4). Pentecost (Shavuot) was in late spring.
16.mean: Paul plans to come through Macedonia and perhaps spend the winter with them, ‘if the Lord permits.’ For now he will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, ‘because a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me.’
16.big: Paul plans his travels around gospel opportunities, even in the face of opposition, and holds his plans loosely before the Lord.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

16.ctx: Timothy was young and perhaps timid (1 Timothy 4:12; 2 Timothy 1:7). The Corinthians had set Apollos up as a rival to Paul.
16.mean: ‘If Timothy comes, see to it that he has nothing to fear while he is with you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am.’ ‘No one, then, should treat him with contempt.’ As for Apollos, Paul had ‘strongly urged him’ to visit, but Apollos ‘was not at all inclined to go now’.
16.big: Paul and Apollos, whom the Corinthians had set up as rivals, were in fact colleagues.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

16.ctx: Five short commands that sum up the letter, written to a church that was divided, proud and careless.
16.mean: ‘Be on the alert. Stand firm in the faith. Be men of courage. Be strong. Do everything in love.’ Paul commends ‘Stephanas and his household’, the first converts in Achaia, who ‘have devoted themselves to the service of the saints’, and asks the church to follow such people. Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus had come to Paul from Corinth and ‘refreshed my spirit and yours as well.’
16.big: Courage and love belong together in Christian character.
16.diff: ‘Be men of courage’ translates one Greek word meaning ‘act like men’: be brave and mature. Paul addresses the whole church, women included. He immediately joins it to ‘Do everything in love.’ Strength without love, or love without courage, falls short.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

16.ctx: Paul dictated his letters to a secretary and added a closing greeting in his own handwriting as a mark that the letter was genuine (compare Galatians 6:11; 2 Thessalonians 3:17).
16.mean: Greetings come from ‘The churches in the province of Asia’, and from ‘Aquila and Prisca… and so does the church that meets at their house.’ This couple had worked with Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:2–3). ‘Greet one another with a holy kiss.’ Then Paul takes the pen: ‘This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus.’
16.big: The letter ends with a prayer for the Lord’s return and a final word of love.

b: Paul writes ‘Come, O Lord!’ (verse 22) in Aramaic, Marana tha, the language of the first Jewish believers in Judea and Galilee, in a Greek letter to a mostly Gentile church. The Didache includes the same prayer in its words for the Lord’s Supper: ‘Maran atha. Amen.’ The phrase shows that the very earliest Aramaic-speaking Christians were already praying to Jesus as ‘Lord’ and asking him to come. It was not a later Greek development.

1.ctx: Written from Macedonia around AD 55–56, after a painful visit and a 'severe letter' (now lost). Paul's authority had been attacked by rival teachers in Corinth. It is the most personal and emotional of his letters.
1.mean: Paul, an apostle by the will of God, and Timothy greet the church of God at Corinth, with all the saints throughout Achaia.
1.big: Paul writes as an apostle by God's will, not by human appointment.
1.diff: Many scholars think 2 Corinthians combines more than one letter, noting sharp changes of tone, especially at chapter 10. Others read it as a single letter written over time. Its teaching does not depend on the answer.

1.ctx: Paul had recently come through a crisis in Asia so severe he expected to die (1:8).
1.mean: Paul blesses the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may comfort others with the comfort we receive. He was so utterly burdened beyond his strength that he despaired of life itself, but that was to make him rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead.
1.big: God comforts his people in affliction so that they can comfort others, and teaches them to rely on him alone.

1.ctx: Paul had changed his travel plans, and critics accused him of being unreliable and double-minded.
1.mean: Paul says he has behaved with simplicity and godly sincerity. His word is not 'yes and no', for the Son of God, Jesus Christ, was not 'yes and no', but in him it is always yes. All the promises of God find their yes in him. It is God who establishes us in Christ, has anointed us, has put his seal on us and given us his Spirit as a guarantee. He did not come because he wanted to spare them.
1.big: Every promise of God is fulfilled in Christ, and God has sealed his people with the Spirit as a guarantee.

2.ctx: Paul explains why he wrote a painful letter instead of visiting.
2.mean: Paul says he decided not to make another painful visit. He wrote out of much affliction and anguish, with many tears, not to cause pain but to let them know his love. The person who caused pain has been punished enough by the majority; now they should forgive and comfort him, so that he is not overwhelmed by excessive sorrow, and reaffirm their love for him, so that Satan does not outwit them.
2.big: Church discipline aims at restoration, and must be followed by forgiveness and comfort.
2.diff: Some identify the offender with the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5; others think he was someone who had personally opposed Paul during his painful visit.

2.ctx: Paul had been anxious waiting to hear from Titus how the Corinthians received his letter.
2.mean: Paul says thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere. We are the aroma of Christ, to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things? We are not peddlers of God's word, but speak as commissioned by God.
2.big: The gospel's messengers spread the knowledge of Christ, which brings life to some and judgement to others.
2.diff: The image is of a Roman triumph, in which a victorious general paraded captives and incense was burned. Paul pictures himself as one of Christ's captives in the procession.

3.ctx: Paul's opponents apparently carried letters of recommendation and questioned Paul's credentials.
3.mean: Paul says he needs no letters of recommendation: the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, on tablets of human hearts. Their sufficiency is from God, who has made them ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
3.big: The changed lives of believers are the proof of a gospel ministry empowered by the Spirit.
3.diff: 'The letter kills' does not mean Scripture's plain meaning is harmful; Paul is contrasting the law written on stone, which exposed sin but could not give life, with the Spirit's work under the new covenant (Jeremiah 31).

3.ctx: Paul compares the ministry of Moses with the ministry of the new covenant, drawing on Exodus 34, where Moses' face shone after meeting God.
3.mean: Paul says if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that Israel could not gaze at Moses' face, will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory? When one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. The Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another.
3.big: Believers see God's glory in Christ and are progressively transformed into his likeness by the Spirit.
3.diff: 'The Lord is the Spirit' has been discussed in relation to the Trinity. Most interpreters understand Paul to mean that 'the Lord' Moses turned to in Exodus 34 is now encountered through the Spirit — not that the Son and the Spirit are the same person.
3.h: The Glory of the New Covenant

4.ctx: Paul defends the openness of his ministry against accusations of trickery.
4.mean: Paul says having this ministry by God's mercy, they do not lose heart. They have renounced disgraceful underhanded ways and do not tamper with God's word. If the gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing, whose minds the god of this world has blinded. We proclaim not ourselves but Jesus Christ as Lord. For God, who said 'let light shine out of darkness', has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
4.big: The God who created light shines the knowledge of his glory into hearts through the face of Christ.
4.diff: Reformed theology draws on verses 4–6 for the need of God's direct work to open blinded minds — conversion as an act of new creation.

4.ctx: Paul explains why his own weakness is no argument against his ministry.
4.mean: Paul says we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us. We are afflicted but not crushed, perplexed but not driven to despair, persecuted but not forsaken, struck down but not destroyed, always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that his life may also be manifested. So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day. This light momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison, as we look to the things that are unseen and eternal.
4.big: God's power is displayed through human weakness, and present suffering prepares an eternal glory.

5.ctx: Paul continues the theme of wasting away and renewal, turning to death and what follows.
5.mean: Paul says if the earthly tent is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. In this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling. God has given us the Spirit as a guarantee. We would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. So we make it our aim to please him, for we must all appear before the judgement seat of Christ.
5.big: Believers can face death with confidence, knowing they will be at home with the Lord, and live to please him.
5.diff: 'Away from the body and at home with the Lord' is one of the main texts for believers being with Christ immediately after death. The judgement seat of Christ here concerns believers giving account for how they have lived, not the question of their salvation.

5.ctx: The heart of the letter. Paul's opponents questioned his motives and sanity; he answers that Christ's love, shown in his death, is what drives him.
5.mean: Paul says the love of Christ controls us, because one has died for all, therefore all have died, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and was raised. If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old has passed away, the new has come. All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation. We are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us: be reconciled to God. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
5.big: In Christ God reconciled the world to himself, and his people are sent as his ambassadors to plead with others to be reconciled.
5.diff: Verse 21 is often called 'the great exchange' and is central to the Reformed doctrine of substitution and imputation: Christ bore our sin, and his righteousness is counted to us. Some scholars understand 'made him to be sin' as 'made him a sin offering'. 'One died for all' features in debates about the extent of the atonement.

6.ctx: Paul appeals to the Corinthians not to waste God's grace, listing his hardships as proof of genuine ministry.
6.mean: Paul says do not receive the grace of God in vain; now is the favourable time, now is the day of salvation. As servants of God they commend themselves by great endurance, in afflictions, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labours, sleepless nights, hunger; by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love; as sorrowful yet always rejoicing, as poor yet making many rich, as having nothing yet possessing everything. He opens his heart wide to them and asks them to do the same.
6.big: The marks of true ministry are endurance, love and joy through hardship, not outward success.

6.ctx: A short passage often applied to marriage and business partnerships. Corinth's social life was bound up with pagan temples, feasts and trade guilds dedicated to gods.
6.mean: Paul says do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. What partnership has righteousness with lawlessness, or light with darkness? What agreement has the temple of God with idols? We are the temple of the living God. Therefore go out from their midst and be separate, says the Lord, and I will welcome you, and be a father to you.
6.big: God's people are his temple and must not bind themselves in partnerships that compromise their faith.
6.diff: The image is of yoking two different animals together (Deuteronomy 22:10). Most Christians apply it to marriage between a believer and an unbeliever, though Paul's immediate concern seems to be involvement in pagan worship and with the false teachers. It does not tell believers to end existing marriages (compare 1 Corinthians 7:12–13).

7.ctx: Paul resumes the story of his anxious wait for Titus, broken off at 2:13.
7.mean: Paul says let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God. When he came into Macedonia he was afflicted at every turn, but God, who comforts the downcast, comforted him by the coming of Titus, with news of their longing and zeal for him. His letter grieved them, but only for a while, and he rejoices because their grief led to repentance. Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.
7.big: Godly sorrow over sin leads to repentance and life; worldly sorrow leads only to despair.

8.ctx: Paul returns to the collection for poor believers in Jerusalem, which the Corinthians had begun but not completed.
8.mean: Paul tells them about the churches of Macedonia, who in extreme poverty overflowed in generosity, giving beyond their means, begging to take part. He asks the Corinthians to excel in this grace too. You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich. The goal is fairness: your abundance supplying their need.
8.big: Christian giving flows from the grace of Christ, who became poor to make us rich.
8.diff: Verse 9 is a brief but profound statement of the incarnation: the eternal Son's riches and his becoming poor as a man.

8.ctx: Paul explains the arrangements for handling the collection. Large sums were being carried across the Mediterranean, and suspicion of misuse was easy to arouse.
8.mean: Paul commends Titus and two brothers who will collect the gift. He says they take precautions so that no one should blame them about this generous gift, aiming at what is honourable not only in the Lord's sight but also in the sight of man.
8.big: Money given to God's work must be handled transparently and honourably before everyone.

9.ctx: Continuing the appeal about the collection, now with principles of giving.
9.mean: Paul says whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will reap bountifully. Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency you may abound in every good work. This service supplies the saints' needs and overflows in thanksgiving to God. Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!
9.big: God loves cheerful, willing giving, and supplies generously to those who give.
9.diff: The 'sowing and reaping' principle is sometimes used to promise financial return for giving. In context Paul says God enriches givers so that they can be generous in every good work, and the 'harvest' is righteousness and thanksgiving to God.

10.ctx: A sharp change of tone. From here to chapter 13 Paul confronts the rival teachers and defends his apostleship.
10.mean: Paul says by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, he who is humble face to face but bold when away. Though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. The weapons of our warfare have divine power to destroy strongholds. We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ. His opponents say his letters are weighty but his bodily presence weak. Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.
10.big: The church's battle is fought with spiritual weapons that bring every thought into obedience to Christ.
10.diff: Verses 4–5 are often applied to spiritual warfare generally; in context the 'strongholds' are arguments and pretensions raised against the knowledge of God, including those of the false teachers.

11.ctx: Paul reluctantly engages in 'foolish' boasting to answer the rival teachers, whom he calls 'super-apostles'.
11.mean: Paul says he feels a divine jealousy for them, having betrothed them to Christ, but fears they are being led astray, accepting another Jesus, a different spirit and a different gospel. He preached to them free of charge. Such men are false apostles, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ; no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.
11.big: False teachers can look impressive and spiritual; the test is whether they preach the true Jesus.
11.diff: Paul's warning about 'another Jesus' and 'a different gospel' is often applied today to groups that use Christian language while denying Christ's deity, such as Jehovah's Witnesses and Mormonism.

11.ctx: Paul lists his sufferings as his real credentials, in deliberate contrast to the opponents' boasting.
11.mean: Paul says he speaks as a fool. Are they Hebrews? So is he. Servants of Christ? He is a better one: far greater labours, far more imprisonments, countless beatings, often near death. Five times he received thirty-nine lashes, three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked, a night and a day adrift at sea; in danger from rivers, robbers, his own people and Gentiles; in toil, hunger, cold and exposure. And daily the pressure of anxiety for all the churches. If he must boast, he will boast of the things that show his weakness — even his escape from Damascus in a basket.
11.big: Paul's credentials as an apostle are his sufferings for Christ, not his achievements.
11.diff: Most of these sufferings are not recorded in Acts, a reminder of how much of Paul's life we do not know.

12.ctx: Paul's opponents apparently boasted of visions and revelations.
12.mean: Paul says he knows a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven — whether in the body or out of the body he does not know — into paradise, and heard things that cannot be told. On behalf of this man he will boast, but on his own behalf only of his weaknesses.
12.big: Paul refuses to build his authority on spiritual experiences, however extraordinary.
12.diff: Most interpreters agree the 'man' is Paul himself, speaking indirectly out of modesty. 'The third heaven' means the highest heaven, the presence of God.

12.ctx: The passage that has comforted countless believers in chronic suffering.
12.mean: Paul says to keep him from becoming conceited, a thorn was given him in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass him. Three times he pleaded with the Lord to remove it. But he said: my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. Therefore he will boast all the more gladly of his weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon him. For when I am weak, then I am strong.
12.big: God's grace is sufficient in suffering that is not removed, and his power is displayed in human weakness.
12.diff: The thorn is unidentified; suggestions include an eye condition, epilepsy, recurring illness, or persistent opposition. Paul's prayer being answered with 'no' — and the thorn being described both as given and as from Satan — shows how God's purposes and evil can be at work in the same event.

12.ctx: Paul turns from boasting to his pastoral concern for the church.
12.mean: Paul says they forced him to be a fool. He is not inferior to the super-apostles, and the signs of a true apostle were performed among them. He is coming a third time and will not be a burden; he seeks not what is theirs but them. He will most gladly spend and be spent for their souls. He fears he may find quarrelling, jealousy, slander and unrepented sin among them.
12.big: Paul's concern is not for himself but for the church's spiritual health.

13.ctx: Paul prepares for his third visit, when he will deal with unrepentant sin.
13.mean: Paul says every charge must be established by two or three witnesses. He will not spare those who sinned before. Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by the power of God, and they too are weak in him but will live with him by God's power. Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Do you not realise that Jesus Christ is in you?
13.big: Believers are called to examine themselves honestly to see whether they are truly in the faith.
13.diff: Self-examination is meant to lead to assurance in Christ, not endless anxiety; Paul expects them to find that Christ is in them.

13.ctx: The letter closes with a final appeal and a well-known benediction.
13.mean: Paul says aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
13.big: The letter ends with the whole Trinity: the grace of Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit.
13.diff: Verse 14 is one of the clearest Trinitarian statements in the New Testament and is used as a blessing in churches every week.

1.ctx: The book’s title is its first word in Greek, apokalypsis, ‘unveiling’. See History & setting of Revelation above.
1.mean: ‘This is the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show His servants what must soon come to pass.’ It came through an angel to John, ‘who testifies to everything he saw.’ It is the first book of the Bible to promise a blessing on its readers: ‘Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and obey what is written in it, because the time is near.’
1.big: Revelation is God’s unveiling of Jesus Christ, given to be read aloud in church and obeyed.
1.diff: How to read it. See How to read Revelation: four approaches above. ‘Soon’ and ‘near’. Preterists take these to mean the main events happened soon after John wrote. Others note that the ‘last days’ began with Christ’s first coming (Hebrews 1:2), and that in God’s timing ‘soon’ is measured differently (2 Peter 3:8). Wesley: ‘The things contained in this prophecy did begin to be accomplished shortly after it was given.’ Notice also that the blessing is for those who ‘hear and obey’, not those who decode it.

src.l: John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Revelation 1
‘Revelation, Book of’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

1.ctx: The seven churches lay on a circular road in the province of Asia, in the order a messenger would reach them. Seven is the number of completeness in Revelation, so they also stand for the whole church.
1.mean: ‘Grace and peace to you from Him who is and was and is to come, and from the seven spirits before His throne, and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.’ Then praise: ‘To Him who loves us and has released us from our sins by His blood, who has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father’. ‘Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him—even those who pierced Him.’ ‘“I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God’.
1.big: Grace comes from Father, Spirit and Son; Jesus, who loves us and freed us by his blood, is coming visibly to rule.
1.diff: ‘The seven spirits’ (BSB footnote: ‘Or the sevenfold Spirit’) is usually understood as the Holy Spirit in his fullness (seven being the number of completeness; compare Isaiah 11:2 and Zechariah 4), since grace comes from them alongside the Father and Jesus. Some take them as seven chief angels. Alpha and Omega (the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet) is said here by ‘the Lord God’, and later by Jesus himself (22:13).

src.l: ‘Revelation, Book of’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

1.ctx: ‘The Lord’s day’ is one of the earliest uses of this name for Sunday, the day of the resurrection.
1.mean: John, ‘your brother and partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance’, was on Patmos ‘because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus.’ ‘On the Lord’s day I was in the Spirit’. He saw seven golden lampstands, ‘and among the lampstands was One like the Son of Man’: white hair, blazing eyes, a voice ‘like the roar of many waters’, a sword from his mouth, his face ‘like the sun shining at its brightest.’ John fell as though dead. ‘Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last, the Living One. I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever! And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades.’
1.big: The risen Christ walks among his churches, holds the keys of death, and tells his people not to be afraid.
1.diff: The figure John sees combines Daniel’s ‘one like a son of man’ (Daniel 7:13) with features Daniel gives to God himself, ‘the Ancient of Days’ (white hair, Daniel 7:9), and to a heavenly being (Daniel 10:5–6). ‘The First and the Last’ is God’s own title in Isaiah 44:6. Revelation repeatedly gives Jesus the titles of God.

b: Patmos is a small, rocky island in the Aegean Sea, about 55 km (35 miles) off the coast of what is now Turkey, roughly 12 km long. The phrase ‘because of the word of God and my testimony’ suggests John was there as a punishment, not as a missionary. Early tradition (Irenaeus, Eusebius, Jerome) says he was exiled there in the 14th year of Domitian (about AD 95) and released to return to Ephesus under the emperor Nerva in AD 96.

2.ctx: Each of the seven letters follows a pattern: a title of Christ from the vision of chapter 1, praise, criticism, a call to repent, and a promise ‘to the one who overcomes’.
2.mean: Christ praises the church’s hard work and endurance and its testing of false apostles. ‘But I have this against you: You have abandoned your first love. Therefore, keep in mind how far you have fallen. Repent and perform the deeds you did at first.’ Otherwise, ‘I will come to you and remove your lampstand’. They rightly hate ‘the works of the Nicolaitans’. ‘To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God.’
2.big: Sound doctrine and hard work are not enough if love has gone.
2.diff: ‘First love’ may mean love for Christ, love for one another, or both. A church can be orthodox, busy and loveless, and Christ counts that a fall.

b: Ephesus was the greatest city of the province of Asia, home of the famous temple of Artemis, and the centre of Paul’s longest ministry (Acts 19). By John’s time it also had its first temple to the emperors, built under Domitian, which made it a ‘temple warden’ of the imperial cult. Early tradition says John himself lived and died there. The ‘Nicolaitans’ cannot be identified with certainty; many think they taught that Christians could take part in pagan guild meals and their immorality (compare 2:14–15).

2.ctx: One of only two churches (with Philadelphia) that receives no criticism.
2.mean: ‘These are the words of the First and the Last, who died and returned to life. I know your affliction and your poverty—though you are rich!’ Some slander them, ‘who falsely claim to be Jews, but are in fact a synagogue of Satan.’ ‘Do not fear what you are about to suffer.’ ‘Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.’ ‘The one who overcomes will not be harmed by the second death.’
2.big: Faithfulness unto death is rewarded with life that death cannot touch.
2.diff: ‘A synagogue of Satan’. These words have been misused to justify hatred of Jewish people. In context they describe particular local opponents who were slandering Christians, perhaps informing on them to the authorities; John, himself a Jew, says they are not living up to the name. They are not a statement about Jewish people in general. Christians must reject antisemitism.

b: Smyrna (modern Izmir) was a rich and beautiful port, fiercely loyal to Rome. It was chosen over rival cities to build a temple to the emperor Tiberius (Tacitus, Annals 4.55–56), and statues and dedications to later emperors, Domitian among them, have been found there. Its bishop Polycarp, who had known John, was martyred there in the mid-2nd century. Asked to curse Christ, he answered: ‘Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?’ The account of his death says local Jews joined in the accusations, which may help explain the harsh words about ‘a synagogue of Satan’.

2.ctx: Balaam advised the Moabite king Balak to lure Israel into idolatry and immorality (Numbers 25; 31:16).
2.mean: ‘I know where you live, where the throne of Satan sits, yet you hold fast to My name.’ They did not deny the faith even when ‘My faithful witness Antipas’ was killed. But some ‘hold to the teaching of Balaam’, eating ‘food sacrificed to idols’ and committing ‘sexual immorality’, and some follow the Nicolaitans. ‘Therefore repent!’ ‘To the one who overcomes, I will give the hidden manna. I will also give him a white stone inscribed with a new name’.
2.big: A church can stand firm under persecution and still be compromised from within.
2.diff: The ‘white stone’ has many suggested backgrounds: a token of acquittal in a trial, a ticket of admission to a feast, or an amulet with a secret name. Whatever its exact background, it promises acceptance and a personal relationship with Christ.

hist.t: Pergamum: ‘where the throne of Satan sits’
b: Pergamum was built on a steep hill rising about 300 metres above the plain, crowded with temples: to Athena, Zeus, Dionysus, and Asclepius, the healing god whose symbol was a serpent. Its huge altar of Zeus, excavated by German archaeologists from 1878, now stands in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. It also had a temple honouring Rome and the deified Augustus, a focus of the imperial cult across the province, and it had been the seat of Roman government, where the governor had ‘the right of the sword’ (compare ‘the sharp, double-edged sword’, verse 12).

What is ‘the throne of Satan’? Suggestions include the great altar of Zeus, the cult of Asclepius, or, most likely in the view of many scholars, the imperial cult and Roman power, which had already cost Antipas his life.

2.ctx: Thyatira was a trade town known for its guilds, including dyers and wool-workers (Lydia, ‘a dealer in purple cloth’, came from there, Acts 16:14). Guild membership involved feasts in honour of pagan gods.
2.mean: Christ praises their growing love, faith, service and perseverance. ‘But I have this against you: You tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess.’ She teaches believers ‘to be sexually immoral and to eat food sacrificed to idols.’ She has had time to repent and refused; judgement will come, so ‘all the churches will know that I am the One who searches minds and hearts’. To the rest: ‘hold fast to what you have until I come.’
2.big: Christ searches hearts, and will not tolerate teaching that makes compromise with idolatry respectable.
2.diff: ‘Jezebel’ is probably a nickname, recalling Ahab’s queen who led Israel into Baal worship (1 Kings 16–21). The issue is not that a woman prophesied (compare Acts 21:9), but what she taught.

3.ctx: See Sardis: caught off guard below.
3.mean: ‘You have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead. Wake up and strengthen what remains’. ‘If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know the hour’. A few ‘have not soiled their garments’; they ‘will walk with Me in white.’ ‘And I will never blot out his name from the Book of Life, but I will confess his name before My Father and His angels.’
3.big: A church can have a lively reputation and be spiritually dead; Christ calls it to wake up.
3.diff: ‘I will never blot out his name’ (verse 5) is a promise. Reformed readers take it as assurance that true believers will never be lost. Arminian readers take it to imply that a name could be removed from someone who does not overcome. Both take the promise as encouragement to persevere.

b: Sardis had been the capital of the wealthy kingdom of Lydia, with a citadel on a high, steep hill thought impossible to capture. Yet in 546 BC Cyrus of Persia took it by surprise, after a defender who dropped his helmet gave away a secret way up. It was captured again by Antiochus III in about 213 BC. ‘To capture the acropolis of Sardis’ became a saying for doing the impossible. Christ’s warning, ‘If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief’, would have stung. The church seems to have taken it to heart: in the 2nd century its bishop Melito was a respected Christian writer.

3.ctx: ‘The key of David’ echoes Isaiah 22:22, where authority over the royal palace is given to a faithful steward.
3.mean: ‘I have placed before you an open door, which no one can shut. I know that you have only a little strength, yet you have kept My word and have not denied My name.’ Their opponents will one day acknowledge ‘that I love you.’ ‘Because you have kept My command to persevere, I will also keep you from the hour of testing that is about to come upon the whole world’. ‘The one who overcomes I will make a pillar in the temple of My God, and he will never again leave it.’
3.big: Christ opens doors for weak but faithful believers, and keeps them.
3.diff: ‘Keep you from the hour of testing’ (verse 10). Dispensational futurists read this as a promise that the church will be removed from the earth (the ‘rapture’) before a future seven-year tribulation. Dallas Theological Seminary’s doctrinal statement, for example, teaches that ‘the translation of the church will be followed by the fulfillment of Israel’s seventieth week’. Most other interpreters (amillennial, postmillennial and historic premillennial) read it as a promise to protect believers through trial, not to remove them from it; Jesus uses the same Greek phrase, ‘keep… from’, when he prays not that the Father would take his disciples out of the world but keep them from the evil one (John 17:15). Wesley, in his day, read it as an exemption for that church: ‘O happy exemption from that spreading calamity!’

hist.t: Philadelphia and the earthquake of AD 17
b: Philadelphia was a smaller city on a major road east, in an earthquake zone. A great earthquake in AD 17 devastated it along with Sardis and other cities; the emperor Tiberius remitted their taxes for five years so they could rebuild (Tacitus, Annals 2.47). To a city that had been shaken apart, the promise ‘I will make a pillar in the temple of My God, and he will never again leave it’ would have meant a great deal.

3.ctx: The only church with nothing good said about it. See Laodicea: rich, lukewarm and blind below.
3.mean: ‘These are the words of the Amen, the faithful and true Witness, the Originator of God’s creation. I know your deeds; you are neither cold nor hot.’ ‘So because you are lukewarm—neither hot nor cold—I am about to vomit you out of My mouth!’ ‘You say, “I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing.” But you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked.’ Christ offers true gold, white clothes and eye salve. ‘Those I love I rebuke and discipline.’ ‘Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me.’
3.big: Self-satisfied religion is useless to Christ, yet he still knocks, offering everything they lack.
3.diff: ‘The Originator of God’s creation’ (BSB footnote: ‘Or Beginning or Ruler’). Jehovah’s Witnesses translate ‘the beginning of the creation by God’ and take it to mean Jesus was the first thing God created. The Greek word archē can mean beginning, origin or ruler; the historic reading is that Christ is the source and ruler of creation (compare John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). Wesley: ‘The Author, Prince, and Ruler’. ‘I stand at the door and knock’ is often used in evangelism, and rightly expresses Christ’s invitation; in context it is addressed to a church that has shut him out.

b: Laodicea was a wealthy banking centre, known for its textiles and wool and for a medical school famous for treating eyes. When an earthquake destroyed it in AD 60, it ‘recovered by its own resources’, refusing help from Rome (Tacitus, Annals 14.27). That background gives force to ‘I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing’, and to Christ’s offer of gold, ‘white garments’ and ‘salve to anoint your eyes’.

Many scholars link ‘neither cold nor hot’ to the city’s water, which came by aqueduct and arrived lukewarm, unlike the hot springs of nearby Hierapolis (useful for healing) and the cold water of Colossae (refreshing). On this reading the point is not ‘cold’ = hostile, ‘hot’ = keen, but that Laodicea was useful for nothing. Others (for example Craig Koester) question this background. The overall point is clear either way.

4.ctx: The scene moves from earth to heaven. Before anything is shown of the troubles to come, John is shown who is in control.
4.mean: John sees ‘a door standing open in heaven’. ‘Come up here, and I will show you what must happen after these things.’ ‘I saw a throne standing in heaven, with someone seated on it.’ The One on it shines like precious stones, encircled by a rainbow like an emerald. Around the throne are twenty-four other thrones, with ‘twenty-four elders dressed in white, with golden crowns on their heads.’
4.big: Before showing the storms of history, God shows his people his throne.
4.diff: The twenty-four elders are usually understood as representing the whole people of God, Old Testament and New: twelve tribes and twelve apostles (compare 21:12–14). Some take them as angelic beings. ‘Come up here’ is read by some dispensational interpreters as a picture of the rapture of the church before the tribulation. Most interpreters see it simply as John being taken up in the Spirit to receive the vision.
