F. F. Bruce, ‘Egyptian, The’ and ‘Ananias’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.

22.ctx: Paul’s second telling of his conversion (compare 9:1–19; 26:9–18), shaped for a Jewish audience.
22.mean: Paul stresses his Jewish credentials: born in Tarsus, ‘raised in this city’, ‘educated at the feet of Gamaliel in strict conformity to the law of our fathers’, zealous for God, a persecutor of ‘this Way’. He tells of the light at noon, the voice, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting’, and Ananias, ‘a devout observer of the law’, who said: ‘Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.’ Later, praying in the temple, the Lord told him to leave Jerusalem: ‘Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’ At that word the crowd explodes: ‘Rid the earth of him! He is not fit to live!’
22.big: Paul’s life story shows that the risen Jesus turned a zealous persecutor into his witness to the Gentiles.
22.diff: ‘Be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name’ (verse 16) is read like 2:38: by some as baptism conveying cleansing, by others as baptism picturing the cleansing received by calling on Christ in faith.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

22.ctx: Flogging with the scourge was a brutal way of extracting information. Roman citizens were legally protected from it without trial. Citizenship could be inherited, granted, or in practice bought.
22.mean: The commander orders Paul to be flogged and interrogated. As they strap him down, Paul asks the centurion, ‘Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen without a trial?’ The commander comes: ‘I paid a high price for my citizenship.’ ‘But I was born a citizen,’ Paul replies. The interrogators step back; the commander is alarmed at having chained a Roman citizen. Next day he brings Paul before the Sanhedrin to discover the real charge.
22.big: Paul uses his legal rights wisely, and his citizenship protects him for the journey to Rome.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

23.ctx: Ananias son of Nedebaeus was high priest about AD 47–58, notorious for greed. Sadducees denied the resurrection, angels and spirits; Pharisees affirmed them.
23.mean: Paul begins: ‘I have conducted myself before God in all good conscience to this day.’ The high priest Ananias orders him struck. Paul flares: ‘God will strike you, you whitewashed wall!’ Told he has insulted the high priest, he says, ‘I was not aware that he was the high priest’, and quotes Exodus 22:28. Then, seeing the council divided, he calls out: ‘I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee. It is because of my hope in the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.’ The Pharisees and Sadducees fall out, some Pharisees defend him, and the commander has to rescue him again. That night ‘the Lord stood near Paul and said, “Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome.”’
23.big: In the middle of conflict and danger, the Lord stands by Paul and promises he will testify in Rome.
23.diff: Why Paul did not recognise the high priest is unclear: poor eyesight, an informal meeting, or irony (‘I did not think a man acting like that could be the high priest’). Opinions differ on whether his appeal to the resurrection was shrewd or questionable; it was true, since the resurrection of Jesus was the heart of the dispute. Luke reports it without comment.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL
F. F. Bruce, ‘Egyptian, The’ and ‘Ananias’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.

23.ctx: Oath-bound assassination plots were not unknown in this troubled period.
23.mean: More than forty men swear not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul, and ask the council to request another hearing so they can ambush him on the way. ‘But when the son of Paul’s sister heard about the plot, he went into the barracks and told Paul.’ Paul sends him to the commander, who listens and tells him to keep it quiet.
23.big: God protects Paul through an ordinary young man’s courage and a Roman officer’s care.
23.diff: This is the only mention of Paul’s family in Acts, and suggests relatives living in Jerusalem.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

23.ctx: Caesarea was the Roman capital of Judea and the governor’s residence. Antipatris was about halfway there.
23.mean: The commander sends Paul by night to Caesarea under a heavy escort: two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen. His letter, from ‘Claudius Lysias, To His Excellency, Governor Felix’, states that Paul is a Roman citizen and that the charges concern Jewish law, with ‘no charge worthy of death or imprisonment.’ (He tactfully says he rescued Paul because he learned he was a citizen; in fact he found out later.) Felix agrees to hear the case and keeps Paul in Herod’s praetorium.
23.big: A Roman officer’s report declares Paul innocent of any capital crime.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

24.ctx: Tertullus was a professional advocate. See the drop-down on Felix and the officials of chapters 24–26.
24.mean: The high priest Ananias comes with elders and the lawyer Tertullus. He opens with flattery of Felix: ‘Because of you, we have enjoyed a lasting peace’. Then the charges: Paul is ‘a pestilence, stirring up dissension among the Jews all over the world. He is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, and he even tried to desecrate the temple’.
24.big: Paul is accused of being a troublemaker, a sect leader and a temple-defiler.
24.diff: The flattery was hollow: Felix’s rule was harsh and his time in office troubled. Verses 6b–8a (Lysias taking Paul by force) are not in the earliest manuscripts (BSB footnote).

hist.t: Felix, Drusilla, Festus, Agrippa and Bernice (chs. 24–26)
b: The officials Paul faced are all known from Roman and Jewish historians. Felix, governor about AD 52–59, was a freed slave whose brother Pallas was a favourite at court. The Roman historian Tacitus wrote that he ‘exercised the powers of a king with the disposition of a slave’; his rule was harsh and corrupt, which fits his hope for a bribe (24:26). His wife Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I. Ananias, high priest about AD 47–58, was notorious for his greed and was killed by Jewish rebels in AD 66.

Porcius Festus succeeded Felix, probably in AD 59, and died in office about two years later; Josephus contrasts him favourably with his predecessor and successor. King Agrippa II, son of Agrippa I, ruled territories north and northeast of Palestine and from AD 48 to 66 had the right to appoint the Jewish high priests; Bernice was his sister. He later tried to prevent the Jewish war against Rome in AD 66. Luke presents each of them in a way consistent with what other sources say.

src.l: ‘Felix’ and ‘Festus’ (E. M. B. Green & C. J. Hemer), New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.
F. F. Bruce, ‘Herod’; J. D. Douglas, ‘Drusilla’; F. F. Bruce, ‘Assassins’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.
F. F. Bruce, ‘Egyptian, The’ and ‘Ananias’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.
Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL
‘Felix’ and ‘Festus’ (E. M. B. Green & C. J. Hemer), New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.

24.ctx: Felix had governed for several years, so knew the situation.
24.mean: Paul answers point by point. He came to Jerusalem only twelve days ago to worship; no one found him arguing or stirring up crowds; they cannot prove their charges. ‘I do confess to you, however, that I worship the God of our fathers according to the Way, which they call a sect. I believe everything that is laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, and I have the same hope in God that they themselves cherish, that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.’ He came ‘to bring alms to my people’ and was found ceremonially clean in the temple. The only charge they could bring is the resurrection.
24.big: Paul’s faith in Jesus is the fulfilment of Israel’s own Scriptures and hope of resurrection, not a betrayal of them.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

24.ctx: Drusilla, born about AD 38, was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I; Felix had persuaded her to leave her first husband, King Azizus of Emesa, and marry him.
24.mean: Felix, ‘well informed about the Way’, postpones the case and gives Paul some freedom. Later, with his wife Drusilla, he sends for Paul to hear about faith in Christ Jesus. ‘As Paul expounded on righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and said, “You may go for now. When I find the time, I will call for you.”’ He was also hoping for a bribe. ‘After two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.’
24.big: Felix is moved by the gospel but puts off a decision, and two years pass.
24.diff: Felix is the clearest biblical picture of someone interested in the gospel who will not act on it. ‘When I find the time’ is one of the most dangerous phrases in the Bible.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL
‘Felix’ and ‘Festus’ (E. M. B. Green & C. J. Hemer), New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.

25.ctx: Festus arrived as governor, probably in AD 59.
25.mean: Three days after arriving, Festus goes to Jerusalem. The leaders ask him to transfer Paul to Jerusalem, planning an ambush. Festus refuses and hears the case in Caesarea. The accusers bring ‘many serious charges that they could not prove.’ Paul: ‘I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews or against the temple or against Caesar.’
25.big: Two years on, the charges against Paul are still unproven.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL
‘Felix’ and ‘Festus’ (E. M. B. Green & C. J. Hemer), New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.

25.ctx: A Roman citizen could appeal to be tried by the emperor (at this time Nero, before his persecution of Christians began).
25.mean: Festus, ‘wishing to do the Jews a favor’, asks Paul if he will go to Jerusalem for trial. Paul refuses: ‘I am standing before the judgment seat of Caesar, where I ought to be tried. I have done nothing wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well. If, however, I am guilty of anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die.…I appeal to Caesar!’ Festus confers and replies: ‘You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!’
25.big: Paul’s appeal to Caesar, a legal right, becomes the means of fulfilling the Lord’s promise that he would testify in Rome.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

25.ctx: Agrippa II was the last of the Herodian kings, with expert knowledge of Jewish affairs.
25.mean: King Agrippa and Bernice visit Festus, who lays out the case. The accusers did not bring the crimes he expected: ‘They only had some contentions with him regarding their own religion and a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive.’ Agrippa wants to hear Paul himself.
25.big: To a Roman governor, the whole dispute comes down to one question: is Jesus, who died, alive?
25.diff: Festus’s summary (‘a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive’) puts the heart of the matter more clearly than he knew.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL
F. F. Bruce, ‘Herod’; J. D. Douglas, ‘Drusilla’; F. F. Bruce, ‘Assassins’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.

25.ctx: A grand public hearing in Caesarea.
25.mean: Agrippa and Bernice enter ‘with great pomp’, with military commanders and leading citizens. Festus explains that he found Paul ‘had done nothing worthy of death’, but needs something definite to write to the emperor.
25.big: A prisoner in chains stands before the powerful, and the pomp of the room cannot hide that he is innocent.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

26.ctx: The third account of Paul’s conversion in Acts, the fullest on his commission.
26.mean: Paul is glad to speak to Agrippa, who knows Jewish customs. He lived as a Pharisee, and is on trial for the hope of Israel: ‘Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?’ He describes his fury against the believers, then the light on the road and the voice: ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’ (Like an ox kicking against a prodding stick, he was resisting the one driving him.) Jesus appointed him ‘as a servant and as a witness’, sending him to the Gentiles ‘to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.’ ‘So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.’ He preached that people ‘should repent and turn to God, performing deeds worthy of their repentance.’ It is all what Moses and the prophets said: ‘that the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.’
26.big: Jesus sends Paul to open blind eyes, turning people from darkness to light and from Satan to God, for forgiveness through faith.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

26.ctx: To a Roman like Festus, resurrection talk sounded absurd.
26.mean: Festus shouts: ‘You are insane, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness!’ Paul: ‘I am not insane…I am speaking words of truth and sobriety.’ These events were ‘not done in a corner.’ ‘King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.’ Agrippa: ‘Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?’ Paul: ‘Short time or long…I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am, except for these chains.’ Leaving, they agree: ‘This man has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.’ ‘This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.’
26.big: Paul’s deepest wish, even for his judges, is that they would become Christians.
26.diff: Agrippa’s reply may be sarcastic, or a half-serious deflection; the older translation ‘Almost thou persuadest me’ is less likely. Paul’s response, ‘except for these chains’, is among the most gracious lines in Acts. ‘Not done in a corner’: Christianity rests on public events that could be checked.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

27.ctx: The ‘we’ narrative resumes: Luke is on board. See the drop-down on the voyage.
27.mean: Paul and other prisoners are handed to Julius, a centurion of the Imperial Regiment. Aristarchus from Thessalonica is with them. At Sidon, ‘Julius treated Paul with consideration, allowing him to visit his friends’. Against contrary winds they reach Myra, transfer to an Alexandrian grain ship bound for Italy, and struggle to Fair Havens on Crete. ‘By now much time had passed, and the voyage had already become dangerous because it was after the Fast.’
27.big: Paul begins the long journey to Rome, as a prisoner but treated with respect.

b: Luke’s account of the voyage is one of the most detailed descriptions of ancient seafaring to survive. F. F. Bruce called it ‘one of our most important documents on ancient seamanship’, and James Smith’s classic study The Voyage and Shipwreck of St Paul (1848) traced the route in detail. Luke notes the sailing season (‘after the Fast’, the Day of Atonement in the autumn, when sailing became dangerous; BSB footnote), the northeast gale (Euraquilo), the undergirding of the ship, the soundings, and the anchors dropped from the stern.

The traditional site of the shipwreck is St Paul’s Bay on Malta, northwest of Valletta, and many scholars accept it, though others have been proposed. On Malta, Luke calls the governor Publius ‘the chief official of the island’ (Greek prōtos, ‘first man’), a title found in inscriptions from Malta.

src.l: B. F. Harris, ‘Malta’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.
F. F. Bruce, ‘Acts, Book of the’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.
Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL
B. F. Harris, ‘Malta’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.

27.ctx: The Syrtis were dangerous sandbanks off the coast of North Africa (modern Libya).
27.mean: Paul warns against sailing on, but the centurion follows the pilot and the owner. A gentle south wind tempts them out, then ‘a cyclone called the Northeaster swept down across the island.’ The ship is driven helplessly. They undergird the hull, lower the sea anchor, throw cargo and tackle overboard. ‘When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the great storm continued to batter us, we abandoned all hope of being saved.’ Then Paul stands up: an angel of ‘the God to whom I belong and whom I serve’ told him, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And look, God has granted you the lives of all who sail with you.’ ‘So take courage, men, for I believe God that it will happen just as He told me.’
27.big: When everyone has given up hope, Paul’s trust in God’s word gives courage to all.
27.diff: Luke’s nautical detail matches what is known of ancient seafaring and is often cited as evidence that he was an eyewitness (see the drop-down).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL
F. F. Bruce, ‘Acts, Book of the’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.

27.ctx: ‘The Adriatic Sea’ then included the central Mediterranean south of Italy.
27.mean: On the fourteenth night, soundings show land is near. They drop four anchors and pray for daylight. The sailors try to escape in the lifeboat, but Paul tells the centurion, ‘Unless these men remain with the ship, you cannot be saved.’ The soldiers cut it loose. At dawn Paul urges everyone to eat; he takes bread, gives thanks to God before them all, breaks it and eats, and all are encouraged. There are 276 on board. They run for a beach, but the ship strikes a sandbar and breaks up. The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them. ‘In this way everyone was brought safely to land.’
27.big: God keeps his promise, and every one of the 276 reaches land, as Paul said.
27.diff: God’s promise (verse 24) and the practical means (staying with the ship, verse 31) are held together, as often in Scripture: God’s sovereignty does not make human action pointless. Paul’s breaking of bread with thanksgiving before pagans was probably an ordinary meal, though Luke’s words echo the Lord’s Supper.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

28.ctx: Malta lies south of Sicily. ‘Justice’ (Greek Dikē) was the Greek goddess of justice (BSB footnote). Publius’s title, ‘first man’, is attested in Maltese inscriptions (see the voyage drop-down at 27:1).
28.mean: The islanders show ‘extraordinary kindness’, lighting a fire in the rain and cold. As Paul puts sticks on the fire, a viper fastens on his hand. The islanders conclude he must be a murderer whom Justice has caught. He shakes it into the fire and suffers no harm; they change their minds and say he is a god. Publius, ‘the chief official of the island’, welcomes them; Paul prays for his father, sick with fever and dysentery, lays hands on him and heals him, and the rest of the sick on the island come and are cured.
28.big: Shipwrecked strangers receive kindness, and God brings healing to a whole island through his servant.
28.diff: This episode is sometimes used, with Mark 16:18, to justify deliberately handling snakes, which most Christians reject as testing God (Matthew 4:7). Paul did not seek out the snake.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL
B. F. Harris, ‘Malta’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.

28.ctx: The Appian Way led to Rome; the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns were stopping points about 43 and 35 miles from Rome (BSB footnotes). The ship’s figurehead was the ‘Twin Brothers’, Castor and Pollux, patrons of sailors (BSB footnote).
28.mean: After three months they sail on an Alexandrian ship, via Syracuse and Rhegium, to Puteoli, where they find believers and stay a week. ‘And so we came to Rome.’ Believers from Rome come out along the Appian Way to meet them. ‘When Paul saw them, he was encouraged and gave thanks to God.’
28.big: The gospel is already in Rome before Paul arrives, and the believers there welcome and encourage him.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL

28.ctx: Paul is under house arrest, chained to a soldier, but free to receive visitors. Philippians, Colossians, Ephesians and Philemon may have been written in this period.
28.mean: Paul calls the Jewish leaders in Rome: he has done nothing against his people; ‘It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.’ They have heard nothing against him personally, but know the ‘sect’ is spoken against everywhere. On an appointed day many come, and ‘He expounded to them from morning to evening, testifying about the kingdom of God and persuading them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets.’ Some are convinced, others not. Paul quotes Isaiah 6: ‘You will be ever hearing but never understanding’, and says that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, ‘and they will listen!’ Acts ends: ‘Paul stayed there two full years in his own rented house, welcoming all who came to visit him. Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ.’
28.big: Acts ends with the gospel proclaimed boldly and freely at the heart of the empire, the story still open.
28.diff: Why does Acts end without telling us the outcome of Paul’s trial? Some think Luke wrote at that point (about AD 62); others that the open ending is deliberate: the gospel has reached Rome ‘unhindered’, and the story continues in the church. Paul attributes Isaiah’s words to the Holy Spirit (verse 25), where Isaiah 6 says the Lord spoke them, another sign that the Spirit is God. Verse 29 is not in the earliest manuscripts (BSB omits it).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Acts, vol. 2 (chs. 14–28), CCEL
F. F. Bruce, ‘Acts, Book of the’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed.

1.ctx: Genealogies mattered in Israel: they established identity, inheritance and the right to an office. Matthew’s opening words echo Genesis (‘the book of the generations’, Genesis 2:4; 5:1).
1.mean: ‘This is the record of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham’: heir of the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed, and of the promise to David of an everlasting king. Matthew arranges the line in three sets of fourteen: Abraham to David, David to the exile, the exile to the Christ. History has been moving towards Jesus. Surprisingly, he names four women besides Mary: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and ‘Uriah’s wife’. All had irregular stories, and most were Gentiles. The line ends carefully: ‘Jacob the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.’
1.big: Jesus is the goal of Israel’s history, the promised son of Abraham and David; and God worked his purpose through Gentiles and sinners as well as kings.
1.diff: Matthew’s and Luke’s lists. From David to Joseph, Matthew’s list (through Solomon and the kings) differs almost completely from Luke’s (through David’s son Nathan, Luke 3:23–38). Three main explanations are offered. Many think Matthew gives the legal, royal line of succession and Luke the actual descent, perhaps through Mary. J. G. Machen suggested that if Joseph’s father in Matthew (Jacob) died childless, his nephew Joseph, son of Heli (Luke), became his heir. Julius Africanus (about AD 230) explained it by a levirate marriage, a tradition he said came from Jesus’ relatives. Matthew’s fourteens also leave out several kings (for example three between Joram and Uzziah), a normal practice in genealogies, which recorded descent, not every generation. Both lists agree on the main point: Jesus was the legal heir of David through Joseph.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 1:1–17 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
F. F. Bruce, ‘Genealogy of Jesus Christ’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996), citing Machen and Julius Africanus (Eusebius, Church History 1.7)

1.ctx: Jewish marriage had two stages: a binding betrothal (‘pledged in marriage’), which could only be ended by divorce, and, some months later, the wife moving into her husband’s home. Unfaithfulness during betrothal counted as adultery.
1.mean: Before they came together, Mary ‘was found to be with child through the Holy Spirit.’ Joseph, ‘a righteous man’ who did not want to shame her publicly, decides to divorce her quietly. An angel tells him in a dream: ‘do not be afraid to embrace Mary as your wife, for the One conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.’ ‘you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins.’ (Jesus, Hebrew Yeshua, means ‘The LORD saves’.) Matthew sees this fulfilling Isaiah 7:14: ‘Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel’ (which means, ‘God with us’). Joseph obeys, takes Mary home, and names the child.
1.big: Jesus is God with us, conceived by the Holy Spirit, and he came to save his people from their sins.
1.diff: ‘Virgin’ in Isaiah 7:14. The Hebrew word almah means a young woman of marriageable age; the Greek Old Testament Matthew quotes uses parthenos, ‘virgin’. Many scholars think Isaiah’s sign had a first fulfilment in his own day (Isaiah 7:16) and that Matthew sees its full meaning in Jesus. Christians agree that the Spirit-given conception is what Matthew narrates, whatever the word in Isaiah. ‘Until’ (verse 25). Joseph ‘had no union with her until she gave birth’. Most Protestants take this to imply normal married life afterwards. Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold Mary’s perpetual virginity, and the New Bible Dictionary notes that ‘The Reformers were virtually unanimous’ in holding it too: Calvin said ‘no just and well-grounded inference can be drawn from these words of the Evangelist, as to what took place after the birth of Christ’, and Wesley likewise: ‘It cannot be inferred from hence, that he knew her afterward’. See the note on Mark 6:1.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 1:18–25 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 1
D. F. Wright and J. S. Wright, ‘Virgin Birth’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)
‘Matthew, Gospel of’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
Catechism of the Catholic Church 499–501 (Mary’s virginity; the ‘brothers’ of Jesus)

2.ctx: ‘Magi’ were a priestly and learned class from Persia or Babylon, known for interpreting dreams and the stars. Herod the Great, an Idumean installed by Rome, was notoriously jealous of any rival. Micah 5:2 named Bethlehem, David’s town, as the Messiah’s birthplace.
2.mean: After Jesus’ birth in Bethlehem, Magi arrive in Jerusalem asking, ‘Where is the One who has been born King of the Jews? We saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him.’ Herod is disturbed, ‘and all Jerusalem with him.’ The chief priests and scribes know the answer from Micah: Bethlehem. Herod secretly finds out when the star appeared and sends the Magi on, pretending he wants to worship too. The star goes ahead of them to the place, and they rejoice. ‘On coming to the house, they saw the Child with His mother Mary, and they fell down and worshiped Him’, offering gold, frankincense and myrrh. Warned in a dream, they go home another way.
2.big: Gentile seekers come to worship the King of the Jews, while Israel’s king plots against him and its scholars, who know where he is, do not go.
2.diff: Tradition later called the Magi three kings (from three gifts and Psalm 72:10) and gave them names; Matthew says neither. They found Jesus in ‘the house’, not the stable, possibly months later (compare 2:16, ‘two years old and under’). Many have seen meaning in the gifts: gold for a king, incense for worship, myrrh for burial.

hist.t: The star and the date of Jesus’ birth
b: When? Herod the Great died in 4 BC, and Jesus was born before that, probably about 6–4 BC. Our ‘AD’ numbering, worked out centuries later, placed his birth a few years too late. (See also the notes on Luke 2.)

What was the star? Suggestions include a conjunction of the planets Jupiter and Saturn in 7 BC and a short-lived new star recorded by Chinese astronomers in 4 BC. The New Bible Dictionary notes these possible confirmations but says they must be applied with caution. A star that ‘stood over the place’ suggests to many something beyond a natural event. Matthew’s interest is not astronomy but that God drew Gentiles to his Son.

Is the story history? Some scholars doubt it, because no other source mentions the Magi or the killing of the children. Others reply that the account is entirely in keeping with Herod’s character and with the expectation of a royal Messiah, and that its symbolic meaning does not count against its historicity.

‘Herod the Great’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 2:1–6 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
E. E. Ellis, ‘Magi’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

2.ctx: Egypt had a large Jewish population, especially in Alexandria, and had long been a refuge (1 Kings 11:40; Jeremiah 43).
2.mean: An angel warns Joseph in a dream: ‘Take the Child and His mother and flee to Egypt’, because Herod will search for him to kill him. Joseph goes that night and stays until Herod dies. Matthew sees Hosea 11:1 fulfilled: ‘Out of Egypt I called My Son.’ In Hosea those words were about Israel, God’s ‘son’, brought out of Egypt in the exodus. Jesus relives Israel’s story, as the true Son who will be faithful where Israel failed.
2.big: Jesus sums up Israel’s history in himself; even as a refugee child he is under his Father’s care.
2.diff: ‘Fulfilled’. Hosea 11:1 is not a prediction but a memory. Matthew uses ‘fulfil’ in a broad sense: patterns in Israel’s history (typology) reach their fullest meaning in Jesus. Christian interpreters of every tradition read Matthew’s quotations this way.

2.ctx: Bethlehem was a small village, so the number of children killed may have been small. Rachel, Jacob’s wife, was buried near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19). Jeremiah 31:15 pictured her weeping over her descendants taken into exile.
2.mean: Furious at being outwitted, Herod has all the boys in and around Bethlehem two years old and under killed. Matthew quotes Jeremiah: ‘A voice is heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.’ In Jeremiah the lament is followed at once by hope: God promises restoration and a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:16–34).
2.big: The coming of the King provokes violence against the innocent; God does not hide the grief, but sets it within the story of his promised rescue.

hist.t: Herod and the killing of the children
b: No source outside Matthew records the massacre, and some scholars doubt it for that reason. But it fits what Josephus tells us of Herod in his last years: paranoid about rivals, he had his wife Mariamme and several of his sons killed, and as he was dying ordered leading men to be executed so that there would be mourning at his death. The killing of perhaps a few infants in a village would hardly have been noticed by historians recording such atrocities.

2.ctx: When Herod died in 4 BC, Augustus divided his kingdom: Archelaus got Judea, Samaria and Idumea; Herod Antipas got Galilee.
2.mean: After Herod’s death an angel tells Joseph to return. But hearing that Archelaus rules Judea, he is afraid, and, warned in a dream, settles in Galilee, ‘in a town called Nazareth. So was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophets: ‘He will be called a Nazarene.’’
2.big: God guides his Son’s family step by step, and even Jesus’ obscure home town carries meaning.
2.diff: ‘He will be called a Nazarene’ is not found word for word in the Old Testament, and Matthew says ‘the prophets’ (plural). Many think it is a wordplay on Isaiah 11:1, where the Messiah is the ‘branch’ (Hebrew netser) from Jesse’s roots; others think it sums up prophecies that the Messiah would be despised, since Nazareth was an insignificant place (John 1:46).

b: Archelaus ruled Judea from 4 BC with a brutality that matched his father’s worst. Josephus records that in the tenth year of his rule the leading Jews and Samaritans, ‘not being able to bear his barbarous and tyrannical usage of them’, accused him before Augustus, who banished him to Vienne in Gaul (AD 6). Judea then came under direct Roman governors, including later Pontius Pilate. Joseph’s fear was well founded.

3.h: The Mission of John the Baptist
3.ctx: Matthew usually says ‘kingdom of heaven’ where the other Gospels say ‘kingdom of God’; devout Jews avoided saying God’s name. The Pharisees and Sadducees were the two leading religious parties.
3.mean: John preaches in the Judean wilderness: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.’ He is Isaiah’s voice in the wilderness. Crowds come, confess their sins and are baptised. When Pharisees and Sadducees come, he calls them a ‘brood of vipers’: ‘Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance.’ Descent from Abraham will not save them; ‘out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham.’ ‘The axe lies ready at the root of the trees’. One is coming who ‘will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire’, who will gather the wheat and burn the chaff.
3.big: No religious pedigree can substitute for a changed life; the coming one brings both the Spirit and judgment.

b: Josephus calls him ‘John, that was called the Baptist’, ‘a good man’ who urged the Jews to practise righteousness and piety and to come to baptism, and records that Herod Antipas had him executed (see 14:1–12).

3.ctx: Only Matthew records John’s protest.
3.mean: Jesus comes to be baptised; John tries to stop him: ‘I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?’ Jesus replies, ‘Let it be so now’, ‘It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness in this way.’ As he comes up from the water, the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice says, ‘This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!’
3.big: Jesus takes his place with sinners in obedience to the Father, and the Father and Spirit publicly affirm him.
3.diff: See the note on Mark 1:1 for why the sinless Jesus was baptised. Calvin’s summary: he received baptism ‘that he might render full obedience to the Father’, and ‘that he might consecrate baptism in his own body, that we might have it in common with him’.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 3:13–17 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

4.ctx: All three of Jesus’ replies quote Deuteronomy 6–8, where Moses recalls Israel’s forty years of testing in the wilderness.
4.mean: Led by the Spirit into the wilderness, Jesus fasts forty days and is hungry. The devil tempts him three times. ‘If You are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.’ Jesus: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’ On the temple pinnacle, quoting Psalm 91: throw yourself down. Jesus: ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’ On a high mountain, all the world’s kingdoms, ‘if You will fall down and worship me.’ ‘Away from Me, Satan!’ ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’ The devil leaves, and angels serve him.
4.big: Where Israel failed in the wilderness, Jesus the true Son trusts and obeys his Father, using Scripture as his weapon.

4.ctx: Zebulun and Naphtali were the northern tribes first conquered by Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). ‘Galilee of the Gentiles’ had a mixed population.
4.mean: When John is imprisoned, Jesus moves from Nazareth to Capernaum. Matthew sees Isaiah 9:1–2 fulfilled: the region that first fell into darkness is the first to see the light. ‘the people living in darkness have seen a great light’. ‘From that time on Jesus began to preach, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.”’
4.big: The light of the Messiah dawns first on the despised, mixed region of Galilee.

b: Capernaum, on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, was a small fishing town on the road to Damascus, with a tax post (compare Mark 2:14). A Roman milestone was found near the synagogue. The white limestone synagogue visitors see today dates from the 4th or 5th century AD (about 10,000 coins were found beneath its floor), but it stands on the foundations of an earlier one, probably the synagogue of Jesus’ day (compare Luke 7:5).

Just south of it is an octagonal church built over the walls of an earlier house. The excavators believe this was Peter’s house (Mark 1:29), venerated by Christians from early times; Italian archaeologists report the name Peter among graffiti scratched on its walls. The identification is reasonable but cannot be proved.

src.l: ‘Capernaum’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Shanks and Cole)
‘Capernaum’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Shanks and Cole)

4.ctx: See the note on Mark 1:16 for fishing on the lake.
4.mean: Jesus sees Simon called Peter and Andrew casting a net: ‘Come, follow Me,’ ‘and I will make you fishers of men.’ ‘And at once they left their nets and followed Him.’ Then James and John leave the boat and their father.
4.big: Jesus’ call takes priority over work and family.

4.ctx: ‘Syria’ here means the wider Roman province to the north; the Decapolis was Gentile territory.
4.mean: Jesus goes throughout Galilee ‘teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness among the people.’ His fame spreads, and crowds come from every direction with the sick, the demon-possessed, those with seizures and the paralysed, ‘and He healed them.’
4.big: Teaching, preaching and healing: in Jesus’ ministry the kingdom is announced in word and shown in deed.

5.ctx: Matthew gathers Jesus’ teaching into five great discourses (chapters 5–7, 10, 13, 18, 24–25), each ending ‘When Jesus had finished…’. Moses received the Law on a mountain; Jesus teaches from one.
5.mean: Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up the mountain and sits down, as Jewish teachers did. His disciples come to him, and he teaches them. The sermon that follows (chapters 5–7) describes life in the kingdom of heaven.
5.big: The Sermon on the Mount is Jesus’ picture of the life of those who belong to his kingdom.
5.diff: How should the Sermon be read? Christians have read it in several ways. The New Bible Dictionary describes it as ‘a character sketch of those who have already entered the kingdom’, not a way to earn entry, and warns against ‘crude literalism’ with its deliberately extreme sayings. The Anabaptist tradition (Mennonites, Amish, Hutterites) takes its commands, such as non-resistance and refusing oaths, as direct rules for the church. Catholic teaching calls the Sermon the expression of the ‘New Law’, ‘the grace of the Holy Spirit given to the faithful through faith in Christ’ (Catechism 1965–1966). All agree it shows what God’s people are meant to be.

5.ctx: ‘Blessed’ (Greek makarios) describes those who are truly well off in God’s eyes, whatever their circumstances.
5.mean: Jesus pronounces God’s blessing on unlikely people. ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.’ Those who know they have nothing to offer God receive everything. Blessed are those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those persecuted for righteousness. Each receives a promise: comfort, the earth, satisfaction, mercy, the sight of God, the name ‘sons of God’, the kingdom. ‘Blessed are you when people insult you, persecute you, and falsely say all kinds of evil against you because of Me. Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven’.
5.big: God’s kingdom turns the world’s values upside down: it belongs to the humble, the hungry for righteousness and the persecuted.

5.ctx: Salt preserved and flavoured food. Most of Galilee’s towns were built on hills and visible for miles.
5.mean: ‘You are the salt of the earth’, but salt that loses its saltiness is useless. ‘You are the light of the world. A city on a hill cannot be hidden.’ Nobody lights a lamp to hide it. ‘In the same way, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.’
5.big: Disciples are meant to make a visible difference in the world, so that God, not they, gets the glory.

5.ctx: A ‘jot’ is the smallest Hebrew letter (yod); a ‘stroke’ is a tiny mark distinguishing letters. The scribes and Pharisees were known for meticulous law-keeping.
5.mean: ‘Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them.’ Not the smallest letter will pass away ‘until everything is accomplished.’ Whoever relaxes the least commandment will be least in the kingdom. ‘For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.’
5.big: Jesus does not cancel the Old Testament; he brings it to its intended goal, and calls for a righteousness that goes deeper than outward law-keeping.
5.diff: How does Christ fulfil the Law? Reformed theology distinguishes the Law’s moral, ceremonial and civil parts: the ceremonial laws are fulfilled and ended in Christ, the civil laws expired with Israel’s state, and the moral law (summarised in the Ten Commandments) still binds believers as a rule of life, though not as a way of earning salvation (Westminster Confession 19). Lutherans emphasise the distinction between law and gospel and the law’s role in showing sin. Some Protestants hold that the Mosaic law as a whole is fulfilled in Christ and that believers are under ‘the law of Christ’. Calvin stressed that the new covenant God promised ‘would not be different from the first’, but would write the same law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). Where the righteousness that ‘exceeds’ comes from is also discussed: from a changed heart (all traditions), and for Protestants ultimately from Christ’s righteousness counted to believers.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 5:17–19 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text)

5.ctx: ‘Raca’ was an Aramaic insult (‘empty-head’). The Sanhedrin was the Jewish council; ‘the fire of hell’ is Gehenna (BSB footnotes).
5.mean: ‘You have heard that it was said…‘Do not murder’…But I tell you that anyone who is angry with his brother will be subject to judgment.’ Contemptuous words are on the same road as murder. So if you are offering a gift at the altar and remember that someone has something against you, ‘First go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift.’ Settle quickly with an opponent before it is too late.
5.big: God looks at the heart; contempt and anger are murder in seed form, and broken relationships take priority over religious ritual.
5.diff: Jesus’ repeated ‘But I tell you’ is remarkable. He does not cite earlier authorities, as rabbis did, or say ‘Thus says the Lord’, as prophets did; he speaks with God’s own authority (compare 7:29).

5.ctx: Gehenna (BSB footnote) was the valley outside Jerusalem that became a symbol of final judgment.
5.mean: ‘anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.’ Then the shocking picture: if your right eye causes you to sin, gouge it out; if your right hand, cut it off. ‘It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to be thrown into hell.’
5.big: Purity begins in the heart and the eyes; deal ruthlessly with whatever leads you into sin.
5.diff: All Christian traditions read the eye and hand sayings as vivid hyperbole, not literal commands; the New Bible Dictionary calls it ‘tragic’ that some in history took them literally. The point is radical action against sin, for example in what we choose to look at.

src.l: ‘Sermon on the Mount’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

5.ctx: Deuteronomy 24:1–4 regulated divorce by requiring a certificate. The school of Hillel allowed divorce for almost any reason; the school of Shammai only for sexual misconduct.
5.mean: ‘It has also been said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife must give her a certificate of divorce.’ But I tell you that anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, brings adultery upon her. And he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery.’ In a society where a divorced woman usually had to remarry to survive, divorcing her without just cause pushed her into what amounted to adultery.
5.big: Marriage is meant to be permanent; Jesus sharply limits divorce and protects the vulnerable wife.
5.diff: The exception clause (here and 19:9) appears only in Matthew. Reformed and most Protestant churches read it as permitting divorce, and remarriage of the innocent party, for adultery (Westminster Confession 24.5–6). Catholic teaching holds that a valid, consummated marriage cannot be dissolved (Catechism 2382) and does not read the exception as permitting remarriage. See the notes on Mark 10:1 and Matthew 19:1.

5.ctx: Some Jews distinguished binding oaths (in God’s name) from lesser ones (‘by heaven’, ‘by Jerusalem’), which could be broken. Compare 23:16–22.
5.mean: The Law said, do not break your oaths. ‘But I tell you not to swear at all’, not by heaven, earth, Jerusalem or your own head, for all of them belong to God. ‘Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’ Anything more comes from the evil one.’
5.big: Disciples should be so truthful that their plain word is enough.
5.diff: May Christians take oaths? The Anabaptist Schleitheim Confession (1527) held that Christ ‘prohibits all swearing’, and Mennonites and Quakers have refused oaths, affirming instead. Most churches hold that Jesus forbade casual or evasive swearing, not solemn oaths in court: Calvin pointed to the examples that follow, which show the target was ‘circuitous or indirect ways of swearing’; the Westminster Confession calls a lawful oath part of religious worship (22.1–2); and the Catholic Catechism says Jesus’ words do not exclude ‘oaths made for grave and right reasons (for example, in court)’ (2154). Jesus himself answered under oath at his trial (26:63–64), and Paul called God as witness (2 Corinthians 1:23). UK courts allow anyone to affirm instead of swearing.

5.ctx: ‘Eye for eye’ (Exodus 21:24) limited revenge to fair compensation in court. A Roman soldier could compel a civilian to carry his gear for one mile (BSB footnote).
5.mean: ‘But I tell you not to resist an evil person. If someone slaps you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also’, a back-handed insult. Give up your cloak too; go the second mile; give to the one who asks. The Law said love your neighbour (and some added ‘hate your enemy’), ‘But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, that you may be sons of your Father in heaven.’ God sends sun and rain on the evil and the good. Even tax collectors love those who love them. ‘Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.’
5.big: Disciples imitate their Father’s generous love, even towards enemies, rather than demanding their rights.
5.diff: Non-resistance and war. The Anabaptist tradition reads verse 39 as forbidding Christians to use force: the sword is ‘ordained of God outside the perfection of Christ’ (Schleitheim, 1527); Mennonites and Quakers are pacifist. Most churches hold that Jesus forbids personal revenge, not the state’s duty to punish wrongdoers and defend the innocent (Romans 13:4). The Westminster Confession allows magistrates to wage war ‘upon just and necessary occasion’ (23.2), and the Catholic Catechism sets out strict just-war conditions (2309). Calvin noted that a believer may still go to court for a just cause. ‘Be perfect’. Calvin: this ‘does not mean equality, but relates solely to resemblance’. Wesley saw it as a promise as well as a command, part of his teaching on Christian perfection in love. The Catholic Catechism cites it for the universal call to holiness (2013).

6.ctx: Almsgiving, prayer and fasting were the three main acts of Jewish piety. ‘Sound a trumpet’ is probably a vivid picture of showing off, not a literal practice.
6.mean: ‘Be careful not to perform your righteous acts before men to be seen by them.’ Those who give for show ‘already have their full reward.’ Instead, ‘do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing’, ‘And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.’
6.big: Do good for God’s eyes, not for an audience.

6.ctx: Devout Jews prayed at set times, often publicly. Luke gives a shorter form of this prayer (Luke 11:2–4).
6.mean: Do not pray for show, or ‘babble on like pagans’, as if many words force God to listen: ‘your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.’ Then: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’ The prayer puts God’s name, kingdom and will first, then our daily needs, forgiveness and protection. Jesus underlines one line: if you forgive others, your Father will forgive you; if not, neither will he.
6.big: Jesus teaches us to approach God as Father, to seek his glory first, and to depend on him for everything, including forgiveness that makes us forgiving.
6.diff: ‘For Yours is the kingdom…’ The closing doxology is not in the earliest manuscripts of Matthew (BSB footnote), but a form of it appears in the Didache (about AD 100) and it ‘has been used in the Christian church from the earliest times’ (New Bible Dictionary). Many Protestants say it at the end of the prayer. Forgiveness. Jesus does not mean we earn God’s forgiveness by forgiving; rather, an unforgiving heart shows that we have not understood or received his forgiveness (compare 18:21–35).

6.ctx: Pharisees fasted twice a week and some made it obvious by neglecting their appearance.
6.mean: ‘When you fast’, Jesus says, assuming his followers will, do not look gloomy for show. ‘anoint your head and wash your face’, so that only your Father, who sees in secret, knows, ‘And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.’
6.big: Fasting is between you and God, not a performance.

6.ctx: Wealth was often stored as fine clothes (eaten by moths) or coins and metal (which corroded); houses with mud-brick walls could be dug through by thieves.
6.mean: ‘Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth’, where they decay or are stolen. ‘But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven’. ‘For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.’
6.big: What we treasure shows where our heart is; invest in what lasts.

6.ctx: A ‘good’ eye in Jewish idiom meant generosity; an ‘evil’ eye meant stinginess or envy (BSB footnotes cite Proverbs 22:9; 28:22).
6.mean: ‘The eye is the lamp of the body.’ If your eye is good (generous, single-minded), you are full of light; if bad (grasping), full of darkness. ‘No one can serve two masters’. ‘You cannot serve both God and money.’
6.big: Money is a rival master; we cannot give ourselves wholly to both God and wealth.

6.ctx: Most of Jesus’ hearers lived close to subsistence; worry about food and clothing was real.
6.mean: ‘Therefore I tell you, do not worry about your life’, what to eat, drink or wear. Look at the birds: your Father feeds them, ‘Are you not much more valuable than they?’ Worry cannot add an hour to your life. Look at the wild lilies: not even Solomon was dressed so finely. Will God not clothe you, ‘O you of little faith?’ The Gentiles chase after these things; ‘your heavenly Father knows that you need them. But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you.’ Do not worry about tomorrow; today has enough trouble of its own.
6.big: Trust the Father who knows your needs, and put his kingdom first.

7.ctx: A ‘beam’ was a roof timber: a deliberately absurd picture.
7.mean: ‘Do not judge, or you will be judged.’ The standard you use on others will be used on you. Why look at the speck in your brother’s eye and ignore the beam in your own? ‘First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.’ Yet discernment is still needed: ‘Do not give dogs what is holy; do not throw your pearls before swine.’
7.big: Jesus forbids hypocritical, condemning judgment, not all moral discernment; deal with your own sin first, then help your brother.

7.ctx: The Greek verbs are continuous: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking.
7.mean: ‘Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you.’ What father would give his son a stone instead of bread? ‘So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!’ Then the ‘Golden Rule’: ‘In everything, then, do to others as you would have them do to you. For this is the essence of the Law and the Prophets.’
7.big: Pray persistently to a generous Father, and treat others as you want to be treated.

7.ctx: The picture is of two roads and two gates, as in Psalm 1 and Deuteronomy 30:15–20.
7.mean: ‘Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it. But small is the gate and narrow the way that leads to life, and only a few find it.’
7.big: Following Jesus is a definite, costly choice against the flow of the crowd.

7.ctx: False prophets claimed to speak for God; Deuteronomy 13 and 18 gave tests for them.
7.mean: ‘Beware of false prophets. They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves. By their fruit you will recognize them.’ A good tree bears good fruit. ‘Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only he who does the will of My Father in heaven.’ Many will point to prophecies, exorcisms and miracles done in his name, but he will say, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!’
7.big: Words and even spectacular ministry are no proof of belonging to Jesus; a life of obedience is the fruit of real faith.
7.diff: ‘I never knew you’. Reformed readers note that Jesus does not say ‘I once knew you’: those who fall away were never truly his, which fits the perseverance of true believers. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers stress that the warning is real for professing Christians. Both agree that true faith shows itself in doing the Father’s will, and that Jesus here speaks as the final Judge, a claim to divine authority.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 7:21–23 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

7.ctx: In Palestine dry stream beds (wadis) could flood suddenly in the winter rains. Sand in a wadi bed was easy to build on in summer.
7.mean: ‘Therefore everyone who hears these words of Mine and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock.’ The storm comes and it stands. Whoever hears and does not act is like a fool who built on sand: ‘and it fell—and great was its collapse!’
7.big: Hearing Jesus is not enough; only a life built on doing what he says will stand the test.

7.ctx: Scribes taught by quoting earlier authorities.
7.mean: ‘When Jesus had finished saying these things, the crowds were astonished at His teaching, because He taught as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.’
7.big: Jesus spoke with his own authority, and that still demands a response.

8.ctx: See the note on Mark 1:40. Matthew places this healing straight after the Sermon on the Mount: the teacher with authority acts with authority.
8.mean: A leper kneels: ‘Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.’ ‘Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!”’ He sends him to the priest to make the offering Moses commanded.
8.big: Jesus is willing as well as able, and his touch makes the unclean clean.

8.ctx: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers, probably here in Herod Antipas’s service, and was a Gentile. Luke adds that he had built the local synagogue (Luke 7:1–10). A devout Jew would not enter a Gentile’s house.
8.mean: A centurion asks Jesus to heal his paralysed servant. Jesus offers to come. ‘Lord, I am not worthy to have You come under my roof. But just say the word, and my servant will be healed.’ As a soldier he knows how authority works: orders are obeyed from a distance. Jesus marvels: ‘I have not found anyone in Israel with such great faith.’ Many will come ‘from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven’, while ‘the sons of the kingdom’ are thrown out. The servant is healed at that hour.
8.big: Faith that simply trusts Jesus’ word is what he looks for, and it opens the kingdom to people from every nation.
8.diff: The centurion’s words ‘Lord, I am not worthy to have You come under my roof’ are echoed in the Catholic Mass and some other liturgies before Communion. Calvin saw in the centurion ‘a kind of first-fruits’ of the calling of the Gentiles.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 8:5–13 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

8.ctx: See the note on Mark 1:29. Isaiah 53 is the song of the suffering servant.
8.mean: Jesus touches the hand of Peter’s mother-in-law and the fever leaves; she gets up and serves him. That evening he drives out spirits ‘with a word and healed all the sick.’ Matthew quotes Isaiah 53:4: ‘He took up our infirmities and carried our diseases.’
8.big: Jesus’ healings are signs of the servant who would bear our sin and its effects.
8.diff: Healing in the atonement? Pentecostals such as the Assemblies of God cite this verse for their teaching that deliverance from sickness ‘is provided for in the Atonement, and is the privilege of all believers’, while admitting that not all are healed in this life. Most other traditions agree that Christ’s work will finally end all sickness (Revelation 21:4), but do not see physical healing as guaranteed now. Calvin argued that Matthew points to the purpose of the healings: Christ healed bodies to show he was sent ‘to relieve us from all evils and miseries’. Wesley saw a ‘lower sense’ here and the ‘highest sense’ in Christ bearing our sins on the cross.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 8:14–18 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Assemblies of God, ‘Divine Healing’ (position paper, quoting the Statement of Fundamental Truths, sec. 12)
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 8

8.ctx: Burying one’s father was a sacred duty that overrode other obligations. The man’s father may not yet have died: he may have meant that he would follow once his father had died.
8.mean: A scribe offers to follow Jesus anywhere. Jesus warns him: ‘Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head.’ Another disciple asks first to bury his father. ‘Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead.’
8.big: Following Jesus has no conditions attached and comes before even the most sacred duties.

8.ctx: See the note on Mark 4:35.
8.mean: A violent storm swamps the boat while Jesus sleeps. ‘Lord, save us! We are perishing!’ ‘You of little faith,’ Jesus replied, ‘why are you so afraid?’ He rebukes the winds and the sea, and it is perfectly calm. ‘What kind of man is this? Even the winds and the sea obey Him!’
8.big: The Lord of the storm is in the boat with his people.

8.ctx: Matthew says ‘Gadarenes’ and mentions two men; Mark and Luke focus on one. See the note on Mark 5:1 for the location.
8.mean: Two violent demon-possessed men meet Jesus from the tombs: ‘What do You want with us, Son of God?’ ‘Have You come here to torture us before the appointed time?’ The demons know their judgment is coming. They beg to be sent into the pigs; Jesus says, ‘Go!’, and the herd rushes into the sea. The town begs Jesus to leave.
8.big: Demons recognise Jesus as the Son of God and their coming judge; the townspeople, valuing their pigs, ask him to go.
8.diff: Mark and Luke tell of one man, Matthew of two. Calvin followed Augustine’s suggestion that there were two, and that Mark and Luke mention only the one who ‘was more generally known’ and worse afflicted; Matthew often records pairs (compare 20:30). The accounts do not contradict: where there were two, there was one.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 8:28–34 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
‘Gerasenes’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

9.ctx: ‘His own town’ is Capernaum (4:13). See the note on Mark 2:1.
9.mean: Seeing the faith of those who brought the paralysed man, Jesus says, ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.’ Scribes think, ‘This man is blaspheming!’ To show ‘that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins’, he tells the man to get up and go home, and he does. The crowds glorify God, ‘who had given such authority to men.’
9.big: Jesus has the authority only God has: to forgive sins.

9.ctx: Matthew, called Levi in Mark and Luke, sat at a tax booth in Capernaum on the trade route. Hosea 6:6 says God desires ‘mercy, not sacrifice’.
9.mean: Jesus sees Matthew at the tax booth: ‘Follow Me’, and he does. At dinner many tax collectors and sinners eat with Jesus. The Pharisees object. Jesus: ‘It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’ For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.’
9.big: Jesus came for sinners; religion without mercy has missed what God wants.

src.l: ‘Matthew, Gospel of’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

9.ctx: See the note on Mark 2:18.
9.mean: John’s disciples ask why Jesus’ disciples do not fast. ‘How can the guests of the bridegroom mourn while He is with them? But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.’
9.big: While Jesus is present it is a wedding; his followers would fast after he was taken.

9.ctx: See the note on Mark 2:21.
9.mean: New cloth on an old garment tears it; new wine bursts old wineskins. ‘Instead, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.’
9.big: The new life Jesus brings needs new forms.

9.ctx: Matthew tells this more briefly than Mark 5:21–43. Flute players and wailers were hired for mourning, even by poor families.
9.mean: A synagogue leader kneels: ‘My daughter has just died’, ‘But come and place Your hand on her, and she will live.’ On the way a woman bleeding for twelve years touches the fringe of Jesus’ cloak. ‘Take courage, daughter,’ He said, ‘your faith has healed you.’ At the house Jesus says, ‘The girl is not dead, but asleep’, and they laugh. He takes her hand and she gets up.
9.big: Jesus has power over long illness and over death itself.

9.h: Jesus Heals the Blind and Mute
9.ctx: ‘Son of David’ was a messianic title. The Messiah was expected to open blind eyes (Isaiah 35:5).
9.mean: Two blind men follow him crying, ‘Have mercy on us, Son of David!’ ‘Do you believe that I am able to do this?’ ‘Yes, Lord’. He touches their eyes: ‘According to your faith will it be done to you.’ Then a mute demoniac speaks after the demon is driven out. The crowds are amazed: ‘Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!’ But the Pharisees say, ‘It is by the prince of demons that He drives out demons.’
9.big: The same miracles produce wonder in some and hostility in others.

9.ctx: Ezekiel 34 condemned Israel’s leaders as shepherds who neglected the sheep.
9.mean: Jesus goes through all the towns teaching, preaching and healing. Seeing the crowds, ‘He was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.’ ‘The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest.’
9.big: Jesus’ compassion for the crowds leads to prayer for more workers, and then (chapter 10) to sending them.

10.ctx: ‘Apostle’ means ‘one sent’. See the note on Mark 3:13.
10.mean: Jesus gives the Twelve authority over unclean spirits and every disease. Matthew lists them in pairs, ‘first Simon, called Peter’, and calls himself ‘Matthew the tax collector’, a humble reminder of his past, ending with ‘Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus.’
10.big: Jesus shares his authority with ordinary people he has chosen.
10.diff: ‘First Simon’. Catholic teaching sees Peter’s place at the head of every list as reflecting his primacy (Catechism 552). Other Christians agree Peter was the leading apostle but do not see this as establishing a continuing office. See the note on 16:13.

src.l: Catechism of the Catholic Church 552–553 (Peter and the keys)

10.ctx: Samaritans were despised by Jews as half-breeds with a corrupted religion. ‘Sodom and Gomorrah’ were the proverbial example of God’s judgment (Genesis 19).
10.mean: ‘Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles or enter any town of the Samaritans. Go rather to the lost sheep of Israel.’ They are to preach, ‘The kingdom of heaven is near’, heal, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, drive out demons: ‘Freely you have received; freely give.’ They travel light, depending on hospitality, ‘for the worker is worthy of his provisions.’ Towns that reject them will fare worse on judgment day than Sodom.
10.big: God’s offer came first to Israel; after the resurrection it would go to all nations (28:19).

10.ctx: Much of this would be fulfilled after Pentecost, when the apostles were flogged and brought before councils and kings (Acts 4–5; 12; 24–26).
10.mean: ‘Behold, I am sending you out like sheep among wolves; therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves.’ They will be handed over to councils, flogged, brought before governors and kings. They need not worry what to say: ‘it will not be you speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.’ Families will divide. ‘You will be hated by everyone because of My name, but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.’ ‘you will not reach all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.’ If they called the master Beelzebul, they will slander his servants too.
10.big: Disciples should expect opposition, act with both wisdom and integrity, and rely on the Spirit.
10.diff: ‘Before the Son of Man comes’ (verse 23) is one of the hardest sayings in Matthew. Wesley took it as the coming of the Son of Man ‘To destroy their temple and nation’ in AD 70. Others think of the resurrection, or of the mission to Israel continuing until Christ’s return.

src.l: John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 10

10.ctx: A sparrow was the cheapest food sold in the market; an ‘assarion’ was a small copper coin (BSB footnote).
10.mean: ‘So do not be afraid of them.’ What is hidden will be revealed; proclaim openly what Jesus told them privately. ‘Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Instead, fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell.’ Not a sparrow falls ‘apart from the will of your Father. And even the very hairs of your head are all numbered.’ ‘So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.’
10.big: Fear of God drives out fear of people; and the God to be feared is the Father who cares for every detail of his children’s lives.
10.diff: ‘Destroy both soul and body in hell’. Those who hold conditional immortality (such as Seventh-day Adventists) see this verse as teaching that the lost will finally be destroyed. Those who hold the traditional view of hell as eternal punishment (the historic position of Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches) read ‘destroy’ as ruin, not ceasing to exist, alongside texts such as 25:46. See the note on Mark 9:42.

src.l: Seventh-day Adventist Church, 28 Fundamental Beliefs, nos. 26–27
Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text)

10.ctx: Mark’s and Matthew’s first readers faced trials in which denying Christ could save their lives.
10.mean: ‘Therefore everyone who confesses Me before men, I will also confess him before My Father in heaven. But whoever denies Me before men, I will also deny him before My Father in heaven.’
10.big: How we stand by Jesus now matters eternally; yet Peter’s denial and restoration show that failure is not necessarily final.

10.ctx: Verses 35–36 quote Micah 7:6, a picture of a society falling apart.
10.mean: ‘Do not assume that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.’ Jesus brings ultimate peace with God, but his coming divides, even within families. ‘Anyone who loves his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me’. ‘and anyone who does not take up his cross and follow Me is not worthy of Me. Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.’
10.big: Loyalty to Jesus must come before every other loyalty, even family.
10.diff: The ‘sword’ is division, not violence; Luke has ‘division’ (Luke 12:51). Jesus forbade his followers to use the sword to defend him (26:52).

10.ctx: Travelling preachers depended entirely on hospitality.
10.mean: ‘He who receives you receives Me, and he who receives Me receives the One who sent Me.’ Whoever welcomes a prophet or righteous person shares their reward; even ‘a cup of cold water’ given to ‘one of these little ones because he is My disciple’ will be rewarded.
10.big: Jesus identifies so closely with his messengers that kindness to them is kindness to him.

11.ctx: John was imprisoned by Herod Antipas, according to Josephus at the fortress of Machaerus. He had expected a Messiah who would bring fiery judgment (3:10–12).
11.mean: From prison John sends to ask, ‘Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?’ Jesus answers by pointing to Isaiah’s promises being fulfilled (Isaiah 35:5–6; 61:1): ‘The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor. Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.’
11.big: Even the greatest prophet could struggle with doubt; Jesus answers with evidence and Scripture, not rebuke.

src.l: Josephus, Antiquities 18.116–119 (Whiston): John the Baptist

11.ctx: Malachi 3:1 and 4:5 promised a messenger, Elijah, before the day of the Lord.
11.mean: Jesus praises John: not a reed in the wind, not a courtier in fine clothes, but a prophet ‘and more than a prophet’, the promised messenger. ‘among those born of women there has risen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet even the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.’ ‘he is the Elijah who was to come.’ But this generation is like sulky children who will not join in any game: John fasted and they called him demon-possessed; Jesus eats and drinks and they say, ‘Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ ‘But wisdom is vindicated by her actions.’
11.big: John stood at the hinge between the old age and the new; the least in the kingdom now sees more than he could.
11.diff: ‘The kingdom of heaven has been subject to violence’ (verse 12) is obscure. Some take it negatively: violent men (such as Herod) attack the kingdom. Others take it positively (BSB footnote: ‘has been forcefully advancing’): Wesley wrote that people ‘rush into my kingdom with a violence like that of those who are taking a city by storm.’

src.l: John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 11

11.ctx: Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum were small towns at the north end of the lake where Jesus did most of his miracles. Tyre and Sidon were pagan cities condemned by the prophets.
11.mean: ‘Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!’ If Tyre and Sidon had seen such miracles, they would have repented. ‘And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades!’ Even Sodom would have repented. Judgment will be more bearable for them.
11.big: Greater privilege brings greater responsibility; seeing Jesus’ works and not repenting is worse than the sins of Sodom.
11.diff: Jesus says Tyre, Sidon and Sodom ‘would have repented’. Theologians have discussed what this shows about God’s knowledge of what would have happened, and why he did not send them such miracles. Calvin warned against raising ‘thorny questions’ about God’s secret decrees here, since the saying is ‘accommodated to the ordinary capacity of the human mind’. All agree the main point is the guilt of those who saw and did not repent.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 11:20–24 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

11.ctx: ‘Yoke’ was a common Jewish image for the Law and its obligations. The rabbis spoke of taking on ‘the yoke of the kingdom’.
11.mean: Jesus praises his Father: ‘You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight.’ ‘All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father. No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.’ Then the great invitation: ‘Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.’
11.big: Only the Son truly knows the Father and makes him known; and the Son invites all the weary to come to him.
11.diff: Election and invitation side by side. Reformed readers see in verses 25–27 God’s sovereign choice: Calvin says it is ‘a distinction which depends entirely on the will of God, that the wise remain blind, while the ignorant and unlearned receive the mysteries of the Gospel’. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers stress the universal invitation of verse 28; Wesley read verse 25 as God having ‘suffered these things to be hid’ from the proud. Both views hold the two truths together: God reveals, and all who are weary are invited. Verse 27 is also one of the clearest statements in the first three Gospels of the unique relationship between the Father and the Son.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 11:25–30 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 11

12.ctx: See the note on Mark 2:23. Priests worked hard on the Sabbath in the temple, offering the extra sacrifices the Law required (Numbers 28:9–10).
12.mean: The Pharisees object to the disciples picking grain on the Sabbath. Jesus cites David eating the consecrated bread, and the priests who ‘break the Sabbath and yet are innocent’. ‘But I tell you that One greater than the temple is here.’ ‘If only you had known the meaning of ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the innocent. For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.’
12.big: Jesus is greater than the temple and Lord of the Sabbath; mercy is the key to understanding God’s law.
12.diff: For the different ways Christians keep the Lord’s Day or the Sabbath, see the note on Mark 2:23.

src.l: Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text)

12.ctx: Jewish teachers debated what could be done for an animal in danger on the Sabbath.
12.mean: Asked, ‘Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?’, Jesus replies that any of them would lift a sheep out of a pit. ‘How much more valuable is a man than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.’ He heals the man’s withered hand; the Pharisees plot to kill him.
12.big: Doing good is always lawful on God’s day.

12.ctx: Isaiah 42:1–4 is the first of Isaiah’s ‘servant songs’.
12.mean: Jesus withdraws, heals the crowds and tells them not to make him known. Matthew sees Isaiah 42 fulfilled: ‘Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul delights.’ The Spirit is on him; he will bring justice to the nations, but quietly: ‘A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish’. ‘In His name the nations will put their hope.’
12.big: Jesus is the gentle servant who will not crush the weak, and the hope of the Gentiles.

12.ctx: Jewish exorcists existed (‘your sons’). See the note on Mark 3:20.
12.mean: Jesus heals a blind and mute demoniac, and the crowds ask, ‘Could this be the Son of David?’ The Pharisees say he works by Beelzebul. Jesus answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand. ‘But if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.’ He has tied up the strong man. ‘He who is not with Me is against Me’.
12.big: Jesus’ victory over demons shows God’s kingdom has arrived; there is no neutral ground.

12.ctx: Said in response to the Pharisees calling the Spirit’s work in Jesus the devil’s.
12.mean: ‘every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the one to come.’
12.big: Every sin can be forgiven, except the settled rejection that calls God’s saving work evil.
12.diff: See the note on Mark 3:28. Some Catholic writers have seen in ‘the one to come’ a hint that some sins can be forgiven after death (Catechism 1031 cites this verse for purgatory); Protestants read it as a Jewish way of saying ‘never’.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 12:25–32 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Catechism of the Catholic Church 1030–1032 (purification after death)

12.ctx: John the Baptist had called the Pharisees a ‘brood of vipers’ too (3:7).
12.mean: A tree is known by its fruit. ‘For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks.’ ‘But I tell you that men will give an account on the day of judgment for every careless word they have spoken. For by your words you will be acquitted, and by your words you will be condemned.’
12.big: Our words reveal our hearts, and God takes them seriously.

12.ctx: Jonah preached to Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, and it repented (Jonah 3). The Queen of Sheba travelled to hear Solomon (1 Kings 10).
12.mean: Asked for a sign, Jesus says only ‘the sign of the prophet Jonah’ will be given: ‘as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.’ The pagan Ninevites and the Queen of the South will condemn this generation, ‘and now One greater than Jonah is here’, ‘One greater than Solomon is here.’
12.big: The only sign Jesus gives is his death and resurrection, and he is greater than prophet or king.
12.diff: ‘Three days and three nights’. Jesus died on Friday afternoon and rose early on Sunday. Wesley explained that ‘It was customary with the eastern nations to reckon any part of a natural day…for the whole day’; the Gospels themselves use ‘after three days’ and ‘on the third day’ interchangeably (compare Mark 8:31 and Matthew 16:21). A few have argued for a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion, but most interpreters accept the Friday dating.

src.l: John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 12

12.ctx: Arid places were thought to be the haunts of demons.
12.mean: An evicted spirit wanders, returns, finds its old home ‘vacant, swept clean, and put in order’, and brings seven worse spirits. ‘And the final plight of that man is worse than the first. So will it be with this wicked generation.’
12.big: Reform without filling the heart with God leaves a person, or a nation, worse off.

12.ctx: See the notes on Mark 3:31 and 6:1.
12.mean: His mother and brothers want to speak with him. ‘Who is My mother, and who are My brothers?’ Pointing to his disciples: ‘Here are My mother and My brothers. For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.’
12.big: Doing the Father’s will makes us Jesus’ family.
