13.ctx: This begins Matthew’s third discourse, seven parables of the kingdom. See the note on Mark 4:1.
13.mean: From a boat Jesus tells of seed falling on the path, rocky ground, thorns and good soil, which yields ‘a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold.’ ‘He who has ears, let him hear.’
13.big: The word meets different responses, but where it takes root the harvest is huge.

13.ctx: Matthew quotes Isaiah 6:9–10 in full.
13.mean: Why parables? ‘The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven has been given to you, but not to them.’ ‘Whoever has will be given more’. In those who refuse, Isaiah’s words are fulfilled: ‘this people’s heart has grown callous’. ‘But blessed are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear.’ Prophets and righteous people longed to see what they see.
13.big: The parables reveal to the receptive and conceal from the hardened.
13.diff: See the note on Mark 4:10 for Reformed and Wesleyan readings. Matthew’s wording (‘This is why I speak to them in parables: ‘Though seeing, they do not see’’) stresses that the people’s hearts had already ‘grown callous’.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 13:1–17 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

13.h: The Parable of the Sower Explained
13.ctx: See the note on Mark 4:13.
13.mean: The path: one who hears ‘the message of the kingdom but does not understand it’, and ‘the evil one comes and snatches away’ the seed. The rocky ground: joyful reception, no root, falling away under persecution. The thorns: ‘the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word’. The good soil: one ‘who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit’.
13.big: Hearing with understanding that bears lasting fruit is what counts.

13.ctx: The weed was probably darnel, which looks like wheat until it ripens and whose roots tangle with the wheat’s.
13.mean: A man sows good seed; an enemy secretly sows weeds among it. When both appear, the servants want to pull the weeds. ‘No,’ he said, ‘if you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest.’ Then the weeds will be burned and the wheat gathered.
13.big: Good and evil grow side by side until the end; final separation belongs to God at the harvest.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

13.h: The Parable of the Mustard Seed
13.ctx: See the note on Mark 4:30.
13.mean: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed’, the smallest of seeds, which grows into a tree where birds nest.
13.big: The kingdom begins tiny and grows beyond all expectation.

13.ctx: Three measures of flour was a huge amount, enough bread for a crowd. Leaven is often a picture of evil in Scripture, but here of the kingdom.
13.mean: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened.’
13.big: The kingdom works quietly and invisibly until it transforms everything.

13.h: I Will Open My Mouth in Parables
13.ctx: Psalm 78 is a psalm of Asaph, who is called a ‘seer’ (prophet) in 2 Chronicles 29:30.
13.mean: Jesus speaks to the crowds only in parables, fulfilling Psalm 78:2: ‘I will open My mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world.’
13.big: Jesus’ parables bring hidden purposes of God to light.

13.h: The Parable of the Weeds Explained
13.ctx: Weeping and gnashing of teeth express anguish and anger.
13.mean: The sower is the Son of Man; ‘The field is the world’; the good seed are the sons of the kingdom; the weeds are the sons of the evil one, sown by the devil. ‘The harvest is the end of the age, and the harvesters are angels.’ They will remove ‘every cause of sin and all who practice lawlessness’ into the fiery furnace. ‘Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.’
13.big: God will put everything right at the end; until then his people live alongside evil without being able to root it out themselves.
13.diff: A pure church or a mixed church? Most churches have read this parable as meaning that the visible church will always contain hypocrites until the judgment. Calvin: ‘So long as the pilgrimage of the Church in this world continues, bad men and hypocrites will mingle in it with those who are good’, though he insisted the parable does not forbid church discipline or tolerating false doctrine. The Anabaptist tradition stresses that ‘the field is the world’, not the church, and that the church should be a disciplined community of committed believers (Schleitheim, art. 2). Both sides agree that only God can finally judge hearts.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Schleitheim Confession (1527), arts. 2 and 6 (the ban; separation), trans. J. C. Wenger

13.h: The Parables of the Treasure and the Pearl
13.ctx: With no banks, people often buried valuables. Pearls were among the most prized possessions in the ancient world.
13.mean: The kingdom is like treasure hidden in a field: a man finds it, ‘and in his joy he went and sold all he had and bought that field.’ It is like a merchant who finds ‘one very precious pearl’ and sells everything to buy it.
13.big: The kingdom is worth everything, and giving all for it is not a grim sacrifice but joyful gain.

13.ctx: A dragnet hauled in everything; unclean fish (Leviticus 11:9–12) and inedible ones were thrown away.
13.mean: The kingdom is like a net that catches all kinds of fish, sorted on the shore. ‘So will it be at the end of the age: The angels will come and separate the wicked from the righteous’. Have they understood? Then ‘every scribe who has been discipled in the kingdom of heaven is like a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old.’
13.big: The judgment will sort what the gospel net gathers; disciples understand the new in the light of the old.
13.diff: Some see in verse 52 a self-portrait of Matthew, a scribe trained for the kingdom who brings out Old Testament treasures and new ones.

13.ctx: Matthew calls Jesus ‘the carpenter’s son’; Mark 6:3 has ‘the carpenter, the son of Mary’.
13.mean: In his home synagogue they are astonished, then offended: ‘Isn’t this the carpenter’s son? Isn’t His mother’s name Mary, and aren’t His brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas?’ ‘Only in his hometown and in his own household is a prophet without honor.’ ‘And He did not do many miracles there, because of their unbelief.’
13.big: Familiarity bred contempt; unbelief shut the door on what Jesus could have done.
13.diff: See the note on Mark 6:1 for the three Christian views of Jesus’ brothers.

b: Nazareth was a small Jewish farming village on a ridge in Lower Galilee: current estimates suggest 200–500 people in Jesus’ day. No writer before the New Testament mentions it, not even Josephus, which fits a place of no importance (compare John 1:46). Excavations under the Church of the Annunciation found silos, cisterns, tombs and simple houses.

About 6 km away stood Sepphoris, which Herod Antipas rebuilt as his capital after 4 BC. The word translated ‘carpenter’ (Greek tektōn) means a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Building work at Sepphoris would have drawn craftsmen from the surrounding villages, and many scholars think Joseph and Jesus may have worked there, though the Gospels never mention it.

src.l: ‘Nazareth’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Reed; Bagatti)
‘Sepphoris’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 13:53–58 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Catechism of the Catholic Church 499–501 (Mary’s virginity; the ‘brothers’ of Jesus)
D. F. Wright and J. S. Wright, ‘Virgin Birth’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)
‘Nazareth’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Reed; Bagatti)

14.ctx: Matthew correctly calls Antipas ‘the tetrarch’.
14.mean: Herod the tetrarch hears about Jesus: ‘This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead!’ He had imprisoned John for saying, ‘It is not lawful for you to have her’, Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife. He wanted to kill John but feared the people. At his birthday, Herodias’s daughter dances; he swears to give her anything; prompted by her mother she asks for John’s head on a platter. Grieved but bound by his oaths and guests, Herod gives the order. John’s disciples bury him and tell Jesus.
14.big: Courage to speak God’s truth to the powerful can cost everything.

hist.t: Herod Antipas, Herodias and John’s death
b: The ‘King Herod’ of Mark 6 is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. After his father died in 4 BC, Augustus made him tetrarch (ruler of a quarter) of Galilee and Perea, which he governed for 43 years. Matthew and Luke give his exact title, ‘tetrarch’; Mark uses the popular ‘king’. He rebuilt Sepphoris and founded Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee.

Josephus confirms the outline of Mark’s account. Antipas divorced his first wife, daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, to marry Herodias, who had been married to his half-brother. Josephus calls that first husband Herod; Mark calls him Philip. Since several of Herod the Great’s sons were called Herod, some suggest he bore both names. Aretas later defeated Antipas in battle, and Josephus says many Jews saw the defeat as God’s punishment for his killing of ‘John, that was called the Baptist’, ‘a good man’ who called the Jews to righteousness and baptism.

Josephus gives a political reason for the execution: Antipas feared John’s influence over the crowds might lead to a revolt. Mark gives the personal story. The two fit together easily. Josephus says John was held and killed at Machaerus, Antipas’s fortress east of the Dead Sea.

src.l: Josephus, Antiquities 18.116–119 (Whiston): John the Baptist
‘Herod Antipas’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Hoehner, Herod Antipas)
‘John the Baptist’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
Josephus, Antiquities 18.116–119 (Whiston): John the Baptist
‘Herod Antipas’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Hoehner, Herod Antipas)

14.h: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
14.ctx: See the note on Mark 6:30. Matthew alone notes that the count did not include women and children.
14.mean: Hearing of John’s death, Jesus withdraws, but the crowds follow. ‘He had compassion on them and healed their sick.’ ‘You give them something to eat.’ ‘We have here only five loaves of bread and two fish’. He blesses, breaks and gives; all eat, twelve baskets are left. ‘About five thousand men were fed, besides women and children.’
14.big: Jesus provides abundantly through what his disciples bring him.

14.ctx: See the note on Mark 6:45. Only Matthew tells of Peter walking on the water.
14.mean: Jesus comes to the disciples walking on the sea in the night: ‘Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.’ Peter: ‘Lord, if it is You,’ ‘command me to come to You on the water.’ ‘Come,’ said Jesus. Peter walks on the water, but seeing the wind he is afraid and begins to sink: ‘Lord, save me!’ Jesus catches him: ‘You of little faith,’ He said, ‘why did you doubt?’ In the boat the wind stops, and they worship him: ‘Truly You are the Son of God!’
14.big: Jesus does what only God can do; faith that looks at him can do what seems impossible, and when faith falters he is there to catch us.

14.ctx: See the note on Mark 6:53.
14.mean: At Gennesaret people bring all their sick, begging ‘just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak. And all who touched Him were healed.’
14.big: Jesus’ power to heal reaches all who come to him.

15.ctx: See the note on Mark 7:1. The scribes came from Jerusalem, an official delegation.
15.mean: ‘Why do Your disciples break the tradition of the elders? They do not wash their hands before they eat.’ Jesus turns the question round: ‘And why do you break the command of God for the sake of your tradition?’ Their rule let a son declare money ‘a gift devoted to God’ and so neglect his parents. ‘Thus you nullify the word of God for the sake of your tradition.’ Isaiah described them: ‘These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me.’
15.big: Human traditions must never be allowed to cancel God’s commands.
15.diff: See the note on Mark 7:1 for how Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Christians relate Scripture and tradition.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 15:1–9 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text)
Catechism of the Catholic Church 80–83 (Tradition and Scripture)

15.ctx: See the note on Mark 7:14.
15.mean: ‘A man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of it.’ The disciples warn him that the Pharisees are offended. ‘Every plant that My heavenly Father has not planted will be pulled up by its roots. Disregard them! They are blind guides.’ Peter asks for an explanation: food goes into the stomach, but ‘out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander.’
15.big: Defilement comes from the heart, not the stomach.

15.h: The Faith of the Canaanite Woman
15.ctx: Matthew calls her a ‘Canaanite’, the name of Israel’s ancient enemies; Mark calls her a Syrophoenician Greek. See the note on Mark 7:24.
15.mean: A Canaanite woman cries out, ‘Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me! My daughter is miserably possessed by a demon.’ Jesus says nothing; the disciples want her sent away. ‘I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.’ She kneels: ‘Lord, help me!’ ‘It is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.’ ‘Yes, Lord,’ she said, ‘even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master’s table.’ ‘O woman,’ Jesus answered, ‘your faith is great!’ Her daughter is healed.
15.big: A Gentile woman’s humble, persistent faith wins what she asks; her faith is called great where the disciples’ was ‘little’.

15.h: The Feeding of the Four Thousand
15.ctx: See the note on Mark 8:1. The crowd here ‘glorified the God of Israel’, suggesting many were Gentiles.
15.mean: Jesus heals the lame, blind, crippled and mute, ‘And they glorified the God of Israel.’ After three days with him the crowd has no food. With seven loaves and a few fish he feeds ‘four thousand men…besides women and children’, and seven baskets are left.
15.big: Jesus’ compassion and provision extend to Gentiles too.

16.ctx: The Pharisees and Sadducees were normally opponents; they unite against Jesus. Some manuscripts lack the weather saying (BSB footnote).
16.mean: They ask for a sign from heaven. Jesus says they can read the sky’s signs for the weather ‘but not the signs of the times.’ ‘A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah.’
16.big: The signs were already in front of them; what was lacking was the will to read them.

16.h: The Leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees
16.ctx: See the note on Mark 8:14. Matthew explains what the ‘leaven’ means.
16.mean: ‘Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.’ The disciples think he means bread. ‘You of little faith’, he says, reminding them of the two feedings. ‘Then they understood that He was not telling them to beware of the leaven used in bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.’
16.big: False teaching spreads like yeast; disciples need discernment.

16.ctx: See the drop-down on Caesarea Philippi at Mark 8:27. ‘Peter’ (Greek Petros) and ‘rock’ (petra) are a wordplay; in Aramaic both would be Kepha (Cephas). ‘Binding and loosing’ was a rabbinic expression for forbidding and permitting.
16.mean: ‘Who do people say the Son of Man is?’ John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, a prophet. ‘But what about you?’ Jesus asked. ‘Who do you say I am?’ ‘Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”’ Jesus: ‘Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! For this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven. And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.’
16.big: Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, known only by the Father’s revelation; on that confession and its confessor Jesus builds a church that death itself cannot overcome.
16.diff: Who or what is the rock? This verse is at the centre of one of the main divisions in Christianity. Catholic teaching: ‘The Lord made Simon alone, whom he named Peter, the “rock” of his Church’, giving him the keys, and this pastoral office ‘is continued by the bishops under the primacy of the Pope’ (Catechism 881; compare 552–553). Orthodox teaching honours Peter as first among the apostles but holds that ‘the Church, as the Body of Christ, can have no other Head than Jesus Christ’ (Longer Catechism 259), and does not accept the Pope’s claim of universal jurisdiction. Protestants have read the rock as Peter’s confession of faith, or Christ himself, or Peter as the first confessor and leading apostle (with no successors in that role). Calvin held that the Church ‘can have no other foundation than Christ alone’, built on the faith Peter confessed; Wesley took it as ‘the faith which thou hast now professed’, or Christ pointing to himself. Binding and loosing is given to the disciples as a group in 18:18. Calvin applied them to ‘the office of teaching’: the gospel opens the kingdom.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 16:13–19 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Catechism of the Catholic Church 881–882 (Peter and the Pope)
Catechism of the Catholic Church 552–553 (Peter and the keys)
The Longer Catechism of the Orthodox Church (Philaret), Q. 258–261 (Christ the one Head of the Church), in Schaff vol. 2
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 16
‘Caesarea Philippi’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

16.ctx: See the note on Mark 8:31. Matthew says ‘From that time on’, marking a turning point (compare 4:17).
16.mean: Jesus begins to show them ‘that He must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things…and that He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life.’ Peter rebukes him: ‘Far be it from You, Lord!’ ‘This shall never happen to You!’ ‘Get behind Me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to Me. For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.’
16.big: Minutes after being called a rock, Peter becomes a stumbling stone when he resists the cross.

16.ctx: See the note on Mark 8:34.
16.mean: ‘If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.’ Losing life for his sake is finding it. ‘What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?’ The Son of Man will come in glory ‘and then He will repay each one according to what he has done. Truly I tell you, some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom.’
16.big: The way of the cross leads to life and to the Son of Man’s reward.
16.diff: On ‘some who are standing here’, see the note on Mark 9:1. Calvin applied it to ‘the manifestation of heavenly glory, which Christ began to make at his resurrection, and which he afterwards made more fully by sending the Holy Spirit’.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 16:20–28 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

17.ctx: See the note on Mark 9:1. Peter later recalled this event (2 Peter 1:16–18; BSB footnote).
17.mean: On a high mountain Jesus is transfigured: ‘His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as the light.’ Moses and Elijah talk with him. Peter offers to build three shelters. A bright cloud covers them and the voice says, ‘This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!’ They fall down terrified; Jesus touches them: ‘Get up,’ He said. ‘Do not be afraid.’ They see only Jesus. Coming down, he identifies John the Baptist as the Elijah who was to come.
17.big: The Father confirms that Jesus, about to suffer, is his beloved Son, greater than Moses and Elijah; listen to him.

17.ctx: See the note on Mark 9:14. Matthew’s word for the boy’s seizures (verse 15) is often translated ‘epileptic’.
17.mean: A father kneels: his son has seizures and falls into fire and water, and the disciples could not heal him. ‘O unbelieving and perverse generation!’ Jesus rebukes the demon and the boy is healed at once.
17.big: Jesus has power where his followers fail.

17.ctx: The ‘mustard seed’ was proverbially tiny. Later manuscripts add verse 21 about ‘prayer and fasting’ (BSB footnote).
17.mean: ‘Why couldn’t we drive it out?’ ‘Because you have so little faith’. ‘if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move. Nothing will be impossible for you.’
17.big: What matters is not the size of our faith but the greatness of the God it trusts.

17.h: The Second Prediction of the Passion
17.mean: ‘The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. They will kill Him, and on the third day He will be raised to life.’ ‘And the disciples were deeply grieved.’
17.big: Jesus kept preparing his disciples for the cross and the resurrection.

17.ctx: Every Jewish man paid an annual half-shekel (a two-drachma coin) for the temple (Exodus 30:11–16). A four-drachma coin (stater) paid for two.
17.mean: Collectors ask Peter whether his teacher pays the temple tax. ‘Yes’. Jesus asks: do kings tax their own sons? ‘Then the sons are exempt’. As God’s Son, Jesus owes nothing to his Father’s house. ‘But so that we may not offend them’, Peter is to catch a fish and find a four-drachma coin in its mouth, enough ‘for My tax and yours.’
17.big: Jesus is the Son of the house, free from obligation, yet he gives up his rights so as not to cause needless offence, and includes Peter with himself.
17.diff: Calvin saw in this story that Christ paid ‘of his own accord’, by ‘a free and voluntary submission’. The story is found only in Matthew, and Matthew does not even say the fish was caught; the point is Jesus’ sonship and his care not to cause offence.

b: After the temple was destroyed, the emperor Vespasian ordered every Jew everywhere to pay the same two drachmas each year to the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol in Rome instead, as Josephus records. For Matthew’s Jewish-Christian readers, this story about the tax would have had a sharp relevance either way: before 70 as a question of the temple, after 70 as a question of avoiding needless offence.

src.l: Josephus, Jewish War 7.218 (Whiston): the two-drachma tax diverted to the Capitol
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 17:24–27 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

18.ctx: Matthew’s fourth discourse, on life together in the community of disciples.
18.mean: ‘Who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’ Jesus stands a child among them: ‘unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest’. Welcoming such a child in his name welcomes him.
18.big: The way into the kingdom, and up in it, is down: humble dependence like a child’s.

18.ctx: See the note on Mark 9:42.
18.mean: Causing ‘one of these little ones who believe in Me’ to stumble deserves the worst fate. ‘These stumbling blocks must come, but woe to the man through whom they come!’ Cut off hand or foot, gouge out an eye, rather than be thrown into ‘the eternal fire’.
18.big: Leading others into sin is grave; deal radically with sin in yourself.

18.h: The Parable of the Lost Sheep
18.ctx: Luke tells this parable to Pharisees about sinners (Luke 15); Matthew applies it to how disciples treat straying members. Verse 11 is found only in later manuscripts (BSB footnote).
18.mean: ‘See that you do not look down on any of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of My Father in heaven.’ A shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to look for the one lost sheep, and rejoices when he finds it. ‘In the same way, your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish.’
18.big: God cares intensely for each vulnerable believer, and so must his people.
18.diff: Guardian angels. Catholic and Orthodox teaching draws from this verse that ‘Beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd’ (Catechism 336, quoting Basil). Calvin agreed that angels guard believers, but thought the idea ‘that God assigned to each believer his own angel, does not rest on solid grounds’. Scripture clearly teaches angels’ care for God’s people (Psalm 91:11; Hebrews 1:14).

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 18:6–10 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Catechism of the Catholic Church 336 (guardian angels)

18.ctx: Deuteronomy 19:15 required two or three witnesses. ‘The church’ here means the local gathering of believers.
18.mean: ‘If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. If he listens to you, you have won your brother over.’ If not, take one or two others; if he still refuses, ‘tell it to the church’; if he refuses even the church, ‘regard him as you would a pagan or a tax collector.’ ‘whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.’
18.big: Sin within the church is to be dealt with privately first, aiming to win the brother back, with discipline as the last resort.
18.diff: Church discipline is practised in different ways: by elders and congregations in Reformed and Baptist churches (Westminster Confession 30), and in the Catholic and Orthodox churches through bishops and the sacrament of penance; the Catholic Catechism links binding and loosing with reconciliation to the Church (1444–1445). Wesley understood binding as excommunication and loosing as ‘absolution from that sentence’. ‘A pagan or a tax collector’ does not mean hostility: Jesus welcomed both. It means treating the person as one who needs to be won to Christ.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 18:15–20 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text)
Catechism of the Catholic Church 1444–1445 (binding and loosing)
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 18

18.ctx: Ten men were needed for a synagogue; Jesus promises his presence to far fewer.
18.mean: ‘if two of you on the earth agree about anything you ask for, it will be done for you by My Father in heaven. For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them.’
18.big: Jesus is present with even the smallest gathering of his people.

18.ctx: Rabbis suggested forgiving three times. A talent was about twenty years’ wages (BSB footnote); ten thousand talents was an unimaginable sum. A hundred denarii was about four months’ wages.
18.mean: Peter offers seven times. ‘I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times!’ A king forgives a servant a debt of ten thousand talents. That servant then chokes a fellow servant over a hundred denarii and has him jailed. The king summons him: ‘You wicked servant! I forgave all your debt because you begged me. Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?’ He hands him over to the jailers. ‘That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother from your heart.’
18.big: We have been forgiven an unpayable debt by God; refusing to forgive others shows we have not grasped his mercy.
18.diff: Does verse 35 mean God takes back forgiveness? Reformed readers see a warning that an unforgiving heart shows forgiveness was never truly received. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers more readily take it as a real danger of forfeiting grace. Both take it as a serious warning to forgive.

19.ctx: Matthew’s version of the question, ‘for any reason’, reflects the debate between the schools of Hillel (any reason) and Shammai (only sexual immorality). See the note on Mark 10:1.
19.mean: ‘Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?’ Jesus goes back to creation: male and female, one flesh. ‘Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.’ Moses permitted divorce ‘because of your hardness of heart. But it was not this way from the beginning. Now I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery.’ The disciples: then it is better not to marry. Jesus: not everyone can accept this; some are eunuchs from birth, some made so by men, ‘and still others live like eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.’
19.big: Marriage is God’s lifelong joining; and singleness for the kingdom is also an honourable gift.
19.diff: The exception. See the notes on Mark 10:1 and Matthew 5:31. Celibacy (verses 10–12). Catholic teaching sees here a call to celibacy ‘for the sake of the kingdom of heaven’, required of most Latin-rite priests and of religious (Catechism 1579). Protestants honour celibacy as a gift (1 Corinthians 7:7) but do not require it of ministers. Calvin stressed that ‘the gift of continence is a special gift’, not given to all, and warned against binding oneself to celibacy without it.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 19:3–9 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 19:10–12 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Catechism of the Catholic Church 1579–1580 (celibacy)
Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text)

19.ctx: See the note on Mark 10:13.
19.mean: Children are brought for Jesus to lay hands on and pray for them; the disciples rebuke the people. ‘Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.’ He lays his hands on them.
19.big: Jesus welcomes children; the kingdom belongs to the dependent.
19.diff: See the note on Mark 10:13 for how this passage has been used in the debate over infant baptism. Wesley on 28:19 explains why he baptised infants: ‘in discipling their children, to baptize them before they were taught’.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 19:13–15 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 28

19.ctx: See the note on Mark 10:17. ‘The renewal of all things’ (verse 28; BSB footnote ‘regeneration’) is the new creation.
19.mean: ‘Teacher, what good thing must I do to obtain eternal life?’ ‘There is only One who is good. If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.’ He claims to have kept them: ‘What do I still lack?’ ‘If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.’ He goes away sad. ‘it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.’ ‘Who then can be saved?’ ‘With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.’ Those who have left everything will sit on thrones ‘in the renewal of all things’, and receive a hundredfold and eternal life. ‘But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.’
19.big: No one can earn eternal life; it is impossible for us and possible only for God, and following Jesus means letting go of whatever holds our heart.
19.diff: ‘If you want to be perfect’. Catholic tradition has seen here the ‘evangelical counsels’, a call to some to embrace voluntary poverty, while insisting that all are called to keep the commandments and to holiness (Catechism 2053, 2013). Calvin, commenting on 5:44, rejected the idea that some of Jesus’ commands are only ‘advices’ for a few. Protestants generally read the command as aimed at this man’s particular idol, his wealth. All agree Jesus demands first place.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 19:16–22 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 5:43–48 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Catechism of the Catholic Church 2052–2054 (the rich young man; the counsels)

20.ctx: Day labourers waited in the marketplace to be hired; a denarius was the usual day’s wage. The workday ran from about 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.; ‘the eleventh hour’ was about 5 p.m. (BSB footnote).
20.mean: A landowner hires workers at dawn for a denarius, then more at nine, noon, three and five. At evening he pays the last first, a full denarius each. The first expect more and get the same, and grumble: ‘you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden and the scorching heat of the day.’ ‘Friend, I am not being unfair to you. Did you not agree with me on one denarius?’ ‘Or are you envious because I am generous?’ ‘So the last will be first, and the first will be last.’
20.big: God’s kingdom runs on grace, not merit; latecomers receive the same gift, and the only fitting response is joy, not envy.

20.h: The Third Prediction of the Passion
20.ctx: Only Matthew says ‘crucified’ in the predictions.
20.mean: Going up to Jerusalem, Jesus tells the Twelve that the Son of Man will be condemned and handed to the Gentiles ‘to be mocked and flogged and crucified. And on the third day He will be raised to life.’
20.big: Jesus went to the cross knowingly and willingly.

20.ctx: In Mark 10:35 James and John ask for themselves; here their mother asks for them. She was probably Salome (compare 27:56 with Mark 15:40).
20.mean: The mother of Zebedee’s sons asks for her sons to sit at Jesus’ right and left in his kingdom. ‘You do not know what you are asking’. ‘Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?’ They can, and will, but the seats are for those ‘for whom My Father has prepared them.’ The others are indignant. Jesus: Gentile rulers lord it over people; ‘It shall not be this way among you.’ ‘just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.’
20.big: Greatness in Jesus’ kingdom is service, modelled on his giving his life as a ransom.
20.diff: See the note on Mark 10:35 for ‘a ransom for many’ in Reformed, Wesleyan and Catholic teaching.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 20:24–28 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Catechism of the Catholic Church 605 and 616 (‘a ransom for many’; Christ died for all)
Canons of Dort (1619), Second Head, arts. 3 and 8, in Schaff vol. 3

20.h: The Blind Men by the Road
20.ctx: See the notes on Mark 10:46 (Bartimaeus) and the ‘two Jerichos’ drop-down there.
20.mean: Leaving Jericho, two blind men shout, ‘Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!’ The crowd tells them to be quiet; they shout louder. ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’ ‘Lord,’ they answered, ‘let our eyes be opened.’ ‘Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes, and at once they received their sight and followed Him.’
20.big: Persistent cries for mercy are heard; the healed follow Jesus on the road to Jerusalem.
20.diff: Mark and Luke mention one blind man (Bartimaeus). Calvin rejected the idea that these are different events, noted that one Evangelist often passes over what another mentions, and called the detail of entering or leaving Jericho ‘a puzzling contradiction’ he tried to resolve. See the note on Mark 10:46.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 20:29–34 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

21.ctx: Zechariah 9:9 promised Zion’s king would come ‘gentle and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey’.
21.mean: Jesus sends for a donkey and her colt. Matthew quotes Zechariah: ‘See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’ Crowds spread cloaks and branches and shout, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David!’ ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!’ The city asks, ‘Who is this?’ ‘This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.’
21.big: The King comes to his city humble and peaceful, as the prophets foretold.
21.diff: Two animals? Only Matthew mentions both a donkey and a colt, and says Jesus sat ‘on them’ (the cloaks, or the animals). Some critics claim Matthew misread Zechariah’s Hebrew parallelism as two animals. Others reply that Matthew, a Jew who knew Hebrew poetry well, was simply reporting that the colt’s mother came too, as she naturally would with an unbroken young animal, and that Mark and Luke mention only the one Jesus rode.

src.l: ‘Matthew, Gospel of’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

21.ctx: See the note on Mark 11:15. Psalm 8:2 speaks of praise from the mouths of children.
21.mean: Jesus drives out the traders: ‘It is written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer.’ But you are making it ‘a den of robbers.’’ The blind and lame come to him in the temple and he heals them. Children shout ‘Hosanna to the Son of David!’ The chief priests are indignant; Jesus quotes Psalm 8: ‘From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise’.
21.big: Jesus cleanses the temple for prayer and healing, and accepts praise reserved for God.

21.ctx: See the notes on Mark 11:12 and 11:20. Matthew tells the cursing and withering together.
21.mean: Hungry, Jesus finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit: ‘May you never bear fruit again!’ It withers at once. ‘if you have faith and do not doubt’, you could move ‘this mountain’. ‘If you believe, you will receive whatever you ask for in prayer.’
21.big: Fruitless religion faces judgment; believing prayer has great power.
21.diff: Calvin insisted ‘it was not the fury of passion that led him to curse the tree’; it was an acted parable of judgment on fruitless religion.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 21:10–22 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

21.ctx: See the note on Mark 11:27.
21.mean: ‘By what authority are You doing these things?’ Jesus asks about John’s baptism, from heaven or from men? They will not answer, so neither will he.
21.big: Those unwilling to respond honestly to God’s messenger forfeit the right to judge Jesus.

21.h: The Parable of the Two Sons
21.ctx: Found only in Matthew.
21.mean: One son says ‘I will not’ to his father but later goes to work; the other says ‘I will, sir’ but does not. ‘Which of the two did the will of his father?’ ‘The first’. ‘Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God before you.’ They believed John; the religious leaders did not, even after seeing it.
21.big: What counts is not religious talk but repentance and obedience.

21.h: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
21.ctx: See the note on Mark 12:1. Verse 44 is missing from some early manuscripts (BSB footnote).
21.mean: The tenants beat and kill the owner’s servants and finally his son. The leaders themselves pronounce the verdict: ‘He will bring those wretches to a wretched end’, and give the vineyard to others. Jesus quotes Psalm 118 on the rejected stone. ‘Therefore I tell you that the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people who will produce its fruit.’ The chief priests and Pharisees know he means them.
21.big: Rejecting God’s Son forfeits the kingdom; it goes to those who produce its fruit.
21.diff: ‘Taken away from you’. Jesus addresses the leaders who rejected him, and the ‘people’ who receive the kingdom is the community of his followers, Jew and Gentile. Christians have sometimes misused such texts to condemn the Jewish people as a whole, with terrible consequences. The Catholic Church teaches that ‘the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God’ (Nostra Aetate 4; compare Catechism 839). Protestant traditions also differ on Israel’s future: many Reformed and Catholic readers see the church as the continuation of Israel, while dispensationalists maintain a distinct future for ethnic Israel; Paul expects a future turning of Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25–29).

src.l: Second Vatican Council, Nostra Aetate (1965), §4
Catechism of the Catholic Church 839 (the Church and the Jewish people)
Dallas Theological Seminary, Doctrinal Statement

22.ctx: Wealthy hosts sent a first invitation and then, when the feast was ready, a second summons; refusing the second was a grave insult. Luke has a similar parable (Luke 14:15–24).
22.mean: A king prepares a wedding banquet for his son. The invited guests refuse; some go off to their business, others kill his servants. The enraged king destroys them ‘and burn their city.’ Then he sends his servants to the crossroads to invite everyone, ‘both evil and good’, and the hall is filled. But one guest has no wedding clothes; speechless, he is thrown out ‘into the outer darkness’. ‘For many are called, but few are chosen.’
22.big: God’s invitation goes out to everyone, good and bad; but no one can stay at the feast on their own terms.
22.diff: The wedding clothes. Some (especially Protestants) see the garment as the righteousness of Christ God provides; others (especially Catholics) as the holy life of the guest. Calvin called this ‘a useless controversy; for faith cannot be separated from good works, nor do good works proceed from any other source than from faith’. ‘Many are called, but few are chosen’. Reformed theology distinguishes the general call of the gospel, which many hear, from God’s effectual calling of the elect. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers take ‘chosen’ as those who accept the call. Calvin drew a practical lesson: ‘Let us not flatter ourselves with the empty title of faith’. Verse 7 (the burned city) is often seen as a pointer to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 22:1–14 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

22.ctx: See the note on Mark 12:13.
22.mean: Pharisees’ disciples and Herodians flatter Jesus, then ask, ‘Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?’ ‘Show Me the coin used for the tax.’ ‘Whose image is this,’ He asked, ‘and whose inscription?’ ‘Caesar’s’. ‘Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.’ They are amazed.
22.big: Governments have a real but limited claim; God’s claim is total.
22.diff: See the note on Mark 12:13. Calvin: if rulers ‘claim any part of the authority of God, we ought not to obey them any farther than can be done without offending God’.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 22:15–22 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

22.ctx: See the note on Mark 12:18.
22.mean: The Sadducees, ‘who say there is no resurrection’, pose the riddle of the woman married to seven brothers. ‘You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.’ In the resurrection people do not marry; they are like the angels. And God said, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’. ‘He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.’
22.big: God’s faithfulness to his people outlasts death.

22.ctx: See the note on Mark 12:28.
22.mean: An expert in the law asks which is the greatest commandment. ‘‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ This is the first and greatest commandment. And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.’
22.big: Love for God and neighbour is the hinge on which the whole Bible’s teaching turns.

22.ctx: See the note on Mark 12:35.
22.mean: ‘What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is He?’ ‘David’s’. ‘How then does David in the Spirit call Him ‘Lord’?’ He quotes Psalm 110:1. ‘So if David calls Him ‘Lord,’ how can He be David’s son?’ No one can answer, and from then on no one dares question him.
22.big: The Messiah is David’s son and David’s Lord.

23.ctx: ‘Moses’ seat’ was the place of authoritative teaching in the synagogue. Phylacteries were small boxes containing Scripture verses, tied to the forehead and arm (Deuteronomy 6:8); tassels were worn on cloak corners (Numbers 15:38). Not all Pharisees were hypocrites: Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea and Paul came from their ranks.
23.mean: ‘The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat. So practice and observe everything they tell you. But do not do what they do, for they do not practice what they preach.’ They load others with burdens and do it all for show. Disciples are not to seek titles: ‘you have one Teacher, and you are all brothers. And do not call anyone on earth your father, for you have one Father, who is in heaven.’ ‘The greatest among you shall be your servant.’ Then seven woes: they shut the kingdom in people’s faces; make converts ‘twice as much a son of hell’; split hairs over oaths; tithe herbs but neglect ‘the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness’; ‘strain out a gnat but swallow a camel’; clean the outside of the cup but not the inside; are ‘like whitewashed tombs’; and honour the prophets their fathers murdered. All the righteous blood from Abel to Zechariah will come on ‘this generation’.
23.big: God hates religious show that neglects justice, mercy and faithfulness; leadership in his kingdom means humble service.
23.diff: ‘Call no one father’. Some Protestants object to calling priests ‘Father’; Catholics, Orthodox and many Anglicans use the title for clergy, as Paul called himself a father to his converts (1 Corinthians 4:15). Calvin said the point is that God alone is the source of spiritual life, and that ‘it is not only lawful to call men on earth fathers, but it would be wicked to deprive them of that honor’. All agree Jesus forbids status-seeking. Zechariah son of Berechiah (verse 35) is usually identified with Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–22), the last murder in the Hebrew Bible’s order of books, as Abel’s is the first. Calvin suggested Jehoiada had two names or that the name was confused in copying. A warning. These words were addressed to particular leaders by a Jew to fellow Jews; they have sometimes been misused to fuel hostility to Jews in general, which the Gospel itself does not do.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 23:1–12 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 23:29–39 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Second Vatican Council, Nostra Aetate (1965), §4

23.ctx: Psalm 118:26 was sung by pilgrims at the festivals and shouted at Jesus’ entry (21:9).
23.mean: ‘O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling! Look, your house is left to you desolate.’ They will not see him again until they say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.’
23.big: Jesus’ judgment comes with tears; he longed to gather Jerusalem, and its refusal brought desolation.
23.diff: ‘You were unwilling’. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers see here God’s sincere desire to save that people can resist. Reformed readers agree that the offer is sincere and the refusal culpable, while holding that God’s saving purpose for his elect is not finally thwarted. Both see Jesus’ real grief.

24.ctx: Matthew’s fifth discourse. See the note and history drop-down at Mark 13:1.
24.mean: ‘Truly I tell you, not one stone here will be left on another’. On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask, ‘when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age?’, three questions in one. ‘See to it that no one deceives you.’ False Christs, wars, famines and earthquakes will come, but ‘the end is still to come.’ ‘All these are the beginning of birth pains.’
24.big: The temple’s fall is certain; but disasters are not in themselves signs that the end has come.

b: In AD 70 the Roman general Titus captured Jerusalem. Josephus, an eyewitness with the Roman army, describes the temple being set on fire and burned on the tenth of Ab. Herod’s retaining walls still stand in places, most famously the Western Wall, but the temple itself has never been rebuilt.

src.l: Josephus, Jewish War 6.249–266 (Whiston)
‘Temple, Herod’s’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

24.mean: Persecution, betrayal, false prophets and love growing cold will come. ‘But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved. And this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.’
24.big: The church’s task until the end is to take the gospel to every nation, and to persevere.

24.ctx: See the note on Mark 13:14. Matthew names Daniel and adds ‘or on the Sabbath’, a concern for Jewish-Christian readers.
24.mean: ‘So when you see standing in the holy place ‘the abomination of desolation,’ spoken of by the prophet Daniel (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.’ It will be ‘great tribulation, unseen from the beginning of the world until now’, but cut short ‘for the sake of the elect’. False Christs will deceive ‘even the elect, if that were possible.’
24.big: Jesus warns his people in advance so they can escape disaster and not be deceived.
24.diff: See the note on Mark 13:14 for the main views (fulfilled in AD 70; double fulfilment; a future tribulation). The Lexham Bible Dictionary suggests that in Matthew, where the question concerns ‘the end of the age’, the abomination likely refers to both AD 70 and the end times. ‘If that were possible’: Reformed readers see a hint that the elect cannot finally be deceived; Arminian readers that the danger is real.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 24:15–28 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
A. Boyd Luter, ‘Abomination of Desolation’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
Dallas Theological Seminary, Doctrinal Statement

24.h: The Return of the Son of Man
24.mean: Do not go looking for the Christ in the wilderness or in secret rooms: his coming will be as obvious as lightning from east to west. After the tribulation the heavens will be shaken; ‘the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn. They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.’ With a loud trumpet call his angels will gather his elect.
24.big: Christ’s return will be public, unmistakable and glorious; no secret Messiah need be sought.

src.l: Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed (381), in Schaff vol. 2

24.h: The Lesson of the Fig Tree
24.mean: When the fig tree sprouts leaves, summer is near. ‘So also, when you see all these things, you will know that He is near, right at the door. Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened. Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.’
24.diff: On ‘this generation’, see the note on Mark 13:28. Calvin: ‘within fifty years the city was destroyed and the temple was razed’.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 24:32–36 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

24.ctx: Grinding grain with a hand mill was women’s daily work, often done in pairs. Some later manuscripts omit ‘nor the Son’ in verse 36 (BSB footnote), perhaps out of reverence.
24.mean: ‘No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.’ It will be like Noah’s day: people carried on as normal ‘until the flood came and swept them all away.’ ‘Two men will be in the field: one will be taken and the other left.’ So keep watch. A homeowner would guard his house if he knew when the thief was coming. The faithful servant will be found working when his master returns; the wicked one, who says ‘My master will be away a long time’ and abuses others, will be caught out.
24.big: Be ready at every moment, by being faithful in what Christ has given you to do.
24.diff: ‘One will be taken’. Dispensational premillennialists (for example Dallas Theological Seminary) often read this as the ‘rapture’, believers being taken to meet Christ before a time of tribulation. Many other interpreters point to the comparison just made: in Noah’s day the flood ‘swept them all away’, so ‘taken’ may mean taken in judgment, and ‘left’ spared. Either way the point is readiness. On ‘nor the Son’, see the note on Mark 13:32.

src.l: Dallas Theological Seminary, Doctrinal Statement
Definition of Chalcedon (451), in Schaff vol. 2

25.h: The Parable of the Ten Virgins
25.ctx: At a wedding the bridegroom went to fetch his bride, often late in the evening, and the bridesmaids met him with torches or lamps to escort the procession to the feast.
25.mean: Ten bridesmaids wait for the bridegroom; five foolish ones bring no spare oil, five wise ones do. The bridegroom is delayed and they all sleep. At midnight he comes; the foolish ones’ lamps are going out, and the wise cannot share. While the foolish go to buy oil, ‘the bridegroom arrived. Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding banquet, and the door was shut.’ ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’ ‘Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.’
25.big: Readiness for Christ’s return cannot be borrowed or arranged at the last minute.
25.diff: Interpreters have long debated what the oil represents: faith, good works, the Holy Spirit, or grace. Calvin took it as the ‘incessant supplies’ believers need to keep the flame of faith burning. The parable’s point does not depend on decoding every detail.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 25:1–13 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

25.ctx: A talent was a weight of silver worth about twenty years’ wages (BSB footnote). Our word ‘talent’, meaning ability, comes from this parable.
25.mean: A man going away entrusts his servants with five, two and one talent, ‘each according to his own ability.’ Two put the money to work and double it; the third buries his. On his return the master says to both faithful servants, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master!’ The third, calling his master ‘a hard man’, returns the talent untouched. ‘You wicked, lazy servant!’ He could at least have banked it. His talent is given to the one with ten, and he is thrown out.
25.big: Christ entrusts his people with gifts and opportunities, and expects faithful use of them, not fearful burial.

25.ctx: Mixed flocks of sheep and goats grazed together by day and were separated at night. The right hand was the place of favour.
25.mean: When the Son of Man comes in glory, ‘All the nations will be gathered before Him, and He will separate the people one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.’ To those on his right: ‘Come, you who are blessed by My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave Me something to eat’, thirsty, a stranger, naked, sick, in prison, and you helped me. Surprised, they ask when. ‘Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me.’ Those on his left, who did none of this, are sent ‘into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.’ ‘And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.’
25.big: Jesus the King and Judge identifies himself with his needy brothers and sisters; how we treat them is how we treat him.
25.diff: Who are ‘the least of these brothers of Mine’? Many interpreters, including Calvin, take them as Jesus’ disciples in need (compare 10:40–42; 12:50): ‘Believers only are expressly recommended to our notice; not that he bids us altogether despise others’. Others, including much Catholic social teaching, apply it to all the poor and needy; the Catechism lists the corporal works of mercy drawn from this passage (2447). Saved by works? Protestants read the deeds as the evidence of genuine faith, not its cause (the kingdom was ‘prepared for you from the foundation of the world’); Catholics read them as the fruit of grace that God rewards. Both agree that faith which never shows love is not saving faith (James 2). ‘Eternal’. Wesley argued: ‘Either therefore the punishment is strictly eternal, or the reward is not: the very same expression being applied to the former as to the latter.’ Those who hold conditional immortality read ‘eternal punishment’ as a final, irreversible destruction. See the note on Mark 9:42.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 25:31–46 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Catechism of the Catholic Church 2443–2449 (love for the poor; works of mercy)
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 25
Catechism of the Catholic Church 1033–1037 (hell)
Seventh-day Adventist Church, 28 Fundamental Beliefs, nos. 26–27

26.ctx: See the note on Mark 14:1. Matthew names the high priest, Caiaphas.
26.mean: Jesus tells his disciples, ‘the Passover is two days away, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.’ Meanwhile the chief priests and elders meet at Caiaphas’s house to plot his arrest, ‘But not during the feast’.
26.big: Jesus foretells the very timing his enemies wanted to avoid.

b: Mark does not name the high priest, but Matthew and John do: Caiaphas. Josephus calls him ‘Joseph Caiaphas’ and records his appointment under the governor Valerius Gratus. He held office from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long time, covering the whole of Pilate’s governorship.

The Caiaphas ossuary (Widely accepted). In 1990 builders accidentally uncovered a family tomb in modern Jerusalem. One finely decorated bone box (ossuary) is inscribed ‘Joseph, son of Caiaphas’. Many scholars think it is the high priest’s. It cannot be certain, because Joseph was a common name and the inscription does not mention the high priesthood.

src.l: Josephus, Antiquities 18.33–35 (Whiston): Joseph Caiaphas made high priest
‘Caiaphas’ (Archaeological Evidence), Lexham Bible Dictionary
Josephus, Antiquities 18.33–35 (Whiston): Joseph Caiaphas made high priest
‘Caiaphas’ (Archaeological Evidence), Lexham Bible Dictionary

26.mean: A woman pours expensive perfume on Jesus’ head. The disciples call it a waste. ‘She has done a beautiful deed to Me.’ ‘By pouring this perfume on Me, she has prepared My body for burial.’ Her deed will be told wherever the gospel goes.
26.big: Costly love for Jesus is never wasted.

26.ctx: Thirty pieces of silver was the compensation for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32), and the insulting wage paid to the shepherd in Zechariah 11:12.
26.mean: Judas asks the chief priests, ‘What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?’ ‘And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver.’
26.big: Jesus was valued at the price of a slave.

26.ctx: See the note on Mark 14:12 on the date of the Last Supper.
26.mean: The disciples ask where to prepare the Passover. Jesus sends them to a certain man: ‘My time is near. I will keep the Passover with My disciples at your house.’ They prepare it.

src.l: ‘Last Supper’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Jeremias)

26.ctx: See the note on Mark 14:17. Only Matthew adds ‘for the forgiveness of sins’.
26.mean: Jesus says one of them will betray him. Judas asks, ‘Surely not I, Rabbi?’ ‘You have said it yourself.’ Then: ‘Take and eat; this is My body.’ ‘Drink from it, all of you. This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.’ He will not drink wine again until he drinks it new ‘in My Father’s kingdom.’
26.big: Jesus’ death seals a new covenant and brings forgiveness of sins; the Supper looks back to it and forward to the kingdom.
26.diff: For the main Christian views of Christ’s presence in the Supper, see the note on Mark 14:17 and the glossary entry. Wesley took ‘This is’ to mean ‘signifies or represents’, citing similar sayings such as ‘This is the Lord’s passover’ (Exodus 12:11). ‘Drink from it, all of you’ was cited by the Reformers for giving the cup to all communicants; medieval practice in the West had given only the bread to lay people.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 26:26–30 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 26
Catechism of the Catholic Church 1373–1381 (the real presence; transubstantiation)
Luther’s Small Catechism (1529), Baptism and the Sacrament of the Altar, in Schaff, Creeds of Christendom vol. 3
The Longer Catechism of the Orthodox Church (Philaret), in Schaff, Creeds of Christendom vol. 2

26.mean: ‘This very night you will all fall away on account of Me.’ But ‘after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.’ Peter: ‘Even if all fall away on account of You, I never will.’ ‘before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.’
26.big: Jesus knew his followers’ weakness and planned their restoration in advance.

26.mean: ‘My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death.’ Falling facedown he prays, ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will.’ The disciples sleep. A second time: ‘My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, may Your will be done.’ A third time. Then: ‘Rise, let us go! See, My betrayer is approaching!’
26.big: Jesus’ human will, in real anguish, submits to the Father’s will to save us.
26.diff: See the note on Mark 14:32 on Christ’s two wills. Calvin noted that by the second prayer Christ ‘no longer asks to have the cup removed from him’ but insists ‘rather on obeying the purpose of God’.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 26:36–44 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Third Council of Constantinople (680–681), Definition of Faith, New Advent

26.ctx: A legion was about 5,000 soldiers; twelve legions of angels would be 60,000.
26.mean: Judas greets Jesus with a kiss. ‘Friend,’ Jesus replied, ‘do what you came for.’ One disciple cuts off the high priest’s servant’s ear. ‘Put your sword back in its place,’ Jesus said to him. ‘For all who draw the sword will die by the sword.’ He could call ‘more than twelve legions of angels’, ‘But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled’? ‘Then all the disciples deserted Him and fled.’
26.big: Jesus goes to the cross by choice, refusing both violence and rescue, to fulfil the Scriptures.
26.diff: ‘All who draw the sword’. Anabaptists and other pacifists read this as forbidding Christians to use lethal force. Most traditions read it as forbidding violence to defend or advance Christ’s cause, while still allowing the state’s use of force for justice (see the note on 5:38).

src.l: Schleitheim Confession (1527), art. 6, trans. J. C. Wenger

26.ctx: See the note and history drop-downs at Mark 14:53. Matthew says Jesus was put ‘under oath’.
26.mean: False witnesses fail until two report: ‘This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days.’’ Jesus is silent. The high priest: ‘I charge You under oath by the living God: Tell us if You are the Christ, the Son of God.’ ‘You have said it yourself,’ Jesus answered. ‘But I say to all of you, from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.’ ‘He has blasphemed!’ ‘He deserves to die,’ they answered. They spit on him and strike him: ‘Prophesy to us, Christ! Who hit You?’
26.big: Under oath, Jesus confesses he is the Christ, the Son of God, the coming Son of Man; for this he is condemned.
26.diff: Jesus’ answer under oath is one reason most churches hold that his words in 5:34 do not forbid solemn oaths in court.

src.l: Mishnah, Sanhedrin 4:1 (Sefaria, William Davidson translation)
Josephus, Antiquities 18.33–35 (Whiston): Joseph Caiaphas made high priest

26.mean: A servant girl: ‘You also were with Jesus the Galilean’. Peter denies it before them all. Another: ‘This man was with Jesus of Nazareth.’ He denies it with an oath. Then: ‘Surely you are one of them’, ‘for your accent gives you away.’ He curses and swears, ‘I do not know the man!’ The rooster crows, Peter remembers, ‘And he went outside and wept bitterly.’
26.big: Even the leading apostle failed utterly; bitter tears were the beginning of his restoration.

27.mean: At dawn the chief priests and elders resolve to put Jesus to death, bind him and hand him over to ‘Pilate the governor.’
27.big: The religious leaders need Rome to carry out their verdict.

b: Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36/37 and is one of the best-attested figures of the period. Josephus describes him bringing Roman standards bearing the emperor’s image into Jerusalem by night, backing down when crowds offered to die rather than see their law broken, and later using temple funds for an aqueduct and having protesters clubbed. The Roman historian Tacitus writes that ‘Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of the procurator Pontius Pilatus’.

The Pilate Stone. In 1961 Italian archaeologists excavating the theatre at Caesarea Maritima found a reused limestone block with a Latin inscription recording that Pilate dedicated a building in honour of the emperor Tiberius. It gives his title as ‘prefect of Judea’ and is now in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

src.l: Josephus, Jewish War 2.169–177 (Whiston): Pilate’s standards and aqueduct
Tacitus, Annals 15.44 (Loeb), LacusCurtius
‘Pontius Pilate’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
Center for Online Judaic Studies, ‘Pontius Pilate’s Tiberium Inscription’ (Israel Museum)
‘Pontius Pilate’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

27.ctx: The ‘potter’s field’ was probably in the Hinnom Valley south of Jerusalem, where potters’ clay was found; the traditional site of Akeldama (‘Field of Blood’) is there.
27.mean: Seeing Jesus condemned, Judas is ‘filled with remorse’ and returns the silver: ‘I have sinned by betraying innocent blood’. ‘What is that to us?’ they reply. He throws the money into the temple and hangs himself. The priests, scrupulous about ‘blood money’, buy the potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners, ‘the Field of Blood’. Matthew sees prophecy fulfilled: ‘They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price set on Him by the people of Israel, and they gave them for the potter’s field’.
27.big: Remorse without turning to God leads to despair; the leaders who kept ritual scruples had no scruple about condemning the innocent.
27.diff: Judas’s death. Acts 1:18–19 says Judas fell headlong and burst open in a field bought with the money. Augustine suggested the two accounts fit together: he hanged himself and the body later fell. Acts can say Judas acquired the field because it was bought with his money, as Matthew says, by the priests. ‘Jeremiah’. The quotation is mainly from Zechariah 11:12–13, though Jeremiah also bought a field and visited a potter (BSB footnote: Jeremiah 19; 32). Many think Matthew combines the two and names the major prophet, as Mark 1:2 names Isaiah for a combined quotation. Calvin, characteristically frank, wrote that ‘the name of Jeremiah has been put down by mistake, instead of Zechariah’, without thinking this affected the substance.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 27:1–10 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
‘Judas Iscariot’ and D. F. Payne, ‘Akeldama’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

27.mean: ‘Are You the King of the Jews?’ ‘You have said so,’ Jesus replied. To the many accusations he gives no answer, ‘much to the governor’s amazement.’
27.big: Jesus’ silence fulfils the servant who ‘did not open His mouth’ (Isaiah 53:7).

27.ctx: Some manuscripts call him ‘Jesus Barabbas’ (BSB footnote); Barabbas means ‘son of the father’. See the history drop-down at Mark 15:6.
27.mean: Pilate offers a choice: ‘Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?’ His wife sends word: ‘Have nothing to do with that innocent man, for I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him.’ The chief priests persuade the crowd. ‘What then should I do with Jesus who is called Christ?’ ‘Crucify Him!’ ‘Why?’ asked Pilate. ‘What evil has He done?’ They shout louder.
27.big: The crowd chooses the guilty man, and the innocent Son of the Father takes his place.

src.l: Michelle J. Morris, ‘Barabbas’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

27.ctx: Hand-washing as a sign of innocence of bloodshed was a Jewish custom (Deuteronomy 21:6–9; Psalm 26:6).
27.mean: Seeing a riot starting, Pilate washes his hands before the crowd: ‘I am innocent of this man’s blood,’ ‘You bear the responsibility.’ ‘All the people answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!”’ He releases Barabbas, has Jesus flogged, and hands him over to be crucified.
27.big: Pilate could not wash away his responsibility; and the blood the crowd called down on themselves is the very blood that brings forgiveness (26:28).
27.diff: A verse misused. Verse 25 was for centuries used by Christians to blame all Jews for Jesus’ death, with terrible results. The Catholic Church teaches that his passion ‘cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today’ (Nostra Aetate 4), and that we cannot ‘extend responsibility to other Jews of different times and places, based merely on the crowd’s cry’ (Catechism 597); it adds that all sinners share responsibility (598). Protestant churches agree. The crowd’s words were spoken by a particular crowd on a particular day; and Christians believe Jesus’ blood is shed for the forgiveness of all who trust him.

src.l: Catechism of the Catholic Church 597–598 (responsibility for Christ’s death)
Second Vatican Council, Nostra Aetate (1965), §4

27.ctx: See the note on Mark 15:16. A soldier’s scarlet cloak served as the mock royal robe.
27.mean: The soldiers strip Jesus, put a scarlet robe on him, a crown of thorns on his head and a staff in his hand, kneel and mock: ‘Hail, King of the Jews!’ They spit on him and beat him, then lead him away to crucify him.
27.big: The true King is crowned with thorns.

b: Christian tradition since the Middle Ages placed the trial at the Antonia Fortress beside the temple, and visitors are still shown a paved area under the Sisters of Zion convent there. Archaeologists now date that pavement to the 2nd century AD, after Jesus’ time.

Most scholars now think Pilate stayed at Herod’s former palace on the western hill when he came to Jerusalem, and that this is the ‘Praetorium’ (Mark 15:16). Josephus says a later governor, Florus, set up his judgment seat there. The exact spot is not certain.

src.l: ‘Praetorium’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
‘Praetorium’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

27.ctx: See the note on Mark 15:21. Psalm 22 lies behind many details here (verses 7–8, 18).
27.mean: Simon of Cyrene carries the cross. At Golgotha Jesus tastes wine mixed with gall and refuses it. They crucify him, divide his clothes, and sit to watch. The charge reads, ‘THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.’ Passers-by, chief priests and robbers mock: ‘He saved others, but He cannot save Himself.’ ‘He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him. For He said, ‘I am the Son of God.’’
27.big: Jesus stays on the cross precisely in order to save others.

b: Crucifixion was the Romans’ most shameful punishment, used for slaves and rebels. Ancient writers describe it often, but physical remains are rare, because bodies were usually left to decay or thrown away. In 1968, in a tomb at Giv’at ha-Mivtar in northern Jerusalem, archaeologists found an ossuary containing the bones of a crucified man from the 1st century AD, with an iron nail about 11.5 cm long still driven through his heel bone. It confirms that victims were nailed, and that a crucified Jew could be given a proper family burial, as Jesus was.

src.l: ‘Crucifixion’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
‘Crucifixion’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

27.ctx: See the note and drop-down on the darkness at Mark 15:33.
27.mean: Darkness from noon to three. ‘Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?’ which means, ‘My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?’ Some think he calls Elijah. ‘When Jesus had cried out again in a loud voice, He yielded up His spirit.’ The temple veil is torn from top to bottom, the earth quakes, rocks split, ‘The tombs broke open, and the bodies of many saints who had fallen asleep were raised. After Jesus’ resurrection, when they had come out of the tombs, they entered the holy city and appeared to many people.’ The centurion and guards say, ‘Truly this was the Son of God.’ Many women watch, including Mary Magdalene.
27.big: Jesus’ death opens the way to God, shakes creation, and breaks the power of death itself.
27.diff: The raised saints (verses 52–53) appear only in Matthew. Most Christians through history, including Calvin, took them as a real event; Calvin thought that ‘when Christ died, the graves were immediately opened: and that, when he rose, some of the godly, having received life, went out of their graves’. In 2010 the evangelical scholar Michael Licona suggested they might be Matthew’s use of apocalyptic imagery to signal that the Son of God had died; this provoked strong objections from Norman Geisler, Albert Mohler and others, and Licona later said he was ‘just as inclined’ to read it as a literal event. On ‘forsaken’, see the note on Mark 15:33.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 27:45–56 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Bobby Ross Jr., ‘Interpretation Sparks a Grave Theology Debate’, Christianity Today (November 2011)

27.ctx: See the note on Mark 15:42. Matthew calls Joseph rich, recalling Isaiah 53:9 (‘with a rich man in His death’).
27.mean: Joseph of Arimathea, ‘a rich man…who himself was a disciple of Jesus’, asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in clean linen and lays it ‘in his own new tomb that he had cut into the rock’, rolling a great stone across the entrance. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit opposite the tomb.
27.big: Jesus was truly dead and buried, in a known tomb watched by witnesses.

hist.t: Where are Golgotha and the tomb?
b: Two sites are shown today.

The Church of the Holy Sepulchre. In the 4th century the emperor Constantine built a church over a site local Christians identified, under a temple Hadrian had built about AD 135. It is now inside the Old City walls, but excavations, including Kathleen Kenyon’s in the 1960s, showed that in Jesus’ time the area was an old quarry outside the walls, with rock-cut tombs of the 1st century. Most archaeologists regard it as the most likely location.

The Garden Tomb. North of the Damascus Gate, identified by General Charles Gordon in 1883, it is a peaceful place to visit. But excavations by Gabriel Barkay and Amos Kloner indicate that the tomb was first cut in the Iron Age (8th–7th centuries BC), so it would not have been a new tomb in Jesus’ day. Few archaeologists now think it was Jesus’ tomb.

src.l: ‘Golgotha’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
‘Joseph of Arimathea’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
‘Golgotha’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

27.ctx: Only Matthew records the guard. The tomb was sealed, probably with a cord and wax or clay stamped with an official seal.
27.mean: The chief priests and Pharisees remind Pilate that ‘that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise again.’’ They fear the disciples will steal the body. ‘You have a guard,’ Pilate said. ‘Go, make the tomb as secure as you know how.’ They seal the stone and post the guard.
27.big: Jesus’ enemies remembered his promise to rise better than his friends did, and their precautions became evidence for the empty tomb.

28.ctx: Women’s testimony counted for little in court then; Josephus says it should not be admitted. Yet all four Gospels make women the first witnesses.
28.mean: At dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary go to the tomb. An earthquake; an angel rolls back the stone and sits on it; the guards become like dead men. ‘Do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified. He is not here; He has risen, just as He said! Come, see the place where He lay.’ They run ‘in fear and great joy’ to tell the disciples, and Jesus meets them: ‘Greetings!’ They hold his feet and worship him. ‘Do not be afraid,’ said Jesus. ‘Go and tell My brothers to go to Galilee. There they will see Me.’
28.big: Jesus has risen as he said; the first witnesses were women, and the risen Lord calls his failed disciples ‘My brothers’.
28.diff: The four Gospels differ in details of the resurrection morning (the number of women and angels, the order of appearances), as independent witnesses do. They agree on the central facts: the tomb was empty, women found it, and the risen Jesus appeared to his followers.

src.l: Josephus, Antiquities 4.219 (Whiston): the testimony of women

28.ctx: A soldier who fell asleep on duty could face severe punishment; the priests promise to protect them.
28.mean: Some of the guards report to the chief priests. The priests bribe them to say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole Him away while we were asleep.’ ‘And this account has been circulated among the Jews to this very day.’
28.big: The earliest explanation from Jesus’ opponents admits that the tomb was empty.

b: Matthew says the story that the disciples stole the body was still told in his day. About AD 155–160 Justin Martyr, in his Dialogue with Trypho, confirms that it was circulating: he says Jewish leaders had sent men out to say that ‘his disciples stole him by night from the tomb’. The story assumes what both sides agreed on: the tomb was empty.

src.l: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 108, ANF vol. 1, New Advent
Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 108, ANF vol. 1, New Advent

28.ctx: The mountain in Galilee recalls the mountain of the Sermon (5:1) and of the Transfiguration (17:1).
28.mean: The Eleven meet Jesus on the mountain in Galilee; ‘they worshiped Him, but some doubted.’ Jesus comes to them: ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.’
28.big: The risen Jesus has all authority, sends his church to make disciples of every nation, and promises his presence to the end: Immanuel, God with us (1:23).
28.diff: One name, three persons. Jesus speaks of ‘the name’ (singular) of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, one of the clearest roots of the doctrine of the Trinity; Calvin said it shows ‘the full and clear knowledge of God’ now revealed. Baptism. All traditions baptise in this threefold name. On whom to baptise, Wesley explained the practice of infant-baptising churches: adults are taught before baptism, while ‘in discipling their children’, they are baptised ‘before they were taught’, as Jewish children were circumcised first. Calvin likewise defended infant baptism here. Baptists note that the command joins baptism to making disciples, and baptise those who profess faith. See the glossary entry. ‘Some doubted’: Matthew does not hide the disciples’ hesitation, an honest detail.
